Takes back unspent money from the IRS

supporters: Supporters say funding Iron Dome and David's Sling gives Israel the ability to shoot down rockets and missiles aimed at civilians, and that replacing equipment the U.S. already sent keeps American stockpiles ready.
Supporters say labeling the spending as emergency funding lets the U.S. respond quickly to the October 7 attacks without waiting for the normal budget process.
Supporters say rescinding unspent IRS funds offsets part of the cost, so not all of the money adds to the deficit.
critics: Critics say expanding the President's power to transfer defense articles to Israel without the usual congressional approval reduces oversight of how and when U.S. weapons are used.
Critics say the bill funds offensive military procurement, like the Iron Beam system still in development, on top of defensive systems, which goes beyond replacing what was already given.
Critics say pulling back unobligated IRS funds weakens tax enforcement capacity that was set aside to collect revenue the government is owed.

118-hr-662.one_liner: Give states block grants to help farmers with 2022 disaster losses
provisions: Lets the Department of Agriculture give block grants to states and territories
Uses existing funding to help farmers who lost crops or livestock in 2022
Covers losses from droughts, wildfires, hurricanes, floods, and other natural disasters
Only applies to disasters that happened in calendar year 2022

supporters: Supporters say this would help farmers and ranchers who lost crops and livestock during the droughts, wildfires, hurricanes, and other natural disasters that hit in 2022.
Supporters say block grants let states decide how to distribute the aid to farmers who need it most in their area.
Supporters say this uses existing Department of Agriculture funding instead of requiring new taxpayer money.
critics: Critics say limiting aid to only 2022 disasters leaves out farmers who suffered losses from natural disasters in 2021, 2023, and other years.
Critics say block grants could lead to unequal distribution of aid, with some states getting more help per affected farmer than others.
Critics say this sets a precedent of using federal money to bail out farmers for weather-related losses that are part of normal farming risks.

118-hr-6363.one_liner: Fund the federal government through early 2024 to prevent shutdown
provisions: Funds most federal agencies through February 2, 2024 at 2023 spending levels
Funds farm, energy, veterans, and transportation agencies through January 19, 2024
Extends farm programs that were set to expire
Extends public health programs and the U.S. Parole Commission
Prevents government shutdown that would start November 17, 2023

supporters: Supporters say this prevents a government shutdown that would start November 17, 2023 by funding federal agencies through February 2024.
Supporters say this extends farm programs and public health programs that were set to expire, keeping essential services running.
Supporters say this maintains funding for veterans affairs, transportation, and agriculture agencies through January 19, 2024 at 2023 levels.
critics: Critics say this only provides temporary funding through February 2024 instead of full-year budget certainty for federal agencies.
Critics say maintaining 2023 spending levels fails to account for inflation affecting government operations.
Critics say extending programs temporarily instead of long-term reauthorization creates ongoing uncertainty.

118-hr-6914.one_liner: Require colleges to provide pregnancy information to students
provisions: Requires colleges that receive federal student aid to give students information about pregnancy rights and resources
Colleges must list places that help pregnant students carry their baby to term and care for the baby after birth
Colleges must explain what support they offer pregnant students and new parents
Colleges must tell students how to report pregnancy discrimination

supporters: Supporters say colleges that get federal student aid must give pregnant students a list of resources to help them carry their baby to term and care for the baby after birth, which they often do not receive today.
Supporters say the bill fills a gap by requiring schools to explain what accommodations are available to pregnant students and new parents, helping them stay enrolled.
Supporters say requiring colleges to tell students how to file a pregnancy discrimination complaint gives students a clear path to protect their rights under existing law.
critics: Critics say the bill only requires colleges to share information about carrying a pregnancy to term and parenting, and does not require schools to inform students about all legal options, leaving out part of what students may need.

Critics say the bill does not set a standard for what resources colleges must actually offer, only what they must list, so students in areas with few services may get information that does not lead to real help.
Critics say the bill places new reporting and disclosure requirements on colleges without providing federal funding to cover the cost of creating and distributing the required materials.

118-hr-6678.one_liner: Make Social Security fraud grounds for deportation and blocking entry for non-citizens
provisions: Makes creating fake IDs without permission grounds for deporting non-citizens
Makes lying on Social Security disability applications grounds for deporting non-citizens
Blocks non-citizens from entering the U.S. if convicted of these Social Security fraud crimes
Applies to people convicted of the crimes or who admit to doing them

supporters: Supporters say that making fake ID creation grounds for deportation will stop non-citizens from using false documents to collect Social Security disability benefits they are not entitled to.

Supporters say that linking lying on a Social Security disability application to deportation protects a program that pays benefits to about 8 million disabled Americans, reducing fraud that drains those funds.
Supporters say the bill covers people who admit to these acts, not just those convicted in court, which closes a loophole that lets admitted fraudsters stay in the country.
critics: Critics say the bill could lead to deportation for a single false statement on a disability application, which may be too harsh a punishment for a paperwork error versus intentional fraud.
Critics say the bill does not set a dollar threshold or define how serious the false statement must be, meaning minor mistakes and large-scale fraud are treated the same way.
Critics say applying this rule to people who only admit to the acts — without a court conviction — removes standard legal protections that non-citizens normally have before facing deportation.

118-hr-6679.one_liner: Block Hamas members and October 7 attackers from US immigration benefits
provisions: Blocks Hamas members from entering the United States
Blocks Palestinian Islamic Jihad members from entering the United States
Blocks people who took part in the October 7, 2023 attacks on Israel from entering the United States
Blocks all Palestinian Liberation Organization members from entering the United States
Stops October 7 attackers from seeking asylum
Stops October 7 attackers from getting protection from deportation

supporters: Supporters say the bill protects the U.S. by blocking Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad members from entering the country, keeping out people tied to groups the U.S. already labels as terrorist organizations.
Supporters say that people who took part in or helped plan the October 7, 2023 attacks on Israel should not be able to use U.S. asylum laws or deportation protections as a way to stay in the country.
Supporters say expanding the PLO admissions bar to cover all PLO members, not just officers and spokespersons, closes a gap that let some members enter the U.S. while others were blocked.
critics: Critics say the bill bars all PLO members from the U.S., which could block Palestinian leaders, diplomats, and civilians with past PLO ties who were not involved in any violence.

Critics say removing deportation protections from anyone linked to the October 7 attacks — even before a court has ruled on their case — takes away a legal process that exists to prevent people from being sent to places where their life is at risk.

Critics say the bill does not define what it means to have 'facilitated' the October 7 attacks, which could allow immigration officials to bar people based on loose or unclear connections to the events.

118-hr-676.one_liner: Require NOAA to work with local communities on ocean acidification problems
provisions: NOAA must work with state, local, and tribal groups on ocean acidification problems
NOAA must help these groups improve their programs for dealing with acidification
NOAA must help groups share their successful work as examples for other communities
A federal advisory board on ocean acidification must include two tribal representatives

supporters: Supporters say this would help coastal communities fight ocean acidification by requiring NOAA to work directly with state, local, and tribal groups on their programs.
Supporters say adding two tribal representatives to the federal advisory board ensures Native American voices are heard on ocean acidification decisions.
Supporters say this would help communities learn from each other by requiring NOAA to share successful acidification programs as examples.
critics: Critics say this creates new federal mandates requiring NOAA to collaborate with state, local and tribal groups without providing additional funding.
Critics say requiring NOAA to assist groups in improving their programs and share information could create administrative burden and duplicate existing work.

118-hr-6918.one_liner: Block a rule change for pregnancy centers that get welfare program money
provisions: Stops the government from applying a new funding rule to pregnancy centers
Lets pregnancy centers keep getting money from a program that helps poor families
Covers centers that offer pregnancy counseling, testing, diapers, baby clothes, and family support
The blocked rule would make states prove the money is used reasonably for program goals

supporters: Supporters say this bill protects pregnancy centers that give out diapers, baby clothes, and prenatal education to low-income families from losing TANF funding under a new federal rule.

Supporters say the blocked rule would let the federal government cut off state spending for centers that counsel pregnant women, even when those centers provide direct material help to mothers and families.
Supporters say states should be able to use TANF funds for pregnancy centers without having to prove to federal officials that the spending fits a narrow definition of program goals.
critics: Critics say TANF was designed to help poor families reach financial independence, and the bill stops the government from checking whether money spent on pregnancy centers actually serves that goal.

Critics say the federal rule being blocked would simply require states to show that TANF spending meets one of the program's four legal purposes, and exempting pregnancy centers removes that basic accountability check.

Critics say the Administration for Children and Families found that counseling women only after they become pregnant has little connection to TANF's goal of reducing out-of-wedlock pregnancies, and this bill prevents that finding from being enforced.

118-hr-6976.one_liner: Make drunk driving a reason to deport or block non-citizens from entering
provisions: Stops non-citizens from entering the US if convicted of drunk driving
Stops non-citizens from entering the US if they admit to drunk driving
Lets the government deport non-citizens convicted of drunk driving

supporters: Supporters say the bill would bar non-citizens from entering the US if they have been convicted of drunk driving, which they argue protects American communities from repeat offenders who have already shown dangerous behavior on the road.

Supporters say the bill also covers non-citizens who admit to the acts of drunk driving — not just those with a formal conviction — closing a loophole that could let some offenders enter the country anyway.
Supporters say allowing deportation of non-citizens convicted of DUI gives the government a tool to remove people who have broken laws that put other drivers and pedestrians at risk.
critics: Critics say the bill would allow deportation based on a DUI conviction, which in many states can include first-time offenders or people with very low blood alcohol levels, potentially separating long-term residents from their families over a single offense.
Critics say the provision that bars entry for people who only 'admit' to drunk driving — without a conviction — removes standard legal protections, since a formal court process is bypassed.

Critics say the bill does not distinguish between a one-time misdemeanor DUI and more serious repeat offenses, meaning non-citizens could face permanent deportation under the same rules regardless of the details of their case.

118-hr-734.one_liner: Ban people born male from competing in women's and girls' sports at federally funded schools
provisions: Stops people born male from competing in women's and girls' sports at schools that get federal money
Says this rule applies under Title IX, the law that stops sex discrimination in schools
Defines sex by a person's biology at birth
Lets people born male practice with women's teams if it does not take away spots from women

supporters: Supporters say the bill protects female athletes by stopping people born male from competing in women's and girls' sports at schools that receive federal funding, which they argue gives those athletes a physical advantage.
Supporters say defining sex by a person's biology at birth under Title IX creates a clear, consistent rule for all federally funded schools to follow.
Supporters say the bill still allows people born male to practice with women's teams, as long as doing so does not take away spots or opportunities from female athletes.
critics: Critics say the bill requires schools to check students' reproductive biology and genetics at birth, which they argue invades student privacy and could force schools to demand medical records.
Critics say applying this rule under Title IX redefines what counts as sex discrimination, which could be used to exclude transgender girls who have lived as female throughout their school years.

Critics say the bill does not include any process for individual schools to review specific cases, leaving no flexibility for students whose situations do not fit neatly into the birth-biology definition.

118-hr-7217.one_liner: Fund military aid to Israel and US operations after attacks in Israel
provisions: Provides emergency military funding for the year starting October 2023
Pays to replace weapons and equipment the US gave to Israel
Covers costs of current US military operations in the Middle East region
Funds Israel's Iron Dome and other missile defense systems
Increases security funding for US embassies affected by the Israel attacks
Pays for emergency evacuations of US government workers and citizens
Lets the President transfer more military equipment to Israel

supporters: Supporters say the bill replaces weapons and equipment the US already gave to Israel, making sure US stockpiles are not left empty after the transfer.
Supporters say funding Israel's Iron Dome and David's Sling missile defense systems helps protect Israeli civilians from short-range rocket attacks.
Supporters say the bill pays for emergency evacuations of US government workers and citizens in the region, which protects Americans caught in the conflict.
critics: Critics say the bill expands the President's power to transfer military equipment to Israel without the normal approval process, reducing congressional oversight.
Critics say the funding is labeled as emergency spending, which means it is exempt from budget limits and adds to the national debt without offsets.
Critics say covering the costs of current US military operations in the Middle East region could pull the US deeper into the conflict.

118-hr-7024.one_liner: Expand tax credits for families and increase business tax breaks
provisions: Increases tax credits for families with children
Lets businesses write off equipment costs faster to reduce their taxes
Sets different tax rules for Taiwan residents who earn US income
Increases tax breaks for people who lost money in disasters and wildfires
Increases tax credits for building affordable housing

supporters: Supporters say the child tax credit changes would allow parents who earn too little to claim the full $2,000-per-child credit to get more money back, reaching about 16 million children in low-income families who currently get little or nothing.

Supporters say restoring 100% first-year write-offs for business equipment — which had been phasing down to 60% in 2024 — would push companies to buy new tools and machines, which can lead to more hiring.
Supporters say raising the low-income housing tax credit would help developers build more rental units for people who cannot afford market-rate housing.
critics: Critics say the bill costs roughly $78 billion over 10 years, and that the business tax breaks — like the faster equipment write-offs — deliver more in savings to corporations than to working families.
Critics say the special tax rules for Taiwan residents who earn U.S. income create a carve-out that workers from other countries do not get, treating one nationality differently from all others.
Critics say the child tax credit increases are set to expire after a few years, meaning families cannot count on the extra money staying in place.

118-hr-7463.one_liner: Keep the government running through March 2024 and change student aid rules
provisions: Funds federal agencies through March 8, 2024 for some and March 22, 2024 for others to prevent government shutdown
Sets a floor of negative $1,500 for student income when calculating financial aid in 2024-2025
Sets a floor of $0 for student income when calculating financial aid starting in 2025-2026
Provides additional funding for Federal Pell Grants starting in 2025

supporters: Supporters say the bill prevents a government shutdown by keeping federal agencies funded through March 8 or March 22, 2024, which protects workers who depend on federal services and pay.
Supporters say setting a student income floor of -$1,500 for 2024-2025 means more students will qualify for federal aid, because their income calculation cannot drop below that number.
Supporters say adding more money to Federal Pell Grants starting in 2025 will help low-income students pay for college without taking on more debt.
critics: Critics say the bill only extends funding for a few weeks — some agencies through March 8 and others through March 22, 2024 — which means Congress will face the same shutdown risk again very soon.
Critics say changing the student income floor to $0 starting in 2025-2026 is stricter than the 2024-2025 rule of -$1,500, which could reduce aid for students who report zero or negative income.
Critics say the bill does not pass full-year spending bills, so federal agencies are stuck operating at 2023 funding levels with no new investments or program updates.

118-hr-753.one_liner: Require VA hospitals to install on-site medical waste treatment systems
provisions: Requires VA hospitals to install systems that treat medical waste on-site instead of shipping it elsewhere
VA must create a cost analysis to figure out which hospitals would save money with these systems
Only hospitals that would save money get the new waste treatment systems

supporters: Supporters say installing on-site medical waste treatment systems at VA hospitals would save money by ending the need to ship waste to outside facilities.
Supporters say the required cost analysis model ensures taxpayer money is only spent at hospitals that would actually save money.
critics: Critics say the upfront costs to install and operate medical waste treatment systems at VA facilities could be expensive for taxpayers.
Critics say operating medical waste treatment systems on-site at VA hospitals could create safety risks for staff and patients.

118-hr-815.one_liner: Remove the 24-month care requirement for new veterans' emergency treatment reimbursement
provisions: Removes the rule that veterans must have received VA care within 24 months before getting emergency treatment to qualify for reimbursement
Lets veterans get VA reimbursement for emergency treatment at non-VA hospitals if the treatment happens within 60 days of enrolling in VA healthcare
Covers emergency treatment costs for newly enrolled veterans who have not yet used VA services

supporters: Supporters say this helps veterans who just signed up for VA care get emergency treatment paid for at non-VA hospitals within 60 days.
Supporters say removing the 24-month rule means new VA patients can get emergency care covered without waiting two years.
critics: Critics say covering emergency treatment for newly enrolled veterans will cost the VA more money by paying for additional non-VA hospital bills.
Critics say this may cause more veterans to go to non-VA emergency rooms instead of VA hospitals.

118-hr-788.one_liner: Stop the federal government from sending settlement money to outside groups
provisions: Stops the government from making legal settlements that send money to outside groups
Allows payments to repair damage caused by the defendant or pay for services
Lets officials be fired or lose money if they break this rule
Requires agencies to report their settlements for 7 years
Requires government watchdogs to report on rule violations

supporters: Supporters say this stops settlement money from going to outside groups that were not harmed, ensuring taxpayer funds return to the Treasury instead.
Supporters say the 7-year reporting rule will show the public how agencies spend settlement dollars and which groups receive payments.
Supporters say officials who break these rules can be fired or lose money, creating real consequences for violations.
critics: Critics say the narrow exceptions for 'actual harm' and 'services' could block settlement funds from going to community programs that help areas affected by corporate wrongdoing.
Critics say the 7-year reporting requirement will create extra paperwork and costs for agencies that must track and report all settlement details.
Critics say this rule could make companies less willing to settle cases if they cannot direct money to environmental cleanup or community restoration projects.

118-hr-813.one_liner: Require a government study of how well America attracts foreign business investment
provisions: Requires the Department of Commerce and Government Accountability Office to study foreign investment in America
The study examines how well America attracts businesses from trusted countries to invest here
Agencies must review current government policies that affect foreign investment
The study includes recommendations for bringing more foreign businesses to America

supporters: Supporters say the Department of Commerce and GAO review will find specific policy gaps that stop trusted foreign companies from choosing the U.S. over other countries.
Supporters say the required recommendations give Congress a clear action list for bringing more foreign business investment and the jobs that come with it to American communities.
Supporters say reviewing federal policies that affect foreign direct investment will show which rules are working and which ones may be pushing companies away.
critics: Critics say the bill only orders a study and report, with no requirement that the government act on any of the recommendations it receives.
Critics say the terms 'trusted countries' and 'responsible private-sector entities' are not defined in the bill, which could make the review results hard to use or compare.
Critics say the GAO and Commerce Department already track foreign investment data, so a new interagency review may repeat work that has already been done.

118-hr-7888.one_liner: Extend FBI surveillance powers for 5 years with new rules
provisions: Lets the FBI keep using a surveillance program for 5 more years to spy on people outside America
Requires FBI supervisors to approve searches about Americans caught in this surveillance
Makes the FBI Deputy Director approve any searches about elected officials or government workers
Bans political appointees from approving searches about politicians
Creates punishments for FBI agents who break surveillance rules including firing for intentional misconduct
Increases criminal penalties for people who violate surveillance laws
Requires sworn statements for surveillance requests and limits using information from political groups or news sources

supporters: Supporters say this bill adds important oversight by requiring FBI supervisors to approve searches about Americans caught in surveillance.
Supporters say the ban on political appointees approving searches about elected officials prevents partisan misuse of surveillance powers.
Supporters say the penalties including firing for intentional misconduct will stop FBI agents from breaking surveillance rules.
critics: Critics say this extends mass surveillance of people outside America for 5 more years without ending warrantless searches of Americans' data.
Critics say FBI supervisors can still approve searches about Americans without a warrant, which violates privacy rights.
Critics say the exception allowing searches to prevent threats to life or serious harm is too broad and could be misused.

118-hres-104.one_liner: Condemn China for flying a spy balloon over the United States
provisions: Condemns China for violating US territory with a spy balloon
Says China lied about what the balloon was for
States US policy should stop foreign spy aircraft from entering US territory

supporters: Supporters say this resolution makes it official US policy to stop foreign spy aircraft from violating US territory.
Supporters say this condemns China for sending the spy balloon over US airspace without permission.
Supporters say this calls out China for lying about the balloon's true purpose as a surveillance tool.
critics: Critics say this resolution only makes statements but creates no new laws to actually stop spy balloons.
Critics say condemning China could make diplomatic relations worse without fixing the surveillance problem.
Critics say existing US policy already prevents foreign aircraft from entering US territory without permission.

118-hres-11.one_liner: Create a House committee to study competition with China
provisions: Creates a committee in the House of Representatives
Committee has up to 16 members chosen by House leaders
Committee studies how China competes with the US in business, technology, and security
Committee writes recommendations for Congress about competing with China

supporters: Supporters say the 16-member committee will investigate China's economic, technological, and security progress to help the US compete.
Supporters say the committee will write policy recommendations for Congress about competing with China.
critics: Critics say the 16-member committee costs money for staff and operations that could be used elsewhere.
Critics say creating a committee focused on China competition could harm diplomatic relations with China.

118-hres-12.one_liner: Create a House subcommittee to investigate federal agencies' information gathering on citizens
provisions: Creates a House subcommittee with up to 13 members to investigate federal agencies
The subcommittee investigates how executive branch agencies collect information on U.S. citizens
Looks for activities that are illegal, unconstitutional, or unethical
Must report findings by January 2, 2025
The subcommittee ends 30 days after filing its report

supporters: Supporters say the 13-member subcommittee will protect citizens from illegal government spying by investigating how executive agencies collect information on Americans.
Supporters say requiring a final report by January 2, 2025 ensures Congress gets answers about unconstitutional surveillance activities within a clear deadline.
critics: Critics say creating another subcommittee wastes taxpayer money on partisan investigations instead of focusing on real legislative priorities.
Critics say the subcommittee interferes with legitimate law enforcement work by second-guessing how agencies investigate threats to national security.

118-hres-114.one_liner: Remove Representative George Santos from the House of Representatives
provisions: Removes George Santos from his seat in Congress
Stops him from voting in the House
Ends his pay and benefits from Congress
Leaves an empty House seat that needs to be filled

supporters: Supporters say this would remove Santos from his seat in Congress and stop him from voting on laws
Supporters say this would end Santos's pay and benefits from Congress paid by taxpayers
Supporters say this would open the House seat so voters can elect a new representative
critics: Critics say this would remove an elected representative before his term ends
Critics say this would leave the House seat empty until a special election is held
Critics say this removes Santos without letting voters decide in the next regular election

118-hres-166.one_liner: Allow votes on requiring inflation estimates and canceling retirement investment rules
provisions: Allows a House vote on requiring inflation estimates for Executive orders that cost money
Allows a House vote on canceling rules about how retirement plans invest money
Sets time limits for debate on both issues

supporters: Supporters say H.R. 347 would require the Executive Office of the President to publish an inflation estimate before any Executive order with a large budget effect takes place, giving Congress and the public a clearer picture of what each order costs.

Supporters say H.J. Res. 30 would cancel a Department of Labor rule that let retirement plan managers pick investments based on factors beyond financial return, arguing that plan managers should focus only on getting the best financial outcome for workers in those plans.
Supporters say setting time limits for debate on both bills prevents either measure from being blocked through extended delay on the House floor.

118-sjres-24.one_liner: Cancel a rule that made the northern long-eared bat an endangered species
provisions: Cancels a Fish and Wildlife Service rule from November 2022
Stops the northern long-eared bat from being called endangered
Keeps the bat's status as threatened instead of endangered
Brings back rules that applied when the bat was threatened

supporters: Supporters say canceling the November 2022 Fish and Wildlife Service rule would stop new restrictions that come with endangered status from affecting land owners and businesses.
Supporters say keeping the northern long-eared bat as threatened instead of endangered would bring back the old rules that protected the bat without creating strict limits on farming and forestry.
critics: Critics say reversing the northern long-eared bat from endangered back to threatened status would remove stronger protections when the bat population is declining.
Critics say the November 2022 rule was necessary because the bat needs endangered status protections to survive disease and habitat loss.

118-sjres-23.one_liner: Cancel a rule that made it easier to set aside habitat areas for endangered species
provisions: Cancels a 2022 rule from the National Marine Fisheries Service about endangered species habitat
Makes it harder for the government to set aside areas as critical habitat for endangered species
Brings back rules that limited the government's ability to create new habitat protections
Critical habitat areas have restrictions to protect endangered species

supporters: Supporters say this resolution would bring back rules that limited the government's power to designate critical habitat areas, reducing land use restrictions on property owners.
Supporters say the 2022 rule gave the National Marine Fisheries Service too much control over private and public lands through habitat protections.
critics: Critics say this resolution would make it harder for the government to protect areas that endangered marine species need to survive and recover.
Critics say bringing back the old limits would reduce habitat protections for endangered species when many marine animals face threats from development.

118-sjres-18.one_liner: Bring back a rule letting officials deny green cards to people who might need benefits
provisions: Brings back a 2019 immigration rule that was cancelled in 2022
Makes it easier to deny green cards to people who might use government benefits
Applies to people trying to get permanent legal status in the United States
Officials can consider whether someone might need food stamps or Medicaid when deciding

supporters: Supporters say restoring the 2019 rule will help ensure people getting green cards won't rely on government benefits like food stamps and Medicaid.
Supporters say immigration officials should consider whether someone might use public benefits when deciding on permanent legal status.
critics: Critics say bringing back the 2019 rule makes it harder for people to get green cards by considering their potential use of food stamps and Medicaid.
Critics say this affects people trying to get permanent legal status in the United States by making benefit use a factor in immigration decisions.

118-sjres-38.one_liner: Cancel a rule that let companies use foreign parts in electric vehicle chargers
provisions: Cancels a federal rule that let companies use foreign parts in electric vehicle chargers
Brings back the requirement that EV charger parts must be made in America
Applies to charging stations built with federal highway money
Steel and iron housing parts were already required to be American-made

supporters: Supporters say ending the waiver early would protect American manufacturing jobs by requiring EV charger parts to be made in America immediately instead of waiting until June 2024.
Supporters say this ensures federal highway money goes to American workers and companies rather than foreign manufacturers.
critics: Critics say ending the waiver before June 2024 would increase costs for charging stations and could delay meeting the October 2024 installation deadline.
Critics say there are not enough American manufacturers making EV charger components yet, which could slow down the buildout of charging infrastructure with federal money.

118-sjres-32.one_liner: Cancel a Consumer Financial Protection Bureau rule on small business loan data collection
provisions: Cancels a Consumer Financial Protection Bureau rule from May 2023
Banks will not have to collect data when small businesses apply for loans
Banks will not have to report this data to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau
A federal court already blocked this rule

supporters: Supporters say this would eliminate costly data collection requirements that banks must follow when small businesses apply for loans.
Supporters say banks will no longer have to report small business credit application data to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.
Supporters say since a federal court already blocked this rule, Congress should make the block permanent.
critics: Critics say canceling this rule removes the requirement for banks to collect data that shows if small businesses owned by women or minorities are denied loans unfairly.
Critics say without banks reporting small business loan data to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, it will be harder to enforce equal credit laws.
Critics say this eliminates oversight of how banks treat small business loan applications.

118-sjres-44.one_liner: Remove U.S. troops from Niger within 30 days
provisions: Requires the President to pull U.S. troops out of Niger within 30 days
Troops can stay only if Congress declares war or gives specific approval for military action
Applies to any military fighting in Niger or that affects Niger

supporters: Supporters say the 30-day deadline would force Congress to vote on whether U.S. troops should stay in Niger, making lawmakers take responsibility for military decisions.
Supporters say the bill follows the Constitution by requiring Congress to approve military action instead of letting the President send troops without permission.
critics: Critics say the 30-day timeline is too short to safely remove troops and could hurt ongoing fights against terrorist groups in Niger.
Critics say pulling U.S. forces from Niger would weaken America's ability to work with local partners and could let terrorist groups grow stronger in West Africa.

118-sjres-43.one_liner: Cancel a rule creating the SAVE student loan repayment plan
provisions: Cancels a Department of Education rule from July 2023
Prevents the SAVE student loan repayment plan from starting
Stops changes to income-based payments for federal student loans

supporters: Supporters say the resolution would prevent the federal government from spending taxpayer money on loan forgiveness through the SAVE plan for some borrowers while borrowers who already repaid their loans receive no relief.
Supporters say canceling the SAVE rule would require Congress to approve any new student loan repayment programs instead of allowing the Department of Education to create them through regulation.
critics: Critics say blocking the SAVE plan would keep millions of federal student loan borrowers in existing income-driven plans with higher monthly payments.
Critics say the resolution would prevent student loan borrowers from accessing the SAVE plan's reduced payment calculations and loan forgiveness provisions.

118-sjres-51.one_liner: Remove US troops from unauthorized Syria fighting
provisions: Orders removal of US troops from fighting in Syria
Applies only to military operations that Congress never approved
Directs the President to end unauthorized Syria hostilities

supporters: Supporters say this resolution would restore Congress's constitutional power to approve military action by ending Syria operations that lawmakers never authorized.
Supporters say it would bring US troops home from fighting that violates the War Powers Act since Congress did not vote to approve these Syria hostilities.
Supporters say the President should not be able to keep troops in combat without getting approval from Congress first.
critics: Critics say removing US forces from Syria operations could hurt efforts to fight ISIS terrorists who still operate in the region.
Critics say ending these military actions could abandon Kurdish allies who have fought alongside American troops against terrorist groups.
Critics say pulling troops from unauthorized Syria hostilities might create a security gap that Iran or Russia could fill.

118-sjres-4.one_liner: Remove the deadline for ratifying the Equal Rights Amendment and declare it valid
provisions: Removes the ratification deadline for the Equal Rights Amendment
Declares the Equal Rights Amendment is now a valid part of the Constitution
Says 38 states have ratified the amendment, which is enough to make it law
Makes it illegal to discriminate based on sex under the Constitution

supporters: Supporters say this would make the Equal Rights Amendment part of the Constitution because 38 states ratified it, which is the number needed under the Constitution.
Supporters say this would make sex discrimination illegal under the Constitution for the first time.
Supporters say the ratification deadline should not matter because the Constitution does not require deadlines for amendments.
critics: Critics say this ignores the original deadlines Congress set in 1972 and extended to 1982, making ratifications after those dates invalid.
Critics say only 33 states have valid ratifications because 5 states rescinded their approval of the amendment.
Critics say this bypasses the proper constitutional process by declaring the amendment valid without following the rules Congress established.

118-sjres-61.one_liner: Cancel a rule requiring states to set greenhouse gas targets for transportation
provisions: Cancels a Federal Highway Administration rule from December 7, 2023
Removes the requirement for states to set declining carbon dioxide targets for highways and transportation
Removes the requirement for states to report their progress on these targets to the federal government
Removes the requirement for metropolitan planning organizations to participate in setting these targets

supporters: Supporters say this would free states from having to set declining carbon dioxide targets for their highway systems.
Supporters say this removes the requirement for state transportation departments to report their emissions progress to the federal government.
Supporters say this eliminates federal rules requiring metropolitan planning organizations to participate in setting carbon targets.
critics: Critics say this removes the requirement for states to track and reduce carbon dioxide emissions from transportation.
Critics say this eliminates the reporting system that shows state progress on reducing highway emissions.
Critics say this ends federal oversight of transportation climate goals.

118-sjres-58.one_liner: Cancel a Department of Energy rule setting energy efficiency standards for gas furnaces
provisions: Cancels a Department of Energy rule requiring gas furnaces to meet new energy efficiency standards
Stops efficiency requirements for non-weatherized gas furnaces and mobile home gas furnaces
Gas furnace manufacturers will not need to meet the canceled energy standards

supporters: Supporters say canceling this rule will save gas furnace manufacturers from having to meet new efficiency standards that would increase production costs.
Supporters say the rule would have made it harder for people to buy affordable non-weatherized gas furnaces and mobile home gas furnaces.
critics: Critics say canceling the energy efficiency standards means consumers will miss out on lower energy bills from more efficient gas furnaces.
Critics say stopping these conservation standards for non-weatherized and mobile home gas furnaces will waste energy that could have been saved.

118-sjres-60.one_liner: Block a planned military equipment sale to Turkey
provisions: Stops the government from selling military equipment and training to Turkey
Uses Congress's power to review and disapprove weapons sales to other countries
Blocks the State Department and Defense Department from completing the sale

supporters: Supporters say blocking the F-16 fighter jets and modernization kits sale would prevent Turkey from getting advanced weapons after it bought Russian S-400 missiles that threaten NATO security systems.
Supporters say Congress must use its power to review weapons sales to stop the State Department and Defense Department from giving military equipment to countries that work with Russia.
critics: Critics say blocking the F-16 sale would harm relations with Turkey, a NATO ally that controls key military bases used by American forces in the Middle East.
Critics say stopping the Defense Department from completing the sale would hurt American defense companies that build the F-16 jets and modernization equipment.

118-sjres-62.one_liner: Cancel a rule allowing beef imports from Paraguay
provisions: Cancels a 2023 government rule that allowed fresh beef imports from Paraguay
The canceled rule had safety requirements to prevent foot-and-mouth disease
Stops Paraguay from exporting fresh beef to the United States

supporters: Supporters say blocking Paraguay beef imports protects US cattle ranchers from losing market share and facing lower prices due to foreign competition.
Supporters say the risk of foot-and-mouth disease entering the US is too high, even with the 12-month disease-free requirements and government inspections.
critics: Critics say the canceled rule had strong safety measures, including 12-month disease-free periods and government inspections of Paraguay facilities.
Critics say blocking these imports will reduce beef supply and raise prices for American consumers.

118-sjres-57.one_liner: Cancel a Treasury rule about COVID recovery fund spending deadlines
provisions: Cancels a Treasury Department rule from November 20, 2023
The rule let states and cities count administrative costs like reporting and audits toward the December 31, 2024 spending deadline
Without the rule, administrative costs do not count toward the December 31, 2024 deadline
States and cities must still use all COVID recovery money by December 31, 2026

supporters: Supporters say the Treasury rule lets states and cities count paperwork costs like reporting and audits toward the December 31, 2024 deadline instead of spending money to help people recover from COVID.
Supporters say administrative costs should not count as using COVID relief funds because the money was meant to help communities, not pay for bureaucracy.
critics: Critics say removing the Treasury rule will make it harder for states and cities to meet the December 31, 2024 deadline because they cannot count necessary reporting and audit costs.
Critics say states and cities need the administrative time to make sure COVID relief money is spent properly and follows federal rules.

118-sjres-89.one_liner: Stop U.S. military from building and running a pier in Gaza
provisions: Stops U.S. military from building, maintaining, and operating a pier on the Gaza coast
Ends a military operation that Congress did not approve

supporters: Supporters say the bill restores Congressional authority over military operations since the Gaza pier was built without Congressional approval.
Supporters say U.S. Armed Forces should not construct or operate facilities on the Gaza coast without authorization from Congress.
critics: Critics say stopping U.S. military construction and maintenance of the Gaza pier could end humanitarian aid delivery to Palestinians.
Critics say only U.S. Armed Forces have the equipment and skills needed to safely operate the pier on the Gaza coast.

118-sres-21.one_liner: Support observing a month to raise awareness about human trafficking
provisions: Expresses support for National Trafficking and Modern Slavery Prevention Month from January 1 to February 1, 2023
Encourages raising awareness about human trafficking and modern slavery
Expresses opposition to human trafficking and modern slavery

supporters: Supporters say this resolution raises awareness about human trafficking during the January 1 to February 1, 2023 period to help more people learn about modern slavery.
Supporters say expressing opposition to human trafficking through this resolution shows Congress stands against these crimes.
Supporters say the month-long awareness campaign helps identify trafficking victims and connect them with help.
critics: Critics say government time spent on awareness resolutions should go toward actual anti-trafficking enforcement and victim services instead.
Critics say the January 1 to February 1, 2023 timeframe may not be the best time for maximum awareness about trafficking issues.
Critics say this resolution only expresses support for awareness but does not create new laws or funding to actually fight human trafficking.

118-sres-13.one_liner: Designate January 2023 as National Stalking Awareness Month
provisions: Names January 2023 as National Stalking Awareness Month
Expresses Congressional support for police, prosecutors, and groups that help stalking victims
Calls for more public awareness about stalking and better support for victims

supporters: Supporters say naming January 2023 as National Stalking Awareness Month helps educate the public about stalking crimes.
Supporters say the resolution shows Congress backs police, prosecutors, and groups that help stalking victims in their work.
Supporters say calling for more awareness and victim support services will help more people get help when they are stalked.
critics: Critics say Congress should pass laws that give actual money to help stalking victims instead of just naming awareness months.
Critics say the resolution only makes statements but provides no funding or resources for police or victim services.
Critics say designating January 2023 as an awareness month is pointless since that month already ended in 2023.

118-sjres-9.one_liner: Cancel government protections for lesser prairie-chickens under the Endangered Species Act
provisions: Cancels a Fish and Wildlife Service rule from November 2022
Removes lesser prairie-chickens from government protection lists
Stops limits on activities that could harm two groups of these birds
Affects prairie-chickens in northern and southern parts of their range

supporters: Supporters say this removes rules that limit farming and energy work in prairie chicken habitat areas.
Supporters say this cancels November 2022 restrictions on land use that affect both northern and southern prairie chicken groups.
critics: Critics say this removes protection for southern prairie chickens that scientists listed as endangered.
Critics say this cancels November 2022 protections when prairie chicken populations are declining.

118-sres-417.one_liner: Expresses Senate support for Israel against Hamas
provisions: States the Senate stands with Israel as it defends itself
Says Israel has the right to defend itself
Calls on all countries to condemn Hamas' war on Israel
Says the US remains committed to Israel's security
Supports emergency military supplies and other help for Israel
Calls on the US to lead efforts to cut off Hamas funding from Iran and other sources
Says this does not declare war or authorize US military force

supporters: Supporters say this resolution reaffirms Israel's right to defend itself and shows US commitment to a key ally's security.
Supporters say calling on all countries to condemn Hamas' war on Israel builds international pressure against terrorism.
Supporters say supporting emergency military supplies helps Israel protect itself while the resolution clearly states it does not authorize US military force.
critics: Critics say the resolution's one-sided support for Israel could make the conflict worse by not addressing both sides.
Critics say supporting emergency military supplies and aid could increase violence and civilian deaths.
Critics say calling on the US to lead efforts to cut off Hamas funding from Iran could pull America deeper into the conflict.

119-hconres-61.one_liner: Remove U.S. troops from fighting terrorist groups in the Western Hemisphere
provisions: Tells the President to pull U.S. troops out of fights with terrorist groups in the Western Hemisphere
Does not apply if Congress has passed a law allowing the military action
Covers any group the President has labeled a terrorist organization
Applies to military operations in North, Central, and South America

supporters: Supporters say this bill would force the President to get Congress approval before fighting any terrorist group he has labeled in North, Central, and South America.
Supporters say this would stop military operations against presidentially designated terrorist organizations in the Western Hemisphere unless Congress passes a law allowing the fights.
critics: Critics say this could end ongoing U.S. military operations against terrorist groups across the Western Hemisphere.
Critics say this would slow down the President's response to threats from terrorist organizations the President has designated in the Americas.

119-hconres-38.one_liner: Stop U.S. military action against Iran without Congress approval
provisions: Tells the President to end all military action against Iran unless Congress declares war or approves the use of force
Lets the U.S. defend itself if Iran attacks first
Uses the War Powers Resolution to force the President to remove troops

supporters: Supporters say this would make the President follow the Constitution by getting Congress to declare war or approve force before military action against Iran.
Supporters say the War Powers Resolution requires congressional approval for hostilities, and this bill would end unauthorized military action against the Iranian government.
Supporters say the bill protects the right to self-defense if Iran attacks the United States first.
critics: Critics say forcing the removal of U.S. forces could limit the President's ability to respond quickly to Iranian threats against American troops or allies.
Critics say the self-defense exception might not cover protecting U.S. bases or allies from Iranian attacks.
Critics say this could weaken deterrence against Iran by restricting military options unless Congress approves them first.

119-hconres-64.one_liner: Remove U.S. military forces from Venezuela unless Congress declares war or authorizes force
provisions: Tells the President to pull U.S. military forces out of Venezuela
Only applies if Congress has not declared war on Venezuela
Only applies if Congress has not given permission for military action there

supporters: Supporters say this bill would make Congress vote before the U.S. goes to war with Venezuela, as the Constitution requires.
Supporters say this would stop the President from using military force in Venezuela without getting permission from Congress first.
Supporters say this would pull U.S. forces out of Venezuela unless Congress votes to declare war or authorize military action there.
critics: Critics say this bill would tie the President's hands if Venezuela threatens U.S. citizens or allies in South America.
Critics say this could help Venezuela's government by forcing the U.S. to remove military pressure.
Critics say this would require the President to pull forces out even if they are protecting American interests in the region.

118-sres-504.one_liner: Request information from the State Department about Israel's human rights practices
provisions: Asks the State Department to provide Congress with information about Israel's human rights practices
Requests information about steps the US has taken to promote human rights in Israel's activities in Gaza and the West Bank
Asks for an assessment of whether Israel follows international human rights law
Requests information about whether Israel will use US security assistance in armed conflicts in Gaza and the West Bank

supporters: Supporters say this resolution would give Congress the information it needs to oversee how Israel uses US security assistance in Gaza and the West Bank.
Supporters say the State Department assessment of Israel's compliance with international human rights law would help ensure US aid follows existing human rights standards.
critics: Critics say this resolution creates reporting requirements about Israel's human rights practices that other US allies do not have.
Critics say the State Department already provides Congress with information about human rights practices through existing reports.

119-hjres-130.one_liner: Cancel a rule that stopped coal leasing in Wyoming's Buffalo Field Office
provisions: Cancels a Bureau of Land Management rule from November 2024
The rule stopped all future coal leasing in Wyoming's Buffalo Field Office
Brings back coal leasing under the 2015 land use plan
Makes federal coal in this Wyoming area available for companies to lease again

supporters: Supporters say this bill brings back coal leasing in Wyoming's Buffalo Field Office that was stopped by the November 2024 Bureau of Land Management rule.
Supporters say restoring the 2015 land use plan will create coal mining jobs and revenue for Wyoming communities.
critics: Critics say this bill ignores the court ruling that required the Bureau of Land Management to study climate impacts before allowing coal leasing in the Buffalo Field Office.
Critics say canceling the 2024 rule removes protections that made federal coal unavailable for future leasing in this Wyoming area.

119-hjres-140.one_liner: Allow mineral and geothermal leasing on 225,504 acres in Minnesota
provisions: Cancels a 2023 rule that stopped companies from leasing forest land for mining
Affects 225,504 acres in Cook, Lake, and Saint Louis Counties, Minnesota
Lets companies lease this land to look for minerals and geothermal energy
Removes protections that were supposed to last 20 years
Includes areas near the Boundary Waters wilderness

supporters: Supporters say canceling the 2023 rule would create mining jobs in Cook, Lake, and Saint Louis Counties where 225,504 acres would be open for mineral leasing.
Supporters say allowing companies to lease this land for mineral exploration would boost the local economy and provide domestic sources of critical minerals.
Supporters say the 20-year mining ban hurts local communities that depend on resource extraction for jobs and tax revenue.
critics: Critics say removing protections from 225,504 acres near the Boundary Waters wilderness would threaten clean water in the Rainy River Watershed.
Critics say canceling the 2023 rule would break promises to protect the 1854 Ceded Territory of the Lake Superior Chippewa from mining damage.
Critics say mineral leasing in these three Minnesota counties would harm tourism that depends on clean lakes and forests.

119-hconres-68.one_liner: Remove U.S. troops from Venezuela unless Congress votes to keep them there
provisions: Orders the President to remove U.S. troops from Venezuela
Troops can stay only if Congress declares war against Venezuela or votes to authorize military action there

supporters: Supporters say this would make the President remove U.S. troops from Venezuela unless Congress votes to authorize the mission.
Supporters say this follows the Constitution by requiring Congress approval before keeping military forces in another country.
critics: Critics say forcing removal of U.S. troops from Venezuela could hurt American security interests in the region.
Critics say this could end important military partnerships or intelligence work that protects Americans.

119-hjres-131.one_liner: Cancel a rule that limited oil drilling to 400,000 acres in an Alaska wildlife refuge
provisions: Cancels a December 2024 rule from the Bureau of Land Management
The rule limited oil and gas drilling to 400,000 acres in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge
Opens up all 1.6 million acres in the refuge for oil and gas drilling
Removes protections from 1.2 million acres that were off-limits to drilling

supporters: Supporters say this would make an additional 1.2 million acres in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge available for oil and gas drilling.
Supporters say removing the limit of 400,000 acres would increase domestic oil production.
Supporters say the 2024 rule blocked access to areas with the highest potential for finding oil.
critics: Critics say this would remove protections from 1.2 million acres in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge.
Critics say opening all 1.6 million acres to drilling could harm caribou and other wildlife in the refuge.
Critics say this overturns rules designed to protect and conserve resources in the wildlife refuge.

119-hjres-117.one_liner: End the national emergency declared on July 30, 2025
provisions: Ends the national emergency that the President declared on July 30, 2025
Stops any special powers the President got from the emergency declaration
Returns government operations to normal rules

supporters: Supporters say this bill would end the July 30, 2025 national emergency declaration and return the government to normal operating rules.
Supporters say the special presidential powers granted by the July 30, 2025 emergency should be stopped and regular procedures restored.
critics: Critics say ending the July 30, 2025 national emergency could remove needed presidential authorities that are still required.
Critics say this bill would force government operations back to normal rules before the situation that prompted the July 30, 2025 declaration is fully resolved.

119-hr-1005.one_liner: Stop public schools from taking money from China's government
provisions: Public schools cannot take money from China's government or the Chinese Communist Party
Public schools cannot sign contracts with China's government or the Chinese Communist Party
Schools that break these rules lose their federal funding
Schools must tell the Education Department about any foreign funding

supporters: Supporters say blocking public schools from taking Chinese government money protects students from foreign influence.
Supporters say requiring schools to tell the Education Department about foreign funding gives parents and officials important information.
Supporters say schools that follow the ban on Chinese government contracts will keep getting federal education funds.
critics: Critics say schools could lose all their federal education funding if they accidentally sign a contract with someone connected to the Chinese government.
Critics say the requirement to report all foreign funding to the Education Department creates extra work for school staff.
Critics say the ban on contracts with Chinese government groups could end useful student exchange programs.

119-hr-1049.one_liner: Require schools to tell parents about foreign money and influence in their schools
provisions: Schools must tell parents they have the right to ask about foreign money in their schools
Parents can request to see any teaching materials bought with foreign government money
Parents can request to know how many school workers are paid with foreign government money
Parents can request information about contracts or funding from foreign countries
Schools must post notice of these parent rights on their websites
Schools that don't comply lose federal education funding

supporters: Supporters say parents have the right to know if foreign governments are paying school workers or funding teaching materials used in their children's classrooms.
Supporters say schools should post public notices about these parent rights on their websites so families can request information about foreign funding.
Supporters say this bill ensures transparency when foreign countries have contracts or funding agreements with local schools.
critics: Critics say schools will face administrative costs to track foreign funding sources and respond to parent requests for information about contracts and staff compensation.
Critics say the requirement to notify parents about foreign influence could discourage schools from participating in existing international education programs and partnerships.
Critics say schools risk losing all federal education funding if they fail to properly post notices or respond to parent requests about foreign involvement.

119-hr-1047.one_liner: Speed up connections for reliable power plants to the electric grid
provisions: Requires federal energy regulators to create new rules for connecting power plants to the electric grid
Lets reliable power plants that can turn on when needed skip ahead in the waiting list
Allows power companies to request their reliable plants get moved up in line
Gives regulators 60 days to approve or reject these requests

supporters: Supporters say this would help reliable power plants that can turn on when needed connect to the electric grid faster by allowing them to skip ahead in the waiting list.
Supporters say the 60-day deadline for federal regulators to approve or reject these requests would speed up decisions for power companies.
critics: Critics say this would give dispatchable power plants preferential treatment in the interconnection queue over renewable energy projects.
Critics say allowing power companies to request their plants get moved up in line could delay other energy projects already waiting for grid connections.

119-hjres-142.one_liner: Cancel DC's tax law to keep federal tax cuts
provisions: Cancels a DC tax law passed in December 2025
Keeps tips exempt from DC income tax for tipped workers
Keeps the higher standard tax deduction for all DC taxpayers
Blocks DC from restoring its child tax credit for families
Keeps business tax benefits for commercial property

supporters: Supporters say this keeps tips exempt from DC income tax for restaurant workers and other tipped employees.
Supporters say this preserves the higher standard tax deduction that reduces taxes for all DC taxpayers.
Supporters say this maintains business tax benefits for commercial property owners in DC.
critics: Critics say this blocks DC from restoring its child tax credit that would help families with children.
Critics say this prevents DC from making its own tax decisions and forces the city to keep federal tax changes.
Critics say this reduces tax revenue that DC needs to fund local services.

provisions: AI summary temporarily unavailable
119-hjres-72.one_liner: Relating to a national emergency by the President on February 1, 2025.

supporters: Supporters say this bill provides Congress with necessary oversight of the February 1st emergency declaration to ensure proper checks and balances.
Supporters say this legislation clarifies the scope and duration of emergency powers used since February 1st to prevent government overreach.
critics: Critics say this bill undermines the President's ability to respond quickly to the ongoing emergency situation declared on February 1st.
Critics say the legislation creates unnecessary bureaucratic delays when swift executive action is needed to address the national emergency.

119-hr-131.one_liner: Cut costs for Colorado communities paying for a water pipeline project
provisions: Removes interest payments that Colorado communities owe for the Arkansas Valley Conduit water pipeline
Extends the repayment time to 100 years
Pipeline brings water from Pueblo Reservoir to communities in Arkansas River Valley

supporters: Supporters say removing interest payments will help Colorado communities in the Arkansas River Valley afford water from the Pueblo Reservoir pipeline.
Supporters say the 100-year repayment period will make monthly payments more manageable for these communities.
critics: Critics say removing interest payments will force taxpayers to subsidize the Arkansas Valley Conduit construction costs.
Critics say the 100-year repayment period means the Bureau of Reclamation will wait much longer to recover project costs.

119-hr-1608.one_liner: Require DHS to write a report on preventing car and truck attacks
provisions: Requires DHS to write a report about preventing people from using cars and trucks in terrorist attacks
Report must list what threats exist now and what new threats might come
Report must identify places that could be targets like airports and government buildings
Report must explain how DHS works with police to prevent vehicle attacks
Report must suggest new technology to detect and stop vehicle attacks
DHS must give Congress a classified version and post a summary online
DHS must present the findings to Congress in a briefing

supporters: Supporters say the threat assessment requirement would help identify current and emerging vehicle attack threats that DHS may not be tracking.
Supporters say identifying vulnerable locations like airports and government buildings would help protect places where many people gather.
Supporters say the coordination requirements with police agencies would improve information sharing to prevent vehicle attacks.
critics: Critics say the reporting requirement adds paperwork burden to DHS when the agency could use those resources for actual security work.
Critics say the classified report structure limits public oversight since only the summary goes online while Congress gets the full details.
Critics say the bill may duplicate existing DHS assessments of critical infrastructure sites like airports that already have security reviews.

119-hr-1069.one_liner: Block federal funding to schools with Chinese government partnerships
provisions: Blocks federal money to elementary and high schools that partner with Chinese government groups
Cuts funding to schools with Confucius Institutes or Chinese-funded learning centers
Stops funding to schools that get Chinese teaching materials, staff, or money
Lets schools ask for an exception if they prove their Chinese partnership helps America
Requires the Education Department to notify schools about these new rules

supporters: Supporters say cutting federal funding to schools with Confucius Institutes protects students from Chinese government influence in American classrooms.
Supporters say blocking federal money to schools that get Chinese teaching materials and staff prevents foreign control of elementary and high school education.
Supporters say requiring schools to prove their Chinese partnerships help America before getting waivers ensures taxpayer money only supports programs that benefit the United States.
critics: Critics say removing federal funding from schools with Chinese-funded learning centers will eliminate language programs that help thousands of students learn Mandarin.
Critics say the waiver requirement forces schools to choose between losing federal education money and ending partnerships that provide free teaching resources and staff.
Critics say blocking funding to schools that receive Chinese teaching materials will hurt rural schools that depend on these programs for foreign language classes.

119-hr-1366.one_liner: Allow mining waste disposal on federal land without proving minerals exist
provisions: Lets mining companies dispose of waste on federal land even if the land has no valuable minerals
Overturns a 2022 court ruling that limited where mining companies could dispose of waste
Creates a fund to clean up old abandoned mines
Requires fees from mining companies that go into the cleanup fund
Lets mining companies claim as many waste disposal sites as they need

supporters: Supporters say this fixes the legal uncertainty created by the 2022 Rosemont court ruling that blocked mining projects from moving forward.
Supporters say the bill creates a fund paid for by mining company fees to clean up old abandoned mines across the country.
Supporters say mining companies need flexibility to dispose of waste rock and this allows them to claim as many disposal sites as their operations require.
critics: Critics say this lets mining companies dump waste on federal lands even when those lands contain no valuable minerals worth mining.
Critics say the bill overturns court protections that prevented mining companies from using federal land solely for waste disposal.
Critics say mining companies can now claim unlimited waste disposal sites on public land under their approved operations.

119-hr-1531.one_liner: Require federal agencies to exclude China from international financial groups if China threatens Taiwan
provisions: Requires Treasury, Federal Reserve, and SEC to exclude China from six international financial organizations if the President says China threatens Taiwan
Covers organizations like the Group of Twenty and Bank for International Settlements
President can waive this requirement if it serves US national interest

supporters: Supporters say this bill gives the US a way to pressure China by removing them from six important financial groups like the Group of Twenty and Bank for International Settlements when China threatens Taiwan's security or economic system.
Supporters say the President can waive these exclusion rules if keeping China in these organizations serves US national interests, which gives flexibility to avoid hurting America.
Supporters say requiring the Treasury, Federal Reserve, and SEC to take action creates real consequences when China threatens Taiwan instead of just empty warnings.
critics: Critics say excluding China from six major financial organizations like the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision could damage US relationships with other member countries who want to keep working with China.
Critics say this bill gives the President too much power to decide when China threatens Taiwan, which could lead to excluding China from important financial groups over minor disagreements.
Critics say removing China from organizations that help oversee global banking and securities could make the world's financial system less stable and harder to manage.

119-hr-1676.one_liner: Set deadlines for federal approval of state wildlife conservation plans
provisions: Gives the federal government 180 days to approve state wildlife conservation plans
Automatically approves state wildlife plans if the federal government misses the deadline
Requires the federal government to set aside grant money for states when it misses deadlines

supporters: Supporters say the 180-day deadline would speed up approval of state wildlife plans that now sit in federal offices for months or years.
Supporters say automatic approval prevents federal delays from stopping important conservation work that protects local wildlife.
Supporters say states would get their grant money faster when federal agencies miss deadlines instead of waiting indefinitely for approvals.
critics: Critics say automatic approval after 180 days could allow weak conservation plans to pass without proper federal review of whether they meet wildlife protection standards.
Critics say removing federal oversight could let states waste grant money on poorly planned programs that fail to protect endangered species.
Critics say the 180-day deadline is too short for federal experts to properly check if state plans follow conservation science and legal requirements.

119-hr-2189.one_liner: Remove certain TASERs and similar devices from federal gun regulations
provisions: Removes TASERs and similar non-lethal weapons from federal gun laws
Only covers devices that fire projectiles slower than 500 feet per second
Devices cannot be easily changed to shoot regular bullets
The ATF must decide within 90 days if a device qualifies when manufacturers ask

supporters: Supporters say removing TASERs and similar devices from federal gun laws will help police departments get non-lethal tools faster without gun regulation paperwork.
Supporters say the 90-day ATF decision timeline will speed up approval for new de-escalation devices that could save lives.
Supporters say the 500 feet per second speed limit and ban on regular ammunition ensures these devices stay safe and non-lethal.
critics: Critics say removing federal oversight of TASER-type devices could lead to misuse by police without proper safety checks.
Critics say the definition of less-than-lethal devices is too broad and manufacturers could exploit loopholes to avoid gun regulations.
Critics say taking these weapons out of gun control laws could put more dangerous devices on the market without enough safety testing.

119-hr-2262.one_liner: Stop counting voluntary training as paid work time
provisions: Changes federal rules about what counts as work hours
Voluntary training outside regular work hours does not count as paid time
Workers can skip training without it affecting their job
Training cannot include actual work tasks

supporters: Supporters say this helps workers get job training without forcing employers to pay overtime for voluntary programs outside regular work hours.
Supporters say workers are protected because they can skip training without it affecting their job status or working conditions.
Supporters say this clarifies federal rules so employers can offer professional development without wage costs for voluntary training.
critics: Critics say workers may feel pressured to attend unpaid training even though it is called voluntary.
Critics say this reduces worker pay by excluding training time from hours worked under federal labor law.
Critics say employers could use voluntary training programs to get around paying overtime wages.

119-hr-1949.one_liner: Remove government restrictions on natural gas exports to other countries
provisions: Removes the requirement for a government agency to approve natural gas sales to other countries
Cancels rules about free trade agreements for natural gas exports
Gives FERC, a federal agency that regulates energy, control over approving exports and shipping facilities
FERC must decide that exports help the public

supporters: Supporters say giving FERC exclusive authority over LNG facilities would speed up approval by having one agency instead of multiple agencies review projects.
Supporters say removing the DOE approval requirement would allow natural gas companies to export more quickly and boost domestic production.
Supporters say more LNG exports would create jobs in the natural gas industry and help the US sell energy to other countries.
critics: Critics say removing DOE oversight could weaken environmental and safety reviews of LNG export facilities.
Critics say more natural gas exports could raise prices for American families by sending domestic gas overseas.
Critics say FERC may not fully consider climate impacts when deciding if exports help the public interest.

provisions: AI summary temporarily unavailable

119-hr-261.one_liner: Remove Commerce Department permit rules for undersea cables in marine sanctuaries
provisions: Stops the Commerce Department from requiring permits for undersea cable work in marine sanctuaries
If another government agency already approved the cable work, Commerce cannot ask for more permits
Covers installing, fixing, and removing undersea internet cables
Lets NOAA work with other agencies when cable work might damage marine sanctuary areas

supporters: Supporters say this bill cuts red tape by stopping the Commerce Department from requiring extra permits when other federal or state agencies have already approved undersea cable work.
Supporters say this speeds up installation of undersea internet cables that provide internet service to communities.
Supporters say the bill still allows NOAA to work with other agencies when cable work might damage marine sanctuary areas.
critics: Critics say removing Commerce Department permit requirements weakens protection of national marine sanctuaries from cable installation damage.
Critics say other agencies that approve cable work may not have the same expertise about marine sanctuary protection that the Commerce Department has.
Critics say this bill allows undersea cable companies to bypass Commerce Department review even when their work could harm sensitive marine areas.

119-hr-2550.one_liner: Cancel an Executive Order that removed union rights from some federal agencies
provisions: Cancels an Executive Order from March 27, 2025 that removed union rights from some federal agencies
Brings back the right for federal workers at those agencies to form unions and bargain for pay and benefits
Keeps existing union contracts in place through their original end dates

supporters: Supporters say this restores union rights for federal workers that were removed by the March 27, 2025 Executive Order.
Supporters say federal employees at affected agencies should be able to bargain for better pay and working conditions like other workers.
Supporters say keeping existing union contracts in place protects deals workers already made with their agencies.
critics: Critics say this blocks the president's ability to manage federal agencies without union interference.
Critics say union contracts at federal agencies could cost taxpayers more money through higher wages and benefits.
Critics say some federal agencies work better when managers can make quick decisions without union rules.
