119-s-3627.one_liner: Require colleges to tell students about resources for pregnant students who want to have babies
provisions: Colleges that get federal student aid money must give students information about help for pregnant students
Colleges must tell students about community groups and campus services that help pregnant students have babies
Colleges must tell students about help available for pregnant students and new mothers
Colleges must tell students how to file complaints if they face discrimination for being pregnant

supporters: Supporters say this bill would help pregnant students find community groups and campus services that help them have babies while staying in school.
Supporters say the bill would protect pregnant students by requiring colleges to tell them how to file complaints if they face discrimination for being pregnant.
Supporters say this would give pregnant students information about accommodations to help them stay in school during pregnancy and after having babies.
critics: Critics say this bill would force colleges that get federal student aid money to create new paperwork and compliance requirements.
Critics say the bill only requires information about carrying babies to term, not about other pregnancy options.
Critics say this adds new rules for colleges without providing money to help them comply.

119-s-356.one_liner: Extend federal payments to rural counties with federal land through 2026
provisions: Continues payments to states and counties that contain federal land through the year ending September 2026
Provides payments for the years ending September 2024 and September 2025
Lets counties use this money to start projects through the year ending September 2028
Lets local advisory committees propose projects using this money through the year ending September 2028

supporters: Supporters say this bill helps rural counties that lose tax money because they cannot tax federal land within their borders, giving them payments through September 2026.
Supporters say the bill lets local counties and advisory committees control how to spend this money on projects through September 2028, giving communities power over their own needs.
critics: Critics say extending these federal payments through 2026 costs taxpayers money that could be used for other priorities or deficit reduction.
Critics say the bill makes rural counties dependent on federal funding instead of finding ways to grow their own tax base.

119-sjres-98.one_liner: Remove US military forces from Venezuela unless Congress approves the mission
provisions: Tells the President to stop using US military forces for fights in or against Venezuela
Makes an exception if Congress declares war or approves military action against Venezuela
Lets the US defend itself if Venezuela attacks first

supporters: Supporters say this bill makes Congress vote before the President can use US military forces against Venezuela, which follows the Constitution's rule that Congress decides on war.
Supporters say this would stop unauthorized military action in Venezuela unless Congress declares war or approves the use of force.
Supporters say this ensures proper checks and balances between the President and Congress on military decisions.
critics: Critics say this bill could prevent the President from responding quickly to Venezuelan threats against US allies or interests in the region.
Critics say this would limit presidential flexibility to use military force unless Congress passes a declaration of war or authorization first.
Critics say this might hamper ongoing US operations or partnerships in the region involving Venezuela.

119-sjres-84.one_liner: Cancel a health insurance rule about enrollment periods and coverage requirements
provisions: Cancels a rule that sets specific dates when people can sign up for health insurance through government websites
Cancels a rule requiring extra checks on 3 out of 4 people who sign up outside normal enrollment times
Cancels a rule blocking DACA recipients from buying insurance through government marketplaces
Cancels a rule stopping insurers from covering certain medical treatments for changing sex characteristics

supporters: Supporters say canceling the verification rule would help people get insurance faster because exchanges would not have to check 75% of people who sign up during special enrollment periods.
Supporters say the resolution would restore DACA recipients' access to buy health insurance through government marketplaces and state programs.
Supporters say canceling the rule would let insurers cover sex-trait modification procedures again, giving patients more treatment options.
critics: Critics say the verification checks on 75% of special enrollment applicants help prevent people from getting insurance subsidies when they are not eligible.
Critics say the standardized enrollment dates from November 1 to December 31 help insurance companies plan and keep premiums stable.
Critics say blocking coverage for sex-trait modification procedures saves money for insurance plans and keeps essential benefits focused on basic medical care.

119-sjres-86.one_liner: Cancel EPA approval of South Dakota's plan to reduce haze in national parks
provisions: Cancels an EPA rule from August 2025
The rule approved South Dakota's plan to cut air pollution that causes haze
The haze makes it harder to see long distances in national parks
Without approval, South Dakota's plan does not meet EPA requirements

supporters: Supporters say this resolution lets South Dakota control its own air pollution rules instead of following the EPA's August 2025 requirements for reducing haze.
Supporters say this stops the federal EPA from forcing South Dakota to follow specific pollution reduction rules that the state did not want.
Supporters say this gives South Dakota the right to create its own plan for reducing haze without needing EPA approval.
critics: Critics say this resolution blocks South Dakota's plan to cut air pollution that causes haze and makes it harder to see long distances in national parks.
Critics say this means South Dakota's pollution plan will not meet EPA requirements designed to improve visibility in national parks and wilderness areas.
Critics say this will prevent pollution reductions needed to help visitors see clearly across long distances in protected areas.

119-sjres-95.one_liner: Block an IRS rule on corporate minimum tax for partnerships
provisions: Cancels an IRS rule about corporate minimum tax rules for partnerships
Stops the new tax rule from taking effect
Means partnerships keep using the current tax rules
Uses Congress power to overturn rules made by government agencies

supporters: Supporters say this resolution would cancel the IRS rule and keep partnerships using current tax rules instead of new corporate minimum tax requirements.
Supporters say stopping the new tax rule from taking effect protects partnerships from additional compliance costs and paperwork.
Supporters say Congress should use its power to overturn agency rules that change how partnerships handle corporate minimum tax calculations.
critics: Critics say the IRS rule simplifies how partnerships apply corporate minimum tax requirements and makes compliance easier.
Critics say canceling this rule keeps partnerships stuck with current tax guidance that is harder to understand and follow.
Critics say blocking the IRS rule prevents proper enforcement of corporate minimum tax on large partnerships that should pay these taxes.

118-hr-2766.one_liner: Create a State Department coordinator and training for Uyghur human rights issues
provisions: Creates a new coordinator position at the State Department for Uyghur issues
Lets the State Department fund human rights advocates who work for Uyghurs in China
Requires Foreign Service officers to get training in the Uyghur language
Requires the U.S. to have Uyghur-speaking staff at diplomatic missions in China
Funds advocates to speak at public forums about human rights in China

supporters: Supporters say the Special Coordinator position would give Uyghur issues focused attention within the State Department.
Supporters say funding advocates to speak at public forums would give Uyghurs a voice in talks about their treatment.
Supporters say requiring Uyghur language training and Uyghur-speaking staff at missions in China would help U.S. diplomats work directly with Uyghur communities.
critics: Critics say creating a new Special Coordinator position would add costs and bureaucracy to the State Department.
Critics say funding advocates who speak against China's policies toward Uyghurs could harm U.S.-China relations.
Critics say requiring Uyghur language training for Foreign Service officers would take resources away from other diplomatic needs.

118-hr-3391.one_liner: Extend funding for children's medical research at NIH through 2028
provisions: Continues funding a program that studies diseases in children through 2028
Requires NIH to coordinate research on children's diseases to avoid duplicate work
Requires the health department to report to Congress about the research it funds

supporters: Supporters say this continues funding for research that studies diseases affecting children through 2028.
Supporters say this requires NIH to coordinate pediatric research to avoid duplicate work and wasted money.
Supporters say this requires the health department to report to Congress about research spending to ensure accountability.
critics: Critics say this extends government spending on research programs through 2028 without setting clear budget limits.
Critics say the new coordination requirements could slow down important research on children's diseases.
Critics say this creates new reporting burdens for the health department that take time away from actual research.

118-hr-3821.one_liner: Extend funding for a firefighter cancer database through 2028
provisions: Continues funding for a database that tracks cancer in firefighters through 2028
Firefighters can choose to share their health information with the database
The database helps researchers study cancer in firefighters

supporters: Supporters say this database helps researchers study cancer in firefighters through 2028, which could help find ways to protect firefighters from cancer risks.
Supporters say firefighters can choose to share their health information with the database, so it respects their privacy while collecting research data.
critics: Critics say extending funding for this database through 2028 costs taxpayer money that could be used for other health programs.
Critics say since firefighters can choose not to participate, the database might not get enough health information to be useful for research.

118-hr-3838.one_liner: Extend federal funding for programs that track and prevent mothers from dying through 2028
provisions: Extends federal money for state committees that review when mothers die through 2028
Funds committees that study why mothers die during or after pregnancy
Requires tracking of deaths related to pregnancy and giving birth
Makes CDC share ways to prevent mothers from dying with hospitals each year

supporters: Supporters say extending federal funding through 2028 for state committees that review maternal deaths will help identify why mothers die and prevent future deaths.
Supporters say requiring CDC to share best practices with hospitals each year will give doctors better tools to save mothers' lives.
Supporters say tracking all pregnancy-related deaths will provide data needed to reduce maternal mortality rates.
critics: Critics say extending federal spending through 2028 adds to government costs without requiring states to show results.
Critics say making CDC share practices with hospitals each year creates new federal mandates on healthcare providers.
Critics say federal oversight of state death review committees takes control away from local health officials.

118-hr-3202.one_liner: Expand sanctions on Syria and block US recognition of Assad's government
provisions: Stops US officials from recognizing Assad as Syria's leader
Puts sanctions on anyone who gives aircraft or spare parts to Assad's government
Puts sanctions on people who steal humanitarian aid meant for Syrian people
Puts sanctions on people who take property in Syria for personal gain
Extends sanctions to family members of sanctioned people
Requires State Department to create a plan to stop other countries from working with Assad

supporters: Supporters say stopping US officials from recognizing Assad prevents America from legitimizing a leader accused of human rights abuses against Syrian people.
Supporters say the aircraft sanctions would limit Assad's military by blocking anyone from giving planes or spare parts to his government.
Supporters say protecting humanitarian aid from theft ensures food and medicine reaches Syrian families instead of being stolen for personal gain.
critics: Critics say preventing US officials from recognizing Assad removes diplomatic options for future peace talks or negotiations.
Critics say extending sanctions to adult family members of sanctioned people punishes relatives who may not be involved in wrongdoing.
Critics say the aircraft sanctions could hurt civilian aviation and make it harder for Syrian people to travel.

118-hr-2799.one_liner: Loosen rules for companies selling stock and let more people invest in private companies
provisions: Lets small companies sell up to $250,000 in stock without registering with the government
Raises the yearly revenue limit for fast-growing companies to qualify for easier rules to $1.5 billion
Lets investment funds raise up to $150 million instead of $10 million
Lets investment funds have up to 600 investors instead of 250
Lets more people invest in private companies by changing who qualifies as a wealthy investor

supporters: Supporters say the $250,000 exemption will help small businesses raise money without expensive paperwork and lawyers.
Supporters say raising the fund limit from $10 million to $150 million will let venture capital funds invest in more startups.
Supporters say letting more people qualify as wealthy investors will give middle-class families new ways to build wealth.
critics: Critics say the $250,000 exemption removes important protections that help investors know what they're buying.
Critics say raising the revenue limit to $1.5 billion lets very large companies avoid disclosure rules meant to protect shareholders.
Critics say increasing fund investor limits from 250 to 600 people makes it harder for regulators to track who is investing.

118-hr-6544.one_liner: Speed up permits and cut fees for nuclear power plants
provisions: Cuts fees that nuclear power companies pay for plant permits
Lets the Energy Department pay some permit fees for nuclear companies
Speeds up permits for nuclear plants built where nuclear plants already operate
Lets nuclear regulators hire staff faster during worker shortages
Creates a program where the government buys power from nuclear plants for many years
Requires faster environmental reviews for nuclear plant applications

supporters: Supporters say cutting permit fees for nuclear companies will help build more clean energy plants faster.
Supporters say speeding up permits for nuclear plants built at existing nuclear sites will reduce delays for clean energy projects.
Supporters say the government buying power from nuclear plants for many years will help companies get loans to build new reactors.
critics: Critics say cutting permit fees means taxpayers subsidize nuclear power companies instead of the companies paying their own costs.
Critics say requiring faster environmental reviews for nuclear plant applications could skip important safety studies.
Critics say the government buying power from nuclear plants for many years will cost taxpayers money to support one energy industry over others.

118-hr-3843.one_liner: Continue grants to states for dental health workers in areas with shortages
provisions: Continues grants to states for dental health programs through 2028
Helps states get more dentists and dental workers in areas that need them
Targets places where people have trouble finding dental care

supporters: Supporters say the grants through 2028 will help states train more dentists in areas where people cannot find dental care.
Supporters say this targets places with dental worker shortages to improve access for families who need dental services.
critics: Critics say continuing these state grants through 2028 will cost taxpayers money that could be used elsewhere.
Critics say states should fund their own dental workforce programs instead of relying on federal grants.

118-hr-4984.one_liner: Give D.C. control of RFK Stadium land for redevelopment
provisions: Moves control of RFK Stadium land from federal parks to D.C.
D.C. gets the land for free to build on
D.C. can build a new stadium, homes, stores, or parks on the site
If D.C. builds homes and stores, at least 30% must be parks and open space
D.C. must provide enough parking for any new buildings

supporters: Supporters say this gives D.C. the RFK Stadium campus for free to build a new stadium or develop homes and stores that create jobs.
Supporters say the 30% parks requirement protects green space if D.C. chooses commercial and residential development on the site.
Supporters say this puts unused federal land under local control where it can be better developed for the community.
critics: Critics say giving D.C. valuable federal land for no cost wastes taxpayer money that could benefit all Americans.
Critics say commercial development near National Park Service lands could damage those protected areas despite the bill's safety rules.
Critics say this takes public land away from federal control and gives it to one city for private development.

118-hr-5375.one_liner: Create a working group with Japan, Australia, and India
provisions: Tells the State Department to create a working group with Japan, Australia, and India
Requires the State Department to give Congress a plan for working with these three countries
The plan must include preparing for the next pandemic
The plan must include developing new technologies together
The plan must include increasing trade and business ties

supporters: Supporters say creating a working group with Japan, Australia, and India would help the US prepare for the next pandemic by sharing information and resources with key allies.
Supporters say developing new technologies together with these three countries would help America compete with China and protect democratic values.
Supporters say increasing trade and business ties with Japan, Australia, and India would create jobs for American workers and open new markets.
critics: Critics say requiring the State Department to create another working group and strategy report adds more paperwork without clear benefits.
Critics say deeper cooperation with Japan, Australia, and India could drag America into their disputes with China and other neighbors.
Critics say the bill does not set any spending limits or timeline for these new cooperation efforts.

118-hr-533.one_liner: Define Tibet more broadly for U.S. policy and direct efforts to counter Chinese disinformation
provisions: Expands the U.S. definition of Tibet to include areas in four Chinese provinces
Directs a U.S. office to counter disinformation from China about Tibet
Declares the Tibet-China conflict unresolved and Tibet's legal status undetermined

supporters: Supporters say this bill recognizes historical Tibet by including Tibetan areas in Qinghai, Sichuan, Gansu, and Yunnan provinces, not just the Tibet Autonomous Region.
Supporters say directing the U.S. Special Coordinator for Tibetan Issues to counter Chinese disinformation will help protect accurate information about Tibet's history.
Supporters say declaring the Tibet-China conflict unresolved reflects that Tibet's legal status has not been settled under international law.
critics: Critics say expanding the U.S. definition of Tibet to include areas in four Chinese provinces could harm diplomatic relations with China.
Critics say directing a U.S. office to counter Chinese statements about Tibet interferes in China's internal affairs.
Critics say declaring Tibet's legal status undetermined could complicate U.S. cooperation with China on trade and security issues.

118-hr-7176.one_liner: Remove rules that limit natural gas exports and imports
provisions: Removes rules that limit importing and exporting natural gas
Stops requiring Energy Department approval for natural gas exports and imports
Makes the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission the only agency that approves natural gas terminals and export facilities
Currently the Energy Department approves exports while FERC approves facilities, but this puts FERC in charge of both
FERC must decide that exports and imports help the public

supporters: Supporters say this streamlines approval by putting FERC in charge of both export permits and terminal construction instead of splitting authority between the Energy Department and FERC.
Supporters say removing Energy Department approval requirements could speed up natural gas export projects and create jobs in the energy industry.
Supporters say this helps American companies compete in global LNG markets by cutting regulatory delays.
critics: Critics say moving export approval from the Energy Department to FERC could weaken oversight of how much natural gas leaves the country.
Critics say removing restrictions on natural gas exports could drive up heating costs for American families who use natural gas in their homes.
Critics say giving FERC control over both export permits and facility construction concentrates too much power in one agency.

118-hr-7511.one_liner: Require detention of non-citizens arrested for theft and let states sue over immigration
provisions: Requires the government to detain non-citizens who are here illegally and have been arrested for break-ins, theft, or shoplifting
Lets states sue the federal government for immigration decisions that cost the state more than $100
Lets states sue when the government releases non-citizens from jail
Lets states sue when the government fails to properly check people trying to enter the country
Lets states sue when the government keeps giving visas to countries that won't take back their own citizens

supporters: Supporters say this keeps communities safe by requiring the government to detain non-citizens who are here illegally and have been arrested for break-ins, theft, or shoplifting.
Supporters say this gives states the power to hold the federal government accountable by letting them sue when immigration decisions cost the state more than $100.

Supporters say this ensures proper security by letting states sue when the government fails to properly check people trying to enter the country or gives visas to countries that won't take back their own citizens.
critics: Critics say this violates due process by requiring detention of people who have only been arrested, not convicted, for crimes like shoplifting.
Critics say this could flood courts with lawsuits since states can sue for any immigration decision that harms them financially by more than $100.
Critics say this creates expensive detention costs by requiring the government to jail people arrested for minor crimes like theft instead of using cheaper alternatives.

118-hr-7102.one_liner: Create an office in the Small Business Administration for Native American businesses
provisions: Creates an office inside the Small Business Administration
The office connects Native American tribes with government business programs
Helps Native Americans get business loans and government contracts
Supports Native Americans who want to start or grow businesses
Works to bring more business to Native American communities

supporters: Supporters say this office would help Native American tribes connect with Small Business Administration programs for business loans and government contracts.
Supporters say the office would increase the number of businesses owned by Native Americans.
Supporters say targeting SBA programs to Native Americans would bring more economic development to tribal communities.
critics: Critics say creating a new office within the Small Business Administration would add to government bureaucracy.
Critics say existing SBA programs already serve Native Americans without needing a separate office.
Critics say the office would cost taxpayer money without proving it works better than current programs.

118-hr-7454.one_liner: Extend FAA programs and airport funding through May 10, 2024
provisions: Keeps FAA drone testing programs running until May 10, 2024
Keeps giving grants for airport projects until May 10, 2024
Keeps collecting taxes on airline tickets and aviation fuel until May 10, 2024
Keeps weather reporting at airports running until May 10, 2024
Lets security agencies stop dangerous drones near key facilities until May 10, 2024

supporters: Supporters say this keeps weather reporting systems running at airports until May 10, 2024, which helps pilots land safely.
Supporters say this continues grants for airport projects that improve safety and reduce noise for nearby communities.
Supporters say this lets security agencies stop dangerous drones near important facilities until May 10, 2024.
critics: Critics say this only fixes the problem until May 10, 2024, creating another funding deadline in two months.
Critics say this continues collecting taxes on airline tickets and aviation fuel without solving long-term funding issues.
Critics say this short extension forces Congress to rush decisions again instead of making a permanent plan.

118-hres-1052.one_liner: Set House rules for voting on two bills
provisions: Creates the debate and voting procedures for a bill changing capital markets rules
Creates the debate and voting procedures for a bill requiring detention of non-citizens charged with theft

supporters: Supporters say the rule allows Congress to vote on capital markets changes that help American businesses compete with other countries.
Supporters say bringing up the detention bill protects communities by keeping non-citizens charged with theft in custody.
Supporters say the debate procedures give lawmakers proper time to discuss economic reforms and public safety measures.
critics: Critics say the capital markets bill could remove rules that protect investors from financial fraud.
Critics say requiring detention of people only charged with theft violates the right to be presumed innocent before trial.
Critics say the rule limits debate time for complex bills that affect millions of Americans' investments and immigration policies.

118-hres-1061.one_liner: Adopt the Senate version of a government funding bill for 2024
provisions: Passes the Senate version of H.R. 4366, which funds government operations for 2024
Makes changes to the Senate amendment before final adoption

supporters: Supporters say this ensures continued funding for government operations through 2024 by advancing the Consolidated Appropriations Act.
Supporters say this allows the House to make necessary changes to the Senate amendment while still moving the spending bill forward.
Supporters say this prevents potential government shutdown by advancing the appropriations process for fiscal year 2024.
critics: Critics say this moves H.R. 4366 forward quickly without extended review of the specific changes made in the Senate amendment.
Critics say this limits House members' time to fully examine the Senate's modifications to the Consolidated Appropriations Act before voting.
Critics say this procedural approach could bypass normal legislative review processes for the 2024 government funding bill.

117-hr-7108.one_liner: Remove Russia and Belarus from favored trade status and expand human rights sanctions
provisions: Removes Russia and Belarus from the list of countries that get lower import taxes
Lets the President raise taxes on Russian and Belarusian products until January 2024
Expands sanctions to cover people who commit serious human rights abuses or corruption
Lets the President freeze assets and ban travel for sanctioned people and their supporters

supporters: Supporters say removing Russia and Belarus from lower import tax rates puts economic pressure on both governments to stop the war in Ukraine, since higher tariffs raise the cost of their exports to the U.S.

Supporters say expanding sanctions to cover 'serious human rights abuses' — a lower bar than the current 'gross violations' standard — means more officials and their financial backers can have assets frozen and travel banned.
Supporters say directing the U.S. Trade Representative to seek Russia's suspension from the World Trade Organization would cut off Russia from global trade rules that protect its exports.
critics: Critics say the President's authority to raise tariffs on Russian and Belarusian goods expires January 1, 2024, which limits how long economic pressure can be applied without new legislation.

Critics say the expanded sanctions definition — covering anyone who 'provides support' for human rights abuses — is broad enough to affect foreign businesses or individuals with indirect ties to sanctioned people, raising due process concerns.

Critics say allowing the President to restore normal trade relations with Russia and Belarus, subject only to a congressional disapproval vote, gives the executive branch too much control over a major trade policy decision.

119-hres-377.one_liner: Set up House votes on renaming the Gulf of Mexico and restricting education funding
provisions: Lets the House vote on changing the name Gulf of Mexico to Gulf of America
Lets the House vote on stopping DHS money to colleges that work with Confucius Institutes

supporters: Supporters say renaming the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America, as H.R. 276 proposes, would better reflect the United States' role as the dominant nation bordering that body of water.

Supporters say H.R. 881 would cut Department of Homeland Security funding to colleges that keep ties with Confucius Institutes, which the FBI has flagged as a source of Chinese government influence on U.S. campuses.
Supporters say bringing both bills to a House vote gives elected members a chance to go on record about national security and national identity issues.
critics: Critics say changing the official U.S. name of the Gulf of Mexico would not change how Mexico or international bodies refer to it, making the rename largely symbolic while costing federal agencies money to update maps and documents.

Critics say tying DHS funding to Confucius Institute relationships could cut resources from colleges that use those programs for Chinese language classes, affecting thousands of students who have no connection to any security concern.
Critics say the rule allowing these two bills to reach the floor bypasses the normal committee review process, reducing the time members have to examine the funding impact on affected institutions.

119-sjres-13.one_liner: Bring back automatic approvals for some bank mergers
provisions: Cancels a Treasury rule from September 2024 that changed bank merger reviews
Brings back automatic approvals for bank mergers that meet certain requirements
Brings back simpler application forms for banks wanting to merge

supporters: Supporters say this would bring back automatic approvals for bank mergers that meet certain requirements, reducing wait times for smaller banks trying to merge.
Supporters say removing the September 2024 OCC rule would restore simpler application forms that community banks relied on to complete merger filings without extra staff or legal costs.

Supporters say the 2024 rule added steps to the expedited review process that were not required by the Bank Merger Act itself, making the OCC's process stricter than what Congress originally approved.
critics: Critics say this resolution would eliminate the OCC's ability to manually review each merger application under the expedited procedure, reducing federal oversight of bank consolidation.

Critics say restoring automatic approvals removes a checkpoint the OCC added in September 2024 specifically to evaluate whether a merger would reduce competition or harm consumers before it is approved.

Critics say canceling the 2024 rule would allow banks to bypass the expanded review process the OCC put in place to assess financial stability risks in merger applications, returning oversight to a lighter standard.

119-hres-122.one_liner: Allow Congress to overturn multiple last-minute rules in a single vote
provisions: Changes the law to let Congress vote on overturning multiple rules at once
Applies to rules made in the final months before a new president takes office
Makes it faster for Congress to cancel government rules

supporters: Supporters say allowing Congress to vote on multiple rules at once makes it faster to cancel last-minute rules passed in the final months before a new president takes office.
Supporters say the current process forces Congress to vote on each rule one at a time, which supporters say lets too many late-term rules stay in place due to limited floor time.
Supporters say this change gives elected lawmakers more power to review and block regulatory actions made by outgoing administrations.
critics: Critics say voting on multiple rules at once makes it harder for lawmakers to carefully review each rule on its own merits before casting a vote.

Critics say the bill targets rules made in the final months of an administration, which critics say could cancel health, safety, or environmental protections that went through a full public comment process.
Critics say speeding up the disapproval process reduces debate time and may pressure lawmakers to vote against rules they have not fully studied.

117-hr-8404.one_liner: Require recognition of same-sex and interracial marriages
provisions: Changes federal law to recognize any marriage that is valid in any state
Requires all states to recognize same-sex and interracial marriages from other states
Lets the Justice Department sue states that refuse to recognize these marriages
Lets people sue in court if their marriage is not recognized

supporters: Supporters say the bill protects same-sex and interracial couples by writing marriage recognition into federal law, so it cannot be undone without an act of Congress.
Supporters say requiring all states to recognize marriages from other states means a couple legally married in one state will not lose their marriage rights if they move to another state.
Supporters say giving the Justice Department the power to sue states — and letting married couples sue in court — creates real tools to enforce these protections.
critics: Critics say the bill goes beyond what is needed because the Supreme Court already ruled that states must recognize same-sex marriages, making a new federal law unnecessary.

Critics say the bill does not include strong protections for religious organizations, and some faith-based groups worry they could be sued for not recognizing marriages that conflict with their beliefs.
Critics say giving individuals the right to sue in court over marriage recognition could lead to a wave of lawsuits against state and local officials.

117-s-5355.one_liner: Give extra money to federal agencies for disaster relief in 2023
provisions: Gives extra money to federal departments and agencies to respond to natural disasters in 2023
Covers disasters like hurricanes, tornadoes, wildfires, and flooding
Adds to the regular funding these agencies already get

supporters: Supporters say the bill adds money on top of what federal agencies already have, letting them respond faster when disasters like hurricanes or wildfires hit in 2023 without waiting for new funding to be approved.

Supporters say covering multiple disaster types — hurricanes, tornadoes, wildfires, and flooding — in one bill means agencies can act across different regions without needing separate votes for each event.
Supporters say giving supplemental funds to several departments at once lets the federal government coordinate a wider response than any single agency could handle alone.
critics: Critics say the bill does not include a specific dollar amount, making it hard to know if the funding is enough to cover the scale of disasters that hit in 2023.
Critics say the summary names no specific regions or affected communities, so there is no way to confirm that the hardest-hit areas will actually receive help.
Critics say the bill adds money to existing programs but does not set any rules for how agencies must report back on where the money went or how it was used.

117-sconres-14.one_liner: Set the federal budget and spending limits for 2022 through 2031
provisions: Sets government spending and revenue targets for the years 2022 through 2031
Lets certain committees write laws that increase the deficit by set amounts for each committee
Requires two committees to write laws that cut the deficit by at least $1 billion
Creates reserve funds that allow budget changes for infrastructure and tax laws that don't raise taxes on people making under $400,000
Sets up rules for how Congress handles emergency spending and advance funding

supporters: Supporters say the spending instructions allow a majority in Congress to pass a budget covering 2022 through 2031 without being stopped by a procedural block from a minority of senators, making it easier to move spending priorities forward.
Supporters say the reserve funds are designed to protect people making under $400,000 from tax increases while still giving Congress room to fund infrastructure.

Supporters say the resolution requires the Senate Finance Committee and the House Ways and Means Committee to write laws that cut the deficit by at least $1 billion over the 2022 through 2031 period, building a deficit-reduction requirement directly into the budget framework.
critics: Critics say the spending instructions allow multiple committees to each increase the deficit by set amounts, which will grow total government debt over the 2022 through 2031 period.
Critics say the required $1 billion in deficit cuts is small relative to the total deficit increases the resolution permits across the other committees.
Critics say the reserve funds that allow budget changes for infrastructure and other bills could be used to get around the spending limits set elsewhere in the resolution.

118-hconres-57.one_liner: Declare that Israel is not a racist or apartheid state
provisions: States that Israel is not a racist or apartheid state
Rejects all forms of antisemitism and xenophobia
Says the United States will always be a partner with Israel

supporters: Supporters say the resolution's statement that Israel is not an apartheid state pushes back against a label used by groups like Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch, which they argue misrepresents how Israeli law applies to its Arab citizens.
Supporters say the provision rejecting antisemitism and xenophobia gives Congress a formal record it can point to when debating future legislation or foreign aid packages.

Supporters say affirming that the U.S. will always be a partner with Israel reinforces existing agreements, including the 10-year, $38 billion Memorandum of Understanding on defense assistance signed in 2016.
critics: Critics say the provision declaring Israel is not a racist or apartheid state contradicts findings by Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch, which documented separate legal systems applied to Jewish and Palestinian residents in the West Bank.

Critics say the resolution's rejection of antisemitism does not address discrimination faced by Arab citizens of Israel, who make up about 20 percent of the population and are not mentioned in the text.
Critics say the resolution includes no funding, enforcement mechanisms, or policy directives that would change U.S. government action toward Israel or the region.

117-sconres-43.one_liner: Set federal spending and revenue targets for 2023 through 2032
provisions: Sets spending limits for defense, healthcare, education and other government programs for 10 years
Establishes how much money the government plans to collect in taxes through 2032
Gives Congress a plan to follow when writing individual spending bills

supporters: Supporters say the 10-year spending plan gives Congress a clear framework to follow when writing individual spending bills each year, reducing last-minute budget fights.
Supporters say setting tax collection targets through 2032 helps the government plan ahead and avoid surprise shortfalls in funding for defense, healthcare, and education.
Supporters say locking in spending limits for 10 years gives businesses and families more certainty about what government programs will exist in the future.
critics: Critics say a 10-year budget plan made today cannot predict future needs, meaning the spending limits on healthcare and defense could be too low or too high by 2032.
Critics say the resolution sets spending levels but does not specify exact dollar amounts for programs, leaving too much room for Congress to cut education or healthcare later.
Critics say budget resolutions like this one are not signed by the President and are not laws, so the spending limits are not legally binding and may be ignored.

118-hconres-9.one_liner: Oppose socialism and socialist policies in the United States
provisions: Says Congress is against socialism
Says Congress opposes putting socialist policies in place

supporters: Supporters say the resolution puts Congress on record against socialism, making the government's position clear to citizens and other countries.
Supporters say opposing socialist policies, as the resolution states, protects private ownership and free markets from government takeover.
critics: Critics say the resolution does not define what counts as a 'socialist policy,' which could be used to attack programs like Social Security or Medicare that millions of Americans rely on.
Critics say a concurrent resolution has no legal force and changes no laws, making it a symbolic act that does not address any real problem facing Americans.

118-hr-82.one_liner: Restore full Social Security benefits for people with government pensions
provisions: Restores full Social Security benefits for spouses, widows, and widowers who also get government pensions
Restores full Social Security benefits for people who get pensions from jobs that did not pay Social Security taxes
Takes effect for benefits paid after December 2023

supporters: Supporters say the bill restores full Social Security benefits to spouses, widows, and widowers who also receive government pensions, a group that includes many retired teachers and public workers who lost part of their earned benefits under the Government Pension Offset.

Supporters say the Windfall Elimination Provision cut Social Security payments for about 2 million people who worked in jobs that did not withhold Social Security taxes, and this bill would give them back the full amount they were promised.
Supporters say the changes take effect for benefits paid after December 2023, meaning affected retirees and survivors would see higher monthly checks without having to wait years for relief.
critics: Critics say the bill adds an estimated $196 billion to federal costs over 10 years, which could speed up the date when the Social Security trust fund runs out of money.

Critics say the Government Pension Offset and Windfall Elimination Provision were put in place to stop people from collecting both a full government pension and full Social Security at the same time, and removing them allows some workers to receive more than they paid into the system.
Critics say the bill does not include a way to pay for the added costs, which puts more pressure on a Social Security program that already faces funding shortfalls in the coming years.

118-hr-9747.one_liner: Keep the government funded and extend programs through December 2024
provisions: Keeps the government funded at 2024 spending levels until December 20, 2024
Prevents a government shutdown that would start October 1, 2024
Gives the Secret Service extra money to protect presidential candidates
Extends flood insurance so people can still buy policies
Extends cash help for poor families through TANF
Extends the Food for Peace program that sends food to other countries

supporters: Supporters say the bill prevents a government shutdown that would start October 1, 2024, keeping federal workers paid and agencies open through December 20, 2024.
Supporters say extending the National Flood Insurance Program means families in flood-prone areas can still buy coverage during hurricane season.
Supporters say the extra Secret Service funding protects presidential candidates during the 2024 campaign and major security events.
critics: Critics say funding the government through short-term patches instead of a full budget leaves agencies unable to plan spending past December 20, 2024.
Critics say the bill keeps spending at 2024 levels, which some say does not address rising costs that federal programs face in 2025.
Critics say extending programs like Food for Peace and Hong Kong sanctions in the same bill as government funding mixes separate policy issues into one vote.

118-hres-1009.one_liner: Remove limits on buying and selling natural gas with other countries
provisions: Cancels rules that limit selling natural gas to other countries
Cancels rules that limit buying natural gas from other countries

supporters: Supporters say repealing the rules that block natural gas exports would let U.S. producers sell to any country without first getting government approval, removing a step that currently delays or blocks export deals.

Supporters say removing the restrictions on natural gas imports would allow U.S. buyers to purchase gas from any foreign supplier, giving utilities and manufacturers more options to find lower-cost supply.
Supporters say U.S. natural gas producers compete with countries that face no such export limits, and repealing these restrictions would put American companies on equal footing in global markets.
critics: Critics say repealing the export restrictions removes the federal review process that currently checks whether sending natural gas abroad would reduce domestic supply available to U.S. households and businesses.

Critics say the bill ends the government's authority to approve or deny natural gas import deals on a case-by-case basis, eliminating a check that screens whether foreign suppliers could create supply risks if those sources were disrupted.

Critics say removing both the export and import approval rules at the same time takes away all federal oversight of cross-border natural gas trade, with no remaining process to assess the effect on domestic energy prices.

118-hjres-109.one_liner: Cancel an SEC rule requiring companies to report how they handle customer cryptocurrency
provisions: Cancels an SEC rule from March 2022 that set accounting requirements for companies holding customer cryptocurrency
Removes requirements for crypto companies to disclose how they safeguard customer funds

supporters: Supporters say the March 2022 rule required companies that store crypto for customers to list that crypto as a debt in their financial records, which made it harder for banks to offer these services to customers.

Supporters say the SEC issued this rule without going through the required federal process where the public can send in written comments before a rule takes effect, so Congress has the right to cancel it.
Supporters say removing this rule would allow more banks to store crypto for customers, giving people more options for where to keep their digital assets.
critics: Critics say this rule required companies holding crypto for customers to clearly show those holdings in their financial records, and they argue that without it, customers have no way to check whether a company can safely protect their crypto.
Critics say that in 2022, several large crypto platforms shut down and customers lost access to their funds, and they argue this rule's reporting requirements help protect against similar losses.
Critics say removing the reporting requirement lets companies that store crypto for customers hide financial risks that investors and customers have a right to know about.

118-hr-839.one_liner: Require U.S. officials to push China to be more open about currency policies
provisions: Requires U.S. officials to push China to share more information about how it handles its currency
Focuses on how China sets currency values and whether Chinese banks or government companies interfere
Also focuses on whether China answers questions from international financial groups
These requirements last for 7 years unless China becomes more transparent

supporters: Supporters say the bill would push China to share more information about how its banks and government-owned companies affect currency values, which U.S. businesses say makes it hard to compete on price.
Supporters say requiring this transparency for 7 years gives enough time to see if China changes its behavior before the rules expire.
Supporters say having the U.S. use its vote at the IMF to demand answers from China puts pressure on China through an international body, not just the U.S. alone.
critics: Critics say the bill only directs U.S. officials to advocate at the IMF but does not require China to do anything, so it may not produce real changes in how China handles its currency.
Critics say China has refused IMF information requests before, and a 7-year advocacy requirement through one U.S. vote at the IMF is unlikely to change that pattern.
Critics say the bill does not set any penalty or consequence if China continues to deny information requests from the IMF about its exchange rate policies and holdings.

118-hr-1023.one_liner: Cancel the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund
provisions: Ends a fund that gives money to states and nonprofit groups
The money helps communities do projects that reduce greenhouse gas emissions
States and nonprofits will no longer get this federal money and technical help

supporters: Supporters say repealing the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund removes a federal program that sent money to states and nonprofit groups, and that ending it reduces government spending.
Supporters say the fund directed federal dollars to specific nonprofit organizations, and removing it stops what they call picking winners among private groups using taxpayer money.
critics: Critics say ending the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund cuts off financial and technical help that states and nonprofits relied on to run local projects that reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
Critics say communities — especially those that depended on this federal assistance — will lose access to both the money and the technical support needed to carry out emission-reduction work.

119-hconres-58.one_liner: Denounce socialism and oppose socialist policies in the United States
provisions: States that Congress denounces socialism
States that Congress opposes putting socialist policies in place in the United States

supporters: Supporters say the provision formally stating that 'Congress denounces socialism' puts the full weight of the U.S. legislature on record against systems where the government owns or controls industries and private property.

Supporters say the provision opposing 'socialist policies in the United States' sends a signal to lawmakers that proposals expanding government control over businesses, housing, or healthcare will face resistance in Congress.
critics: Critics say the resolution never defines 'socialism,' so the provision opposing 'socialist policies' could later be used to argue against existing programs like Social Security, Medicare, or public education.

Critics say a concurrent resolution has no legal force, meaning the two provisions — denouncing socialism and opposing socialist policies — change no laws, shift no funding, and bind no future Congress.

119-hres-707.one_liner: Set up House votes on DC crime bills and energy project bills
provisions: Sets up votes on bills changing how DC handles juvenile crime and sentencing
Sets up votes on bills setting police car chase rules in DC and trying minors as adults
Sets up votes on bills ending a DC court appointment commission
Sets up votes on bills speeding up approvals for power plants and transmission lines
Sets up votes on bills recreating a coal council and easing cross-border energy approvals

supporters: Supporters say this rule allows a vote on H.R. 5140, which would let courts try minors as young as 14 as adults for certain crimes in DC, and on H.R. 4922, which limits youth offender status to those 18 and under, giving judges fewer options to reduce sentences for older teens.

Supporters say the rule opens floor votes on H.R. 1047 and H.R. 3062, which would speed up federal approvals for power plants and cross-border oil, gas, and electricity lines — steps they say cut years off project timelines.

Supporters say bundling DC crime bills with energy bills into one rule lets Congress move faster on multiple priorities, including recreating the National Coal Council under H.R. 3015 to advise the Energy Secretary on coal industry policy.
critics: Critics say the rule advances H.R. 4922 and H.R. 5125, which would strip the DC Council of power to change criminal sentences and end the DC Judicial Nomination Commission — reducing local control over DC's own courts and laws.

Critics say the rule sets up a vote on H.R. 5140, which lowers the age for adult criminal trials in DC to 14, a change that could expose more young teenagers to longer sentences typically reserved for adults.

Critics say combining DC governance changes with energy deregulation bills — including H.R. 3062, which eases cross-border energy facility approvals — limits debate time on each issue and prevents lawmakers from voting on them separately.

118-sjres-42.one_liner: Cancel a rule treating gender identity discrimination as sex discrimination in food programs
provisions: Cancels a 2022 government rule about discrimination complaints in food programs
The rule said discrimination based on gender identity and sexual orientation counts as sex discrimination
The rule told states to handle these complaints the same as sex discrimination complaints
Food programs would return to their previous way of handling gender identity discrimination complaints

supporters: Supporters say the food agency did not follow required steps — a federal law gives Congress the power to cancel agency rules that were not sent to Congress first, and the 2022 rule skipped this step before taking effect.

Supporters say the 2020 Supreme Court ruling was about job discrimination in the workplace, not food assistance programs, so the food agency went beyond what the court decided when it applied that ruling to food programs.
critics: Critics say canceling this rule removes the process that lets people in food assistance programs file complaints if they face discrimination based on gender identity or sexual orientation.

Critics say state agencies would lose the guidance the 2022 rule gave them on how to handle these complaints, and food programs would return to an earlier process that did not include gender identity or sexual orientation.

118-hconres-86.one_liner: Expresses Congress's opposition to carbon taxes
provisions: States Congress's view that carbon taxes would hurt the economy
Says carbon taxes are not in the country's best interest
Declares carbon taxes would be bad for families and businesses

supporters: Supporters say Congress should go on record that a carbon tax would hurt families and businesses, since the resolution directly states it is 'not in the best interest of the country.'
Supporters say this resolution signals to federal agencies that Congress opposes any carbon pricing policy that could raise energy costs for U.S. households and companies.
Supporters say the resolution protects industries like manufacturing and energy production, which would face higher operating costs under a carbon tax.
critics: Critics say this resolution does not change any law or spending — it only states an opinion, so it has no real effect on carbon tax policy.
Critics say blocking a carbon price leaves out a tool that some economists argue could reduce emissions while generating revenue that could be returned to families.
Critics say the resolution labels carbon taxes harmful to 'families and businesses' without citing any specific cost estimates or economic data to support that claim.

118-hr-2560.one_liner: Create a grant program for sea turtle rescue
provisions: Creates a grant program run by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration
Gives money to groups that rescue sea turtles that get stranded
Helps coordinate quick response when sea turtles need help

supporters: Supporters say the bill would create a grant program run by NOAA that gives money to local groups that rescue sea turtles when they get stranded, helping those groups respond faster.
Supporters say having NOAA run the program would help rescue groups across all U.S. coastal states work together so they can reach stranded sea turtles more quickly.
critics: Critics say the bill does not list a specific dollar amount for the grant program, making it hard to know what it would cost or whether the funding would reach rescue groups in every coastal state.
Critics say NOAA already runs programs that protect sea turtles under the Endangered Species Act, and adding a new grant program could repeat work that is already being done with current resources.

118-hr-3033.one_liner: Make Iran sanctions permanent by removing their expiration date
provisions: Removes the expiration date from a 1996 law that punishes people who do business with Iran
Makes it permanent that the President must punish companies that work with Iran's oil and gas industry
Makes it permanent that the President must punish anyone who helps Iran get chemical, biological, or nuclear weapons

supporters: Supporters say removing the expiration date means the President can no longer let sanctions on Iran's oil and gas industry lapse, closing a gap that could give Iran access to billions in energy revenue.

Supporters say making the sanctions permanent sends a clear signal to companies worldwide that doing business with Iran's energy sector will result in punishment, reducing the chance that foreign firms help fund Iran's government.
Supporters say permanent sanctions on anyone who helps Iran get chemical, biological, or nuclear weapons removes the risk that a future Congress could accidentally let those penalties expire.
critics: Critics say locking in sanctions with no end date removes the President's ability to lift pressure on Iran as a bargaining tool in future nuclear negotiations.
Critics say permanent sanctions on Iran's energy sector can hurt companies in allied countries that trade with Iran, straining relationships with U.S. partners who prefer diplomatic options.
Critics say taking away the sunset clause means Congress loses a regular chance to review whether the 1996 law is still working, making it harder to update the policy if conditions change.

118-hr-1836.one_liner: Ban Chinese logistics platforms at ports and strengthen federal shipping regulation
provisions: Stops port authorities from using LOGINK and other Chinese government shipping software
Lets federal shipping regulators label ships from countries like China as controlled carriers that must charge fair rates
Requires federal shipping regulators to investigate complaints about shipping exchanges
Creates new data standards so shipping companies and ports can share supply chain information
Sets standards for how shipping exchanges publish their price information
Creates a committee to advise regulators on making shipping more competitive

supporters: Supporters say banning LOGINK and similar Chinese government software from U.S. ports will stop the Chinese government from accessing American shipping data, which could be used to track cargo movements and supply chains.

Supporters say giving the Federal Maritime Commission the power to label ships from countries like China as controlled carriers will force those ships to charge fair market rates, making it harder for state-backed companies to undercut U.S. and allied shipping businesses.

Supporters say requiring the commission to investigate complaints about shipping exchanges and set price index standards will give businesses a way to report unfair pricing and get clearer information when booking cargo transport.
critics: Critics say the bill does not include funding to help port authorities pay for replacing LOGINK systems, which could place the cost of new software on ports and terminal operators.

Critics say expanding the definition of controlled carriers to include ships from any country labeled anticompetitive gives regulators broad power that could slow trade with multiple countries, not just China.

Critics say creating new data-sharing standards and a new advisory committee adds federal requirements on shipping companies and ports without a clear timeline or budget for putting those rules into effect.

118-hr-1121.one_liner: Stop the President from banning fracking without Congress approval
provisions: Stops the President from banning fracking unless Congress agrees
Says states should keep control over fracking rules on state and private land

supporters: Supporters say the bill stops the President from banning fracking without a vote in Congress, keeping that power with elected lawmakers.
Supporters say keeping fracking rules at the state level lets states like Texas and Pennsylvania set rules that fit their local land and water conditions.
Supporters say blocking a federal fracking moratorium protects oil and gas jobs in states where fracking is a major part of the economy.
critics: Critics say the bill takes away a tool the President could use to quickly stop fracking if it causes harm to drinking water or public health.
Critics say letting states control fracking rules on private and state land means some states may set weaker protections, leaving nearby communities with less safety.
Critics say Congress should not pass a law limiting presidential action before any moratorium has even been proposed.

118-hr-1752.one_liner: Create grants for high-speed internet projects in underserved areas
provisions: Creates grants from the Commerce Department for high-speed internet projects
Lets companies working with government apply for money to build or expand internet service
Covers planning, training, buying land, and building internet equipment
Requires grants to go to different areas including places with poor internet service
Makes government partners or nonprofits own property bought with grant money
Lets Commerce help pay part of project costs

supporters: Supporters say the bill would bring high-speed internet to underserved rural areas by requiring Commerce to spread grants across different regions, including places with poor internet access.
Supporters say allowing private companies to partner with governments to apply for grants will attract more resources and expertise to build internet infrastructure faster.
Supporters say covering planning, training, and land costs means communities can get help at every stage of a broadband project, not just construction.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set a funding amount, leaving it unclear how many communities will actually receive grants or how far the money will go.
Critics say requiring government partners or nonprofits to hold title to all property bought with grant funds could discourage private companies from joining public-private partnerships.
Critics say without strict rules on how Commerce defines 'underserved markets,' grants may not reach the rural areas that need internet access most.

118-hr-5917.one_liner: Extend sanctions power against groups using human shields through 2030
provisions: Extends the president's power to punish foreign groups that use human shields until 2030
Requires the president to punish Palestine Islamic Jihad members who use human shields
Requires the president to check if people Congress asks about should face punishment and report back
Requires the Defense Department to report to Congress about how Hamas, Hezbollah, and Palestine Islamic Jihad use human shields

supporters: Supporters say the bill closes a gap in current law by making sanctions mandatory for Palestine Islamic Jihad members who use human shields, putting PIJ on the same level as Hamas and Hezbollah members who already face required sanctions.
Supporters say extending the president's sanction authority through 2030 gives the U.S. a longer-term tool to pressure foreign groups that place civilians in danger during conflict.
Supporters say requiring the Defense Department to report to Congress on how Hamas, Hezbollah, and Palestine Islamic Jihad use human shields creates a public record that can inform future policy.
critics: Critics say the bill focuses only on Palestine Islamic Jihad, Hamas, and Hezbollah, leaving out other foreign groups that may also use human shields and could avoid sanctions under this law.
Critics say requiring the president to review and report back on every person Congress requests for sanctions review could slow down the process and create a backlog that delays action.
Critics say the bill does not include any new funding or enforcement mechanism, meaning the added mandatory sanctions on PIJ members may be difficult to carry out in practice.

118-hr-5826.one_liner: Block sanctioned UN representatives from entering the US and require Iran reports
provisions: Lets the President stop certain UN representatives from entering the US if they are sanctioned for terrorism
Requires a report about $6 billion moved from South Korea to Qatar in August 2023
Requires a report on Americans taken hostage by Iran in the last 10 years
Requires a report on frozen Iranian money
Requires a report on whether Americans face danger traveling to Iran
Requires a plan to stop enemies from taking American hostages

supporters: Supporters say the bill would stop the President from having to let sanctioned terrorism-linked UN representatives into the country, closing a gap in current law that only covers people directly targeting the US or its allies.
Supporters say requiring a report on the $6 billion moved from South Korea to Qatar in August 2023 would give Congress facts it needs to check whether that money helped Iran take Americans hostage.
Supporters say the required plan to deter hostage-taking would push the government to act before more Americans are wrongfully held in Iran, rather than only responding after it happens.
critics: Critics say the bill gives the President new power to block UN representatives based on sanction lists that were not designed with diplomatic access in mind, which could disrupt US participation in the UN.
Critics say the required reports do not come with any enforcement rules or deadlines for action, so Congress would get information about hostages and frozen assets but have no new tools to act on it.
Critics say focusing reports only on Iran and the $6 billion Qatar transfer leaves out other countries where Americans have been wrongfully detained, making the oversight one-sided.

118-hr-4723.one_liner: Impose sanctions on foreign people who threaten peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina
provisions: Blocks visas and freezes assets of foreign people who threaten Bosnia and Herzegovina
Requires the President to sanction people involved in corruption in Bosnia and Herzegovina
Lets Treasury restrict foreign banks that do business with sanctioned people
Makes permanent the sanctions from two presidential orders about the Balkans

supporters: Supporters say the bill blocks visas and freezes the assets of people who undermine the Dayton Peace Agreement, which ended the Bosnian War and forms the basis of Bosnia and Herzegovina's government.

Supporters say requiring the President to sanction people involved in corruption in Bosnia and Herzegovina gives the U.S. a legal tool to hold specific individuals and groups accountable, rather than relying on presidential orders that can be reversed.
Supporters say making Executive Orders 13219 and 14033 permanent law means Congress, not just the President, controls when Western Balkans sanctions can be lifted.
critics: Critics say the bill lets Treasury restrict any foreign bank that 'knowingly' conducts a 'significant transaction' with a sanctioned person, but does not define what dollar amount or type of transaction counts as significant.

Critics say the bill gives the President broad power to sanction anyone found to 'threaten the peace, stability, or democracy' of Bosnia and Herzegovina, without setting clear limits on who meets that standard.
Critics say locking in the two executive orders as permanent law removes the President's flexibility to ease sanctions if conditions in the Western Balkans improve over time.

118-hr-3250.one_liner: Name the Strong Museum in Rochester as the National Museum of Play
provisions: Names the Margaret Woodbury Strong Museum in Rochester as the National Museum of Play
Gives the museum official federal recognition under this title
Makes this Rochester museum the official national museum representing play

supporters: Supporters say giving the Margaret Woodbury Strong Museum in Rochester, NY the official federal title of National Museum of Play would make it easier for families, schools, and researchers across the country to find a central place focused on play.
Supporters say federal recognition as the National Museum of Play could help the Rochester museum attract more national partnerships, visitors, and attention to its work.
Supporters say having one officially recognized national museum for play gives the subject a permanent home in the public record, the same way other topics have dedicated national museums.
critics: Critics say naming a single museum in Rochester, NY as the official National Museum of Play through federal recognition leaves out other museums and organizations around the country that also focus on play and child development.
Critics say the federal title of National Museum of Play attached to a private Rochester institution may cause confusion about whether the U.S. government funds or has oversight over the museum.
Critics say designating the Margaret Woodbury Strong Museum with a national title sets a pattern where Congress picks one local institution to represent an entire subject for the whole country.

118-hr-4681.one_liner: Sanction foreign people who make, sell, or profit from captagon stimulant drugs
provisions: Sanctions foreign people who make, sell or deal captagon stimulant drugs
Sanctions foreign people who knowingly receive money or property from captagon dealing
Freezes sanctioned people's money and property in the US
Bans sanctioned people from getting US visas or entering the country
Cancels existing US visas for sanctioned people
Requires the President to report whether Syrian and Hezbollah leaders qualify for sanctions

supporters: Supporters say the bill targets foreign drug dealers by freezing their U.S. assets and blocking their ability to get visas or enter the country, cutting off their access to American financial and travel systems.

Supporters say requiring the President to report on whether Syrian and Hezbollah leaders qualify for sanctions holds specific foreign governments and armed groups accountable for captagon trafficking.
Supporters say sanctioning people who knowingly receive money or property from captagon dealing closes a loophole that lets financial backers profit without directly selling drugs.
critics: Critics say the bill gives the President broad power to sanction foreign persons based on a determination standard that lacks clear court oversight or appeal process for those who are wrongly targeted.
Critics say focusing sanctions on individuals may not disrupt captagon supply chains if production networks in Syria and elsewhere simply shift to new people who are not yet designated.
Critics say the bill does not include funding or staffing for the agencies that would have to identify, investigate, and track captagon traffickers across multiple countries.

118-hr-6009.one_liner: Cancel a proposed rule about oil and gas leasing on public lands
provisions: Cancels a proposed rule that would change how companies lease public land for oil and gas drilling
Stops changes that were part of climate and infrastructure laws passed in 2021 and 2022
Keeps current oil and gas leasing rules in place

supporters: Supporters say the bill keeps current oil and gas leasing rules in place on public lands, which they argue protects energy companies from new costs and delays tied to the proposed rule changes.

Supporters say stopping the rule blocks requirements added to carry out the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022, which raised royalty rates and bonding requirements for oil and gas drillers on federal land.
Supporters say the bill protects jobs in the oil and gas industry by preventing rule changes that would make it harder or more expensive to lease public land for drilling.
critics: Critics say the bill cancels a rule designed to carry out laws passed by Congress — the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 and the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act of 2021 — which they say undermines those laws.

Critics say blocking the rule keeps in place older leasing terms that charge lower royalty rates to oil and gas companies drilling on land owned by the public, reducing money that would go to the federal government.
Critics say the proposed rule included updates to protect public lands from drilling damage, and canceling it removes those protections for communities near federal oil and gas operations.

118-hr-5921.one_liner: Stop U.S. banks and government agencies from financing trade with Iran
provisions: Stops U.S. banks from handling money for trade with Iran
Allows trade in food, medicine, and farm products for Iranian civilians
Tells U.S. officials to oppose international loans to Iran
Stops a U.S. government trade bank from financing Iran deals
Lasts 10 years or until Iran stops supporting terrorism

supporters: Supporters say the bill cuts off U.S. banks from handling any money tied to Iran trade for up to 10 years, which they argue reduces funds available to Iran's government while still allowing food, medicine, and farm products to reach Iranian civilians.
Supporters say requiring U.S. officials to oppose IMF loans and block Iran from exchanging its Special Drawing Rights adds international financial pressure on top of the U.S. bank restrictions.
Supporters say giving the Export-Import Bank a clear legal ban on financing Iran deals removes any ambiguity about whether U.S. government-backed trade financing can reach Iran.
critics: Critics say blocking U.S. banks from all Iran-related transactions for up to 10 years could limit the President's ability to use financial access as a tool in diplomacy, since relief only comes after a formal certification to Congress.

Critics say opposing Iran's access to IMF Special Drawing Rights — which are reserve assets held by member countries — could reduce resources available to ordinary Iranian civilians, not just the government.

Critics say the carve-out for food, medicine, and farm products still leaves U.S. companies uncertain about what transactions are allowed, since banks must avoid any financing tied to Iran even for permitted goods.

118-hr-6245.one_liner: Close bank accounts of Iranian leaders
provisions: The President must report how much money Iranian leaders have in banks
U.S. banks must close accounts belonging to Iranian leaders
The Treasury must ask foreign banks to close these accounts too
Intelligence work, UN duties, and humanitarian aid are not affected

supporters: Supporters say requiring the President to report on Iranian leaders' bank accounts in both U.S. and foreign banks would make it harder for those leaders to hide or move money.
Supporters say forcing U.S. banks to close accounts held by Iranian leaders cuts off a direct financial lifeline, and asking foreign banks to do the same adds more pressure.
Supporters say the exemptions for intelligence work, UN duties, and humanitarian aid mean the bill targets leaders specifically without blocking important government functions.
critics: Critics say the bill does not name which Iranian leaders are covered or set a dollar threshold, which could make it hard to enforce or lead to legal disputes over who qualifies.
Critics say asking foreign banks to close accounts through the Treasury may not work, since foreign governments are not required to follow U.S. requests and may refuse.
Critics say the bill could push Iranian leaders to move money into banks outside U.S. reach, making the funds harder to track rather than easier.

118-hr-5923.one_liner: Block U.S. banks from working with Chinese banks that buy Iranian oil
provisions: Requires the President to check which Chinese banks buy oil from Iran
Stops U.S. banks from opening accounts with Chinese banks that buy Iranian oil
Stops U.S. banks from keeping accounts with Chinese banks that buy Iranian oil

supporters: Supporters say requiring the President to check which Chinese banks buy Iranian oil will help enforce existing U.S. sanctions on Iran by tracking who is still doing business with them.
Supporters say cutting off U.S. bank accounts with Chinese financial institutions that buy Iranian oil gives the U.S. a direct way to pressure China to stop funding Iran's oil sales.
Supporters say this bill closes a gap where Chinese banks could keep helping Iran sell oil while still having access to the U.S. financial system.
critics: Critics say blocking U.S. banks from maintaining accounts with Chinese financial institutions could hurt American businesses that rely on those banks for trade and payments unrelated to Iran.
Critics say the bill does not set a dollar threshold or minimum amount of Iranian oil purchased before a Chinese bank faces penalties, which could pull in banks with small or indirect exposure.
Critics say cutting off large Chinese financial institutions from U.S. accounts could push more global oil trade away from the U.S. dollar and toward other currencies.

118-hr-6015.one_liner: Require new rules for humanitarian aid exemptions to Iran
provisions: Iran faces sanctions that block most business with the U.S., but medicine and food are allowed
Requires the President to write new rules making sure these exemptions do not help sanctioned people
Makes sure the exemptions do not support terrorism
Prevents the exemptions from helping Iran build weapons of mass destruction
Tells the U.S. person at the World Bank to oppose loans to Iran

supporters: Supporters say the bill closes a gap in current law by requiring the President to write new rules making sure that medicine and food exemptions cannot be used by people who are already on the U.S. sanctions list.
Supporters say the bill protects against terrorism by requiring that the same humanitarian exemptions cannot be used to fund groups that carry out international attacks.

Supporters say directing the U.S. representative at the World Bank to oppose loans to Iran keeps financial pressure on Iran's government without changing access to food or medicine for ordinary people.
