Critics say the 'least restrictive means' rule could force the government to use weaker measures even when a broader entry block is needed to fully address a security threat.

Critics say letting people inside the U.S. sue in federal court over entry restrictions could pull national security decisions into long legal battles that delay or block the government from protecting the country.

117-hr-1374.one_liner: Give states federal money and help to build energy emergency plans
provisions: The federal government can give money to states to create or update plans for keeping their energy systems running during a crisis.
Each state plan must look at the risks to its energy systems, including physical attacks and hacking.
State plans must include steps to lower those risks and keep power and fuel running if something goes wrong.
States can ask the Department of Energy for advice and technical help when building or updating their plan.

supporters: Supporters say the bill helps states build plans that cover both physical attacks and hacking threats to power and fuel systems, which the federal government currently does not require.

Supporters say states can ask the Department of Energy for technical help when writing or updating their energy security plans, giving smaller states access to expert guidance they may not have on their own.
Supporters say requiring each state plan to include steps to keep power and fuel running during a crisis could reduce damage from future outages like the 2021 Texas winter storm.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set a funding amount, so states have no guarantee they will receive enough money to actually build or update their energy security plans.
Critics say the bill lets states ask for help but does not require the Department of Energy to provide it, meaning federal assistance is optional and may not reach the states that need it most.
Critics say the bill does not set a deadline for states to complete their plans, so there is no guarantee any state will act on the new requirements.

117-hr-1443.one_liner: Require banks to report credit data for LGBTQ-owned businesses to federal regulators
provisions: Banks must collect and send data about credit applications from businesses owned by LGBTQ people to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.
This data is used to check whether LGBTQ-owned businesses are being treated fairly when they apply for loans.
Right now, banks already report this same data for businesses owned by women, minorities, and small business owners.
This bill adds LGBTQ-owned businesses to that list.

supporters: Supporters say that adding LGBTQ-owned businesses to the credit reporting list — alongside women-owned, minority-owned, and small businesses — would let the CFPB check whether banks are denying loans to LGBTQ business owners at higher rates.
Supporters say that because banks already collect this type of data for other groups, the cost and process of adding LGBTQ-owned businesses to the reporting requirement would be small.
Supporters say the CFPB could use this data to enforce fair lending laws if the numbers show LGBTQ-owned businesses are being turned down or charged more for credit.
critics: Critics say requiring banks to collect and report whether a business owner is LGBTQ raises privacy concerns, since owners would need to self-identify to their lender in order to be counted.
Critics say the bill does not define how a business qualifies as 'LGBTQ-owned,' which could make it hard for banks to collect consistent data and lead to compliance problems.
Critics say adding a new reporting category to the CFPB's small business lending data system could increase costs and paperwork for financial institutions, especially smaller community banks.

117-hr-1446.one_liner: Extend the wait time before gun dealers can sell without a finished background check
provisions: Gun dealers must now wait 10 business days — up from 3 — before selling a gun if the background check is not done yet.
If the background check is still not done after 10 days, the buyer can file a request asking for a final decision.
If another 10 days pass with no final decision, the gun dealer can go ahead and complete the sale.

supporters: Supporters say extending the background check wait time from 3 to 10 business days gives the FBI more time to complete checks, which could stop gun sales to people who are legally blocked from buying firearms.

Supporters say the current 3-day limit has allowed guns to be sold before checks are finished — including the 2015 Charleston church shooting, where the gunman got a gun through a default proceed sale.
critics: Critics say the new 10-business-day wait — plus a possible additional 10 days after filing a petition — could leave law-abiding gun buyers waiting up to 20 business days before receiving a firearm they have a legal right to own.

Critics say the bill does not fix the reason background checks are slow in the first place, and that delays in the federal system should not be used to block or postpone transfers for buyers who have done nothing wrong.

117-hr-1339.one_liner: Create a federal group to plan for flying taxis and cargo drones
provisions: The Department of Transportation must set up a group of federal agencies to work together on new kinds of aircraft, including flying taxis and cargo drones.
The group will look at safety rules, ground infrastructure, cybersecurity, and how much money the government should put into this type of air travel.
The goal is to bring these new aircraft into the same airspace already used by regular planes.
The working group will cover flights in cities, suburbs, rural areas, and between regions.

supporters: Supporters say the bill would require the Department of Transportation to bring multiple federal agencies into one working group, so safety rules, cybersecurity standards, and infrastructure plans for flying taxis and cargo drones are built together instead of separately by each agency.

Supporters say the working group would cover flights in cities, rural areas, and between regions, which means the federal government would plan for the full range of places these new aircraft could operate before they enter shared airspace.

Supporters say having one group look at both ground infrastructure and federal investment needs would give aircraft companies clearer signals about what the government expects before they spend money building new systems.
critics: Critics say the bill sets up a coordination group but does not require any specific funding amounts, safety rules, or deadlines, so there is no guarantee the working group will produce binding results.

Critics say adding a new interagency body on top of existing agencies like the FAA could create overlapping responsibilities and slow down the process of writing the actual rules that flying taxi and cargo drone companies need to operate.

Critics say the bill does not define how many agencies must join the group, what voting or decision-making rules it follows, or what happens when agencies disagree, leaving the structure of the group unclear.

117-hr-1392.one_liner: Block U.S. weapons sales to Saudi Arabia and require reports on Jamal Khashoggi's death
provisions: For 120 days after this bill becomes law, the U.S. cannot sell or ship weapons to Saudi Arabia.
After 120 days, the weapons ban stays unless the President tells Congress Saudi Arabia met three conditions.

Those three conditions are: Saudi Arabia has not silenced or killed people in other countries, has not unjustly jailed U.S. citizens or legal U.S. residents inside Saudi Arabia, and has not tortured people in its custody.
The President must tell Congress that Saudi officials in the U.S. are not using their diplomatic status to track or harass Saudi citizens here.
If the President cannot make that statement, the U.S. must close at least one Saudi embassy or consular office in the country.
Congress gets a report on whether any Saudi officials harassed people inside the United States.
Congress gets a report on whether U.S. intelligence agencies warned journalist Jamal Khashoggi about threats to his life before he was killed in 2018.

supporters: Supporters say the 120-day weapons ban gives Saudi Arabia a clear deadline to change its behavior, and the ongoing certification requirement means the U.S. can stop arms sales any time Saudi Arabia kills or silences people in other countries.

Supporters say requiring the President to close a Saudi embassy if officials are found tracking Saudi citizens in the U.S. gives the government a real tool to protect people living here from foreign harassment.
Supporters say the required report on whether U.S. intelligence warned Jamal Khashoggi about threats to his life before his 2018 killing will hold American agencies accountable for what they knew.
critics: Critics say a 120-day blanket ban on all defense sales to Saudi Arabia could hurt U.S. defense contractors and their workers who depend on those contracts, without a guarantee it changes Saudi behavior.

Critics say the certification conditions — covering actions inside Saudi Arabia, in other countries, and inside the U.S. — set a standard that may be difficult to verify, making the ongoing arms restriction hard to lift even if Saudi Arabia cooperates.
Critics say closing a Saudi diplomatic facility as punishment could damage U.S.-Saudi relations on issues beyond human rights, including regional security cooperation and oil supply agreements.

117-hr-1460.one_liner: Fund carbon monoxide alarm installation in homes of low-income families and older adults
provisions: The government gives money to states and Native American tribal groups to buy and install carbon monoxide alarms.
The alarms go in homes where low-income families or people 65 and older live.
The alarms also go in buildings that regularly serve children or older adults, like day care centers or senior centers.
All alarms installed through this program must meet safety standards set by the government.

supporters: Supporters say the grants will put carbon monoxide alarms in homes of low-income families and adults 65 and older, who may not be able to afford detectors on their own.
Supporters say placing alarms in day care centers and senior centers will protect children and older adults who spend time in these buildings each day.
Supporters say requiring all installed alarms to meet government safety standards means the devices will actually work when carbon monoxide is present.
critics: Critics say the bill creates a new federal grant program that adds to government spending without setting a clear dollar limit on how much states can receive.
Critics say the program focuses only on low-income households and select facilities, leaving out middle-income families who also cannot always afford carbon monoxide detectors.
Critics say the bill gives the Consumer Product Safety Commission new responsibilities without specifying how much staff or funding the agency needs to run the grant program.

117-hr-147.one_liner: Give veterans more information and money options for apprenticeship programs
provisions: When service members leave the military, the Department of Labor must tell them about apprenticeship job training programs.
Veterans using the Post-9/11 GI Bill get a monthly housing payment — this bill lets them use that money for other costs too.
The Department of Veterans Affairs must build a website where veterans can search for apprenticeship programs approved for GI Bill benefits.

supporters: Supporters say that requiring the Department of Labor to share apprenticeship information during the Transition Assistance Program means every service member separating from active duty receives this information at the exact moment they are planning their next steps.

Supporters say that letting veterans use their Post-9/11 GI Bill monthly housing payment for costs beyond housing gives them more flexibility to cover expenses that come up during job training programs.

Supporters say the new VA-run website would let veterans search in one place for apprenticeship programs already approved under GI Bill education benefits, instead of searching across multiple government sources.
critics: Critics say that expanding the Post-9/11 GI Bill housing stipend to cover 'other purposes' removes limits that were designed to make sure those funds go toward housing costs while veterans are in training.

Critics say the bill requires the VA and the Department of Labor to build and maintain a new public-facing website but does not identify a funding source or set a deadline for when it must be completed.

Critics say the Transition Assistance Program already covers a wide range of topics for separating service members, and adding new apprenticeship information requirements without adjusting the program's existing content could reduce the quality of other guidance veterans receive.

117-hr-1482.one_liner: Add oversight rules for companies that help small businesses get SBA loans
provisions: Gives a federal office the job of watching over companies that help small businesses get loans through the SBA's 504 program.
The office must review the files for each loan that closes under the program.
The office can take action — formal or informal — against a company that breaks the rules.
The office can charge each of these companies a fee.
The SBA must write new rules explaining how these companies need to follow environmental requirements.

supporters: Supporters say giving the Office of Credit Risk Management direct oversight of certified development companies (CDCs) in the 504 Loan Program will help catch problems before small businesses are harmed by bad loan practices.
Supporters say requiring the office to review files for every loan closing under the 504 program creates a clear record of what each CDC is doing, making it easier to spot rule-breaking early.

Supporters say allowing the office to take formal or informal enforcement action against CDCs that break the rules gives the federal government real tools to hold these companies accountable, instead of just watching.
critics: Critics say the new fee the office can charge each CDC could raise costs for these companies, and those costs may get passed on to small businesses trying to use the 504 Loan Program.
Critics say requiring file reviews for every single loan closing in the 504 program adds paperwork and review time for CDCs, which could slow down how fast small businesses get approved for loans.

Critics say adding a requirement for the SBA to write new rules on environmental compliance gives CDCs another set of rules to follow, which could make it harder for smaller CDCs to keep up with the program's requirements.

117-hr-1487.one_liner: Require the SBA to report data on its small business microloan program
provisions: The Small Business Administration must report each year on its microloan program, which gives small loans under $50,000 to small businesses.
The report must show how many microloans went unpaid, the total dollar amount of those loans, and what percentage of all microloans went unpaid that year.
The report must show how many microloans went to small businesses in rural areas.
The report must include the average loan size, the interest rate charged, and the fees borrowers paid.

supporters: Supporters say requiring the SBA to report how many microloans went unpaid — and the total dollar amount of those defaults — will help Congress spot problems in the program before they grow.
Supporters say tracking how many microloans go to rural small businesses will show whether those communities are getting a fair share of loans under $50,000.
Supporters say publishing the average loan size, interest rate, and fees will let small business owners compare SBA microloan terms before they borrow.
critics: Critics say the SBA already collects loan data internally, so adding a formal annual report creates paperwork for agency staff without changing how loans are made.
Critics say the bill does not set any rules about what default rates or fee levels are too high, so the reports may be published without anyone acting on them.

117-hr-1490.one_liner: Raise the loan limit for small manufacturers and update SBA 504 loan rules
provisions: The top loan amount for small manufacturers goes from $5.5 million to $6.5 million.
Small manufacturers can now put less of their own money toward a project to get one of these loans.
Small manufacturers must show they kept more jobs to qualify.
Companies that connect businesses to these loans can fix paperwork errors and shift up to 10% of project costs to close a deal.
These loans can now go to businesses in areas hit by disasters, or to businesses that want to cut energy use or make renewable energy.
Every SBA office must team up with a local partner to offer training for small manufacturers.

supporters: Supporters say raising the loan limit for small manufacturers from $5.5 million to $6.5 million gives these businesses access to more money for equipment and facilities they could not afford before.
Supporters say allowing small manufacturers to put less of their own money into a project makes it easier for smaller or newer companies to qualify for a loan without draining their savings.
Supporters say expanding 504 loans to cover disaster areas and energy-efficiency projects helps businesses in struggling communities rebuild and lower their operating costs.
critics: Critics say requiring small manufacturers to show they kept more jobs adds a stricter condition that could disqualify businesses going through hard times or workforce changes.
Critics say allowing loan intermediaries to shift up to 10% of project costs without full review could lead to changes that borrowers did not originally agree to.
Critics say the new training requirement at every SBA district office adds an unfunded obligation that local offices may not have the staff or budget to carry out.

117-hr-1619.one_liner: Add 17 acres of land in North Carolina to the Catawba Indian Nation's reservation
provisions: Makes about 17 acres of land in Cleveland County, North Carolina, part of the Catawba Indian Nation's reservation.
The federal government will hold this land in trust for the tribe.
The tribe can run gambling and gaming on this land.

supporters: Supporters say the bill gives the Catawba Indian Nation formal, long-term federal ownership of about 17 acres in Cleveland County, North Carolina, making it part of the tribe's official reservation.
Supporters say allowing the tribe to run gaming on this land would bring jobs and money to the Catawba Indian Nation and the surrounding area in Cleveland County.
critics: Critics say the bill lets the tribe open a casino on this land without following a federal law that normally requires a state to sign a gaming agreement with a tribe before gambling can begin.

Critics say adding 17 acres in Cleveland County to the Catawba Reservation sets a pattern where Congress bypasses the usual process for approving tribal land and gaming, which could affect how other tribes make similar requests.

117-hr-1620.one_liner: Renew and expand funding for domestic violence and sexual assault programs through 2026
provisions: Keeps funding active through 2026 for programs that help victims of domestic violence, sexual assault, dating violence, and stalking.
Creates new programs to help victims keep their housing and stay financially stable.
Changes federal gun rules so people convicted of abusing a dating partner or stalking someone can no longer legally buy or own a gun.
Before this change, only people who abused a spouse or household member faced that restriction.

supporters: Supporters say the bill closes a gap in federal gun law by extending the ban on gun ownership to people convicted of abusing dating partners or stalking victims, not just spouses or household members.
Supporters say reauthorizing funding through 2026 keeps shelters, hotlines, and legal services running for victims who rely on those programs each year.
Supporters say the new housing and financial stability programs give victims a way to leave dangerous situations without losing their home or income.
critics: Critics say expanding the gun restriction to dating partners and stalking convictions is too broad and could strip gun rights from people based on minor or disputed convictions.
Critics say extending the law through 2026 without a full review of how current funds are being spent adds more federal spending without proof the existing programs are working.
Critics say some of the new housing protections could create legal conflicts with landlords' rights under state property laws.

117-hr-1502.one_liner: Update rules for the Small Business Administration's small-loan program
provisions: Lenders in this program can now offer a line of credit — money a small business can borrow from as needed — instead of only one-time loans.
Lenders who give out bigger average loans to small businesses now qualify for a lower interest rate on the money they borrow from the SBA.
Sets a maximum time limit for borrowers to pay back their loan, and stops the SBA from cutting that time limit shorter.
The SBA must set aside 15% of new loan money for states that have not received many of these loans, and make the other 85% available to any state.
Lenders must share borrower payment records with the major credit bureaus, which affects a borrower's credit score.
Each year, the SBA must report on how loan money is being spread across different groups and states.

supporters: Supporters say allowing lenders to offer lines of credit — instead of only one-time loans — gives small businesses more flexible access to money when they need it most.
Supporters say reserving 15% of new loan funds for underutilized states will send more money to places that have been left out of the program.
Supporters say requiring lenders to report borrower payments to credit bureaus will help small business owners build credit history they can use to get better loans later.
critics: Critics say requiring lenders to report borrower payment records to credit bureaus could hurt small business owners if they miss a payment, lowering their credit scores and making it harder to borrow in the future.
Critics say giving lenders a lower interest rate when they make bigger average loans could push them to favor larger borrowers over the smallest businesses the program is meant to help.
Critics say setting a fixed maximum repayment term and blocking the SBA from adjusting it removes flexibility that may be needed to protect borrowers who run into financial trouble.

117-hr-1573.one_liner: Give people stopped at the U.S. border the right to speak with a lawyer
provisions: People with green cards, visas, or refugee status who are pulled aside for extra questioning at a U.S. border must be allowed to speak with a lawyer within 1 hour of the questioning starting.
During the extra questioning, a lawyer or a relative can speak up for the person and give information to the officer.
Green card holders cannot sign away their green card status during a border stop unless they first had a real chance to talk to a lawyer.
If a green card holder decides to skip their right to a lawyer, they must say so in writing and it must be their own free choice.

supporters: Supporters say the bill would protect green card holders, visa holders, and refugees from losing their immigration status during a border stop without first talking to a lawyer, since officers cannot accept a signed waiver unless the person had a real chance to get legal advice.

Supporters say allowing a lawyer or relative to give information to the officer during secondary questioning could help clear up mistakes faster, since the officer would have more facts about the person being questioned.

Supporters say the 1-hour rule gives people with legal status — like green card holders and refugees — enough time to reach someone who can help them before they say anything that could hurt their case.
critics: Critics say requiring border officers to wait up to 1 hour before continuing secondary inspections could slow down processing at busy ports of entry and delay questioning of all travelers in line.

Critics say letting lawyers speak during secondary inspections could interfere with the officer's ability to ask questions freely, since the bill allows counsel to provide evidence and information directly to the examining officer.
Critics say the bill does not say who must provide or pay for a lawyer, so people who cannot afford one may not actually get meaningful legal help within the 1-hour window the bill requires.

117-hr-1603.one_liner: Give legal work status to undocumented farm workers and change farm visa rules
provisions: Undocumented farm workers who worked at least 1,035 hours on farms in the two years before March 2021 and have stayed in the U.S. since then can apply for a work permit that lasts 5.5 years.
While their application is being decided, the government cannot deport them and they can work legally.
Their spouse and children can also receive protected status.
After getting the permit and continuing to work in agriculture for a set number of years, they can apply for a green card.
Changes how the minimum wage for H-2A farm visa workers is calculated, and opens the program to year-round farm jobs, not just seasonal ones.
Lets H-2A workers who leave a job have 60 days to find a new farm employer before having to leave the country.
Makes a housing program permanent that provides loans and grants to build or fix housing for farm workers in rural areas.

supporters: Supporters say the bill would protect about 1 million undocumented farm workers who already worked at least 1,035 hours in U.S. agriculture before March 2021, letting them stay and work legally without fear of deportation while their application is reviewed.

Supporters say opening the H-2A visa program to year-round farm jobs — not just seasonal ones — and giving workers 60 days to find a new employer after leaving a job would help farms like dairies that need workers all year keep a steady workforce.

Supporters say making the rural farmworker housing program permanent and adding new loans and grants for housing would improve living conditions for farm workers who currently lack safe, stable places to live near their jobs.
critics: Critics say giving undocumented workers a 5.5-year work permit and a path to a green card rewards people who entered the country illegally, and that the bill's employment authorization during the application period means the government cannot remove applicants even before their cases are decided.

Critics say the new electronic work verification system required for all agricultural employers will place a compliance burden on small and mid-size farms that may not have the technology or staff to use it.

Critics say changing how the minimum wage for H-2A visa workers is calculated could raise labor costs for farm operators at a time when food production costs are already high, and that those costs could be passed on to consumers.

117-hr-1664.one_liner: Let a private group build a Medal of Honor memorial in Washington DC
provisions: Lets the National Medal of Honor Museum Foundation build a memorial on federal land in Washington DC
The foundation must raise and spend its own money to build the memorial
No federal tax dollars can be used to pay for the memorial

supporters: Supporters say the bill protects taxpayers because it bars any federal funds from being used to build the memorial, requiring the National Medal of Honor Museum Foundation to raise and spend its own private money.

Supporters say placing the memorial on federal land in Washington DC gives Medal of Honor recipients — a group of fewer than 3,600 people ever awarded the honor — a permanent, visible place of recognition near other national monuments.
Supporters say putting the funding responsibility entirely on the foundation, not Congress, means no federal budget impact while still allowing the memorial to be built in the nation's capital.
critics: Critics say granting a private foundation the right to build a permanent structure on federal land in DC sets a precedent for other private groups to seek the same access, which could increase competition for limited public space.

Critics say the bill includes no cap on how large or expensive the commemorative work can be, and gives Congress no role in approving the foundation's design or construction plans once authorization is granted.

Critics say that while no federal dollars fund construction, the National Park Service or other federal agencies would likely bear ongoing maintenance and security costs for the site, which the bill does not address.

117-hr-1667.one_liner: Fund mental health programs and suicide prevention training for doctors and nurses
provisions: The federal government gives money to hospitals and health groups to train doctors, nurses, and other health workers on suicide prevention and mental health.
Some of that money goes to programs that support health workers who were involved in treating COVID-19 patients.
The Department of Health and Human Services studies what gets in the way of health workers getting mental health care and writes up suggestions for fixing it.
The CDC runs a public campaign to encourage health workers to get help when they are struggling with their mental health.

supporters: Supporters say the bill gives federal grants to hospitals and health groups to train doctors, nurses, and other health workers on suicide prevention, which could help address high rates of burnout and mental health problems in that workforce.

Supporters say the bill directs HHS to study what gets in the way of health workers getting mental health care and write up fix recommendations, which could lead to policy changes that make it easier for providers to seek help without fear of losing their jobs or licenses.
Supporters say the CDC campaign would encourage health workers to seek treatment, reaching a group that often avoids care because of stigma in the medical field.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set a specific dollar amount for the grants, so there is no guarantee that hospitals and health groups will get enough money to run effective training programs.

Critics say some of the grant money is tied to COVID-19 response programs, which may leave out health workers in other settings who face burnout and mental health struggles not connected to the pandemic.

Critics say a study and a CDC awareness campaign do not change the licensing rules and credentialing policies that currently discourage health workers from seeking mental health treatment, so the root barriers may stay in place.

117-hr-1693.one_liner: Equalize federal prison sentence thresholds for crack cocaine and powder cocaine
provisions: Right now, getting caught with 28 grams of crack cocaine triggers the same jail time as 500 grams of powder cocaine.
This bill changes that so both drugs use the same amounts at every penalty level.
People with open cases on the day this becomes law also get the new rules.
People already in prison for a crack cocaine offense can go back to a judge and ask for a lower sentence.

supporters: Supporters say the current law sets the crack cocaine threshold at 28 grams but powder cocaine at 500 grams to trigger the same penalties — a ratio of nearly 18 to 1 — and this bill would apply the same gram amounts to both drugs at every penalty level.

Supporters say roughly 80% of federal crack cocaine convictions involve Black defendants, so the 28-to-500 gram gap has resulted in longer prison terms for Black defendants compared to those convicted of the powder form of the same drug.

Supporters say people already in prison for crack cocaine offenses could go before a judge and ask for a lower sentence under the new equal thresholds, reducing time served for those convicted under the old ratio.
critics: Critics say allowing people already serving federal prison sentences for crack cocaine offenses to request resentencing could lead to the early release of people convicted of large-scale drug distribution.

Critics say crack cocaine is more commonly sold in small amounts near street level, so raising the crack threshold from 28 grams to match powder cocaine's 500 grams could lower the penalty for dealers who sell in smaller quantities.
Critics say the bill applies the new rules to cases still open on the day it becomes law, which could interrupt federal drug prosecutions already in progress.

117-hr-1651.one_liner: Extend COVID-19 bankruptcy protections for people and small businesses through March 2022
provisions: COVID-19 payments, like stimulus checks, do not count as income when a person files for bankruptcy — this rule is extended through March 27, 2022.
Small businesses can use a simpler type of bankruptcy if they owe up to $7.5 million, up from the standard $2.7 million limit — extended through March 27, 2022.
People already on a Chapter 13 repayment plan can ask to change their payment schedule if COVID hurt their finances — previously this was only an option for plans set up before March 27, 2020.
Lenders and landlords cannot turn someone down for COVID mortgage or eviction help just because that person filed for bankruptcy — extended through March 27, 2022.
Utility companies cannot shut off service to people in bankruptcy under certain conditions — extended through March 27, 2022.

supporters: Supporters say that people who received COVID aid, like stimulus checks, and later file for bankruptcy will not have those payments counted as income, which could help them keep more of their assets through March 27, 2022.

Supporters say small businesses that owe up to $7.5 million — up from the standard $2.7 million — can use a simpler, court-supervised debt restructuring process through March 27, 2022, letting more businesses qualify.

Supporters say people already in a Chapter 13 repayment plan can now ask a court to change their payment schedule if COVID hurt their finances, a protection that was previously only available for plans set up before March 27, 2020.
critics: Critics say the bill removes lenders' ability to reject someone for COVID mortgage or eviction help based on their bankruptcy status, meaning lenders must offer relief even to applicants they believe cannot repay.

Critics say raising the debt limit for the simpler restructuring process from $2.7 million to $7.5 million allows more businesses to qualify, which may leave people or companies owed money with fewer protections during the process.

Critics say extending utility protections through March 27, 2022 prevents utility companies from shutting off service in certain cases, which could shift the cost of unpaid bills onto the companies themselves.

117-hr-1629.one_liner: Limit which rare-disease drugs can get 7-year market protection from the FDA
provisions: Right now, the FDA can label a drug an orphan drug if it treats a rare disease. When that happens, the maker gets 7 years where no other company can sell the same drug for the same disease.
This bill adds a new test for getting that 7-year protection. The maker must show it won't earn back its costs within the first 12 years of US sales.
This new test also applies to drugs that already have the 7-year protection before this bill passes.
When checking if a company passes the test, the FDA counts sales from all that company's drugs under the same rare disease label.

supporters: Supporters say the bill stops large drug companies from using the 7-year exclusivity period as a shield when they are already making back their money — the 12-year sales test makes sure only companies that truly cannot recover their costs get the protection.

Supporters say requiring the FDA to count sales from all drugs under the same orphan disease label closes a loophole where a company could sell many related drugs and still claim each one loses money.
Supporters say applying the new rule to drugs that already have the 7-year protection removes an unfair advantage for companies that got exclusivity before this stricter test existed.
critics: Critics say the bill's 12-year cost-recovery test could discourage drug makers from investing in rare disease treatments if they fear losing the 7-year exclusivity period that helps them plan for future sales.

Critics say applying the new rule retroactively to drugs that already received the 7-year exclusivity period changes the rules after companies already spent money on research and development based on the old law.

Critics say counting sales from all drugs under the same orphan designation could unfairly penalize companies that developed multiple treatments for the same rare disease, even if each individual drug did not recover its own costs.

117-hr-1762.one_liner: Require the FTC to study and report on scams targeting Native American tribes
provisions: Tells the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) to talk with Native American tribes about scams and unfair business practices that target them or their members
Requires the FTC to send a written report on those scams to Congress and post it online for anyone to read
Requires the FTC to add information to its website so tribes and their members can spot and avoid scams targeting them

supporters: Supporters say requiring the FTC to consult directly with tribal governments will produce a report that reflects the specific scams targeting Native American communities, rather than generic consumer fraud data.

Supporters say posting the report online and updating the FTC website gives tribal members a free, easy-to-find resource to identify scams that currently go unreported because people do not know where to turn.
Supporters say the bill creates a formal record for Congress of how unfair business practices affect tribes, which could lead to stronger enforcement actions in the future.
critics: Critics say the bill only requires a report and a website update, with no new enforcement powers or funding given to the FTC to actually stop scams targeting tribal members.
Critics say the bill does not set a deadline for when the FTC must complete the consultation with tribes or submit the report to Congress, which could delay any real action.

Critics say tribal governments were not listed as co-authors of the bill's requirements, raising questions about whether the consultation process will give tribes enough say in what gets studied and reported.

117-hr-1917.one_liner: Lets groups get federal disaster money for projects already underway
provisions: Groups working on disaster prevention projects — like flood barriers or firebreaks — can now get federal money even if the project already started before they applied.
Before this bill, federal disaster prevention money could only go to projects that had not yet begun.
This applies to the federal Hazard Mitigation Assistance program, which helps communities reduce damage from floods, wildfires, and other natural disasters.

supporters: Supporters say that communities working on flood barriers, firebreaks, or other disaster prevention projects can now get federal Hazard Mitigation Assistance money even if the project already started before they applied.

Supporters say local governments and nonprofits that began projects quickly during an active threat will no longer be turned away from the Hazard Mitigation Assistance program just because they did not wait for federal approval first.
critics: Critics say that removing the rule requiring projects to not have started before approval means federal reviewers cannot check whether a project meets Hazard Mitigation Assistance program standards before construction begins.

Critics say communities that followed the old pre-approval requirement — stopping work until they received federal sign-off — are now at a disadvantage, because groups that skipped that step can receive the same Hazard Mitigation Assistance funds without having complied with the same rules.

117-hr-1899.one_liner: Set clear rules for when a drug distribution license ends or transfers
provisions: Gives official legal backing to rules about changing, transferring, or ending a license to make, sell, or hand out controlled substances
A license automatically ends when the person or company dies, closes, stops doing business, or gives up the license
Sets rules for what must be reported and when a license can be passed to someone else

supporters: Supporters say the bill writes existing DEA rules into law, so automatic license termination when a person dies or a company closes is no longer just an agency policy that can be changed without Congress.
Supporters say the notification requirements give the DEA a clear timeline to act when a controlled substance license is transferred, reducing gaps where drugs could be diverted.
Supporters say locking transfer conditions into law makes it harder for bad actors to quietly pass a license to another person or company without DEA approval.
critics: Critics say the bill does not add new oversight tools, only codifying rules already in place, which may give false confidence that drug diversion problems are being addressed.
Critics say the automatic termination rules could disrupt pharmacies or distributors mid-operation if a business change triggers a license lapse before a transfer is approved.
Critics say the bill leaves out enforcement funding or staffing, so written-in rules about notification deadlines mean little if the DEA lacks resources to act on them.

117-hr-172.one_liner: Fund the U.S. agency that tests athletes for performance-enhancing drugs through 2030
provisions: Gives USADA, the U.S. agency that runs drug testing for American athletes, continued funding through 2030
Before any international sports organization can drug-test amateur athletes or run competitions inside the United States, USADA must first approve that testing
USADA must spend some of its money on materials that teach kids in youth sports about sportsmanship and healthy performance
If USADA investigates or punishes someone for breaking a rule, it must follow due process — meaning the person gets a fair process before any action is taken against them
The Justice Department, Homeland Security, and the FDA must share information with USADA about performance-enhancing drugs and banned methods

supporters: Supporters say extending USADA's funding through 2030 gives the agency stable resources to keep drug testing American athletes without gaps in oversight.
Supporters say requiring USADA to pre-approve any drug testing by international sports organizations inside the United States stops foreign groups from running tests that may not meet U.S. standards.
Supporters say the new due process rule means USADA must give athletes a fair process before any investigation, punishment, or sanction is carried out against them.
critics: Critics say requiring USADA to certify all international testing before it happens could delay or block drug tests at international competitions held inside the United States, since approval must come in advance.

Critics say directing USADA to spend part of its budget on youth sportsmanship and character-building materials takes money away from its core job of catching athletes who use performance-enhancing drugs.

Critics say forcing the Justice Department, Homeland Security, and the FDA to share drug enforcement information with USADA, a private nonprofit, raises questions about what data is shared and how it will be protected.

117-hr-1975.one_liner: Transfer 721 acres in San Diego County to the Pala Band of Mission Indians reservation
provisions: The federal government takes about 721 acres in San Diego County, California, and holds it in trust for the tribe.
That land becomes part of the Pala Indian Reservation.
The tribe must first sign the land over to the U.S. government before this takes effect.
No gambling is allowed on any of this land.

supporters: Supporters say the bill would add 721 acres to the Pala Indian Reservation in San Diego County, giving the Pala Band of Mission Indians more land for housing, farming, or cultural use.
Supporters say the no-gaming rule written into the bill addresses a common concern about tribal land transfers, since no gambling would be allowed on any of the 721 acres.
Supporters say the process is low-risk because the tribe must first sign the land over to the U.S. government before any trust status takes effect.
critics: Critics say placing 721 acres of private land into federal trust removes that land from San Diego County's tax rolls, which could reduce local government revenue.
Critics say once land is taken into federal trust, the county and state lose most of their ability to enforce local zoning and land-use rules on those 721 acres.

117-hr-2119.one_liner: Extend and expand federal grants for domestic violence shelters and prevention programs
provisions: Keeps the federal program that funds emergency shelters for domestic violence victims running through 2026.
Gives grants to state and tribal groups to run prevention programs in local communities.
Gives grants to groups that serve communities of color and groups that serve people in areas with fewer resources.
Creates a new grant program for tribal groups to support domestic violence services on tribal lands.
Funds a hotline for Native American people affected by domestic violence.

supporters: Supporters say the bill keeps emergency shelter funding running through 2026, so domestic violence victims have a place to go when they leave a dangerous home.
Supporters say grants for communities of color and underserved areas will help groups that currently lack resources to serve domestic violence victims in their own languages and cultural settings.
Supporters say the new tribal grant program and the Native American domestic violence hotline will bring services directly to tribal lands, where victims have had fewer options.
critics: Critics say the bill expands the number of grant programs and eligible organizations without setting clear performance measures to show whether the new prevention programs actually reduce family violence.

Critics say adding grants for population-specific and culturally specific organizations may spread limited federal dollars across too many groups, making it harder for any single program to reach enough people to make a difference.

117-hr-208.one_liner: Rename a Tupelo, Mississippi post office after Colonel Carlyle "Smitty" Harris
provisions: The post office at 500 West Main Street, Suite 102 in Tupelo, Mississippi currently has no special name.
This bill gives it the official name "Colonel Carlyle 'Smitty' Harris Post Office".
The building is located at 500 West Main Street, Suite 102 in Tupelo, Mississippi.

117-hr-2062.one_liner: Let workers win age discrimination cases without proving age was the only reason
provisions: Workers suing for age discrimination no longer have to prove age was the only reason for an employer's decision.
They only need to show age was one of the reasons.
Workers are also protected from retaliation for reporting age discrimination or taking part in a related case.
Workers can use any type of evidence to support their case.
If age discrimination is proven, a court can order the employer to stop the practice.
But if the employer shows it would have made the same decision anyway, the court cannot order back pay or job reinstatement.
This same standard applies to disability discrimination cases and other workplace discrimination claims.

supporters: Supporters say the bill fixes a rule set by the Supreme Court in 2009 that forced older workers to prove age was the only reason they were fired or passed over, a standard that no other discrimination law requires.

Supporters say allowing workers to show age was just one of several reasons for a bad employment decision makes it easier for the estimated millions of workers over 40 covered by the Age Discrimination in Employment Act to bring valid claims to court.

Supporters say expanding the same standard to disability discrimination cases under the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 and the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 closes a legal gap that has made those cases harder to win.
critics: Critics say the bill could expose employers to more lawsuits because workers only need to show age was one motivating factor, even in layoffs or performance decisions driven mostly by other reasons.

Critics say the rule that blocks courts from ordering back pay or reinstatement when an employer proves it would have made the same decision anyway creates an uneven result — a worker wins the case but gets no real relief.

Critics say applying the new standard across the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the ADA, and the Rehabilitation Act at once makes a large change to how courts handle many types of workplace cases, which could create confusion while courts work out what rules apply.

117-hr-2088.one_liner: Transfer land in Tennessee to the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians
provisions: The federal government takes land in Monroe County, Tennessee and holds it on behalf of the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians.
The land includes the Sequoyah Museum, the Chota Memorial, the Tanasi Memorial, and nearby land used for cultural programs.
The Tennessee Valley Authority keeps the right to flood parts of this land when needed for river management.
If the tribe builds on the land in ways that reduce the TVA's ability to generate power, the TVA must be paid for that loss.
The federal government is not responsible for damage caused by flooding on land next to these properties.
No gambling is allowed on any of these lands.

supporters: Supporters say the bill places the Sequoyah Museum, Chota Memorial, and Tanasi Memorial into federal trust for the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians, giving the tribe legal control over historic sites tied to their cultural heritage.
Supporters say holding these lands in trust means they cannot be sold or taken from the tribe, giving the Eastern Band a permanent base for cultural programs in Monroe County, Tennessee.
Supporters say the no-gaming rule removes a common objection to tribal land-in-trust transfers, making it easier for Congress to approve the bill without debate over casino development.
critics: Critics say the TVA keeps the right to flood parts of the trust land for river management, which could damage or destroy the cultural sites and programs the bill is meant to protect.

Critics say that if the tribe builds on these lands and reduces TVA hydropower output, the tribe must pay TVA for that lost power capacity, creating a financial burden on land placed in trust for their use.
Critics say the federal government removes its own liability for flood damage on land next to these properties, leaving the tribe with no legal recourse if TVA water management harms their sites.

117-hr-1996.one_liner: Let banks work with cannabis businesses without facing federal penalties
provisions: Banks can open accounts and give loans to cannabis businesses without being punished by federal bank regulators.
Federal regulators cannot shut down or threaten a bank just because it serves cannabis businesses.
Money from cannabis business transactions will not automatically be treated as illegal under money laundering rules.
Banks cannot lose their federal deposit insurance just for banking a cannabis business.
Banks that give loans to cannabis businesses cannot have those assets seized under federal law.
Federal regulators can still order a bank to close a customer account, but only for real reasons — like national security threats or terrorism — not just because serving that customer looks bad.

supporters: Supporters say the bill would allow banks to open accounts and give loans to cannabis businesses that are legal under state law, without those banks being punished by federal regulators — helping thousands of businesses that are currently forced to operate in cash only.

Supporters say the bill removes the risk of banks losing their federal deposit insurance just for serving a state-licensed cannabis business, which supporters say has blocked these businesses from getting basic financial services.

Supporters say the provision that stops federal regulators from seizing a bank's assets for giving loans to cannabis businesses will help those businesses get the capital they need to operate safely and pay taxes.
critics: Critics say cannabis is still a Schedule I controlled substance under federal law, and letting banks serve cannabis businesses without penalty creates a direct conflict with federal drug law that Congress has not resolved.
Critics say removing the automatic money laundering flag from cannabis business transactions could make it harder for law enforcement to track illegal drug money moving through the banking system.

Critics say the bill protects banks from federal punishment, but does not require banks to actually serve cannabis businesses — meaning the access problem for cannabis businesses may not change in practice.

117-hr-2355.one_liner: Update pharmacist training and grant rules for checking ID at prescription pickups
provisions: Requires HHS to update training guides so pharmacists know how to check the ID of people picking up prescribed medications.
The CDC can give priority to states when handing out overdose prevention grants.
To get priority, a state must run a drug monitoring program that collects specific information about prescriptions.
To get priority, a state must also require pharmacies to check the ID of people picking up certain addictive drugs.

supporters: Supporters say requiring pharmacists to check ID before giving out addictive drugs will help stop people from picking up prescriptions that were not written for them, which can lead to misuse.
Supporters say giving CDC grant priority to states that run drug monitoring programs and require ID checks will push more states to adopt these rules without making them a federal mandate.
Supporters say updating HHS training materials for pharmacists gives them clear guidance on how to verify who is picking up a controlled substance.
critics: Critics say requiring ID verification at pharmacies could create barriers for low-income patients or people without government-issued ID who are trying to pick up legitimate prescriptions.
Critics say tying CDC overdose prevention grant priority to specific state program requirements may disadvantage states that have different but effective approaches to reducing opioid deaths.
Critics say the bill does not include new funding to help pharmacies or states cover the cost of building out drug monitoring programs or training staff on the new ID verification procedures.

117-hr-22.one_liner: Require federal agencies to post budget request documents online for the public
provisions: Each federal agency must post its budget request documents on its own website and on a central government website like USAspending.gov.
The documents must be posted within two weeks of being sent to Congress.
The documents must be in a format that lets anyone download one report, all reports at once, or just their search results.
The Office of Management and Budget must keep a public webpage listing which agencies submitted budget documents, when they were submitted to Congress, and when they were posted online.

supporters: Supporters say that requiring agencies to post budget documents on both their own websites and a central site like USAspending.gov would let any citizen find and download federal spending plans in one place.
Supporters say the two-week posting deadline means the public would see budget requests at nearly the same time as Congress, instead of months later or never.

Supporters say the open-format requirement — which lets users download one report, all reports at once, or just search results — would make it easier for researchers and journalists to study how agencies spend money.
critics: Critics say the two-week deadline for posting after submission to Congress may not give agencies enough time to convert documents into open, downloadable formats, especially agencies with small IT teams.
Critics say the bill does not include funding to help agencies build the new web systems needed to meet the bulk-download and open-format rules, which could shift costs onto existing agency budgets.

117-hr-2278.one_liner: Create an official trail route connecting the three 9/11 memorial sites
provisions: Lets the National Park Service mark an official trail route linking three 9/11 memorial sites.
The route connects the 9/11 Memorial in New York City, the Pentagon Memorial in Virginia, and the Flight 93 Memorial in Pennsylvania.
This bill marks an existing route on a map — it does not fund building a new physical trail.
No money is set aside in this bill for construction or maintenance of the trail route.

supporters: Supporters say that officially linking the 9/11 Memorial in New York, the Pentagon Memorial in Virginia, and the Flight 93 Memorial in Pennsylvania under one named route will make it easier for visitors to find and travel between all three sites.
Supporters say the designation costs nothing because the bill does not set aside any money for construction or maintenance — it only asks the National Park Service to mark an existing route on a map.
Supporters say connecting the three memorials honors the people killed at each location on September 11, 2001 and helps families and the public visit all the sites as one unified tribute.
critics: Critics say the bill gives the National Park Service a new responsibility — managing and promoting a multi-state memorial route — without providing any funding to cover those costs.

Critics say that because no money is set aside for maintenance, the quality and upkeep of the designated route is uncertain, which could affect the experience of visitors traveling between the three memorial sites.

117-hr-2225.one_liner: Fund the National Science Foundation and expand its science and education programs
provisions: Keeps the National Science Foundation funded through the year ending September 2026
Creates at least 3 new centers to research better ways to teach STEM subjects like science, math, and computer science in schools
Builds a network of centers to help students train for science and technical jobs
Starts a national program to bring more students from groups underrepresented in STEM fields into those studies and careers
Creates a new division inside NSF to fund research on national challenges including climate, food, water, and energy
Funds research to better predict extreme weather, natural disasters, and pandemics
Sets up an office inside NSF to manage research security across all its programs

117-hr-2220.one_liner: Require Congress to approve below-market purchase deals in federal building leases
provisions: Some federal building leases include an option to buy the building at less than its real market value.
This bill says the government cannot use that option on its own.
Congress must pass a separate law giving specific approval before the government can use it.
This rule covers any federal building lease signed on or after January 1, 2021.

117-hr-2379.one_liner: Keep funding state programs that help people with drug addiction through 2027
provisions: Keeps the State Opioid Response Grant program running through 2027.
States can now use this money to help people with any drug addiction, not just opioids.
The grants are run by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, a federal health agency.

117-hr-239.one_liner: Remove copays for contraception from veterans using VA healthcare
provisions: Veterans who use VA healthcare will no longer pay out of pocket for contraception.
The VA must cover contraception at no cost, the same way private health insurance plans are required to.
This applies to any contraceptive item that private insurers must cover for free under current law.

117-hr-2365.one_liner: Give a monument foundation more time to build a tribute to Gold Star families
provisions: A group called the Gold Star Mothers National Monument Foundation has permission to build a monument honoring Gold Star families.
Gold Star families are people who lost a family member in military service.
The group's permission to build the monument is extended to January 2, 2027.

117-hr-2364.one_liner: Require federal agencies to teach the public and first responders about fentanyl dangers
provisions: The CDC must run a public education campaign about the dangers of fentanyl and other synthetic opioids.
A federal workplace safety office called NIOSH must create training materials for people who may come into contact with synthetic opioids on the job.
First responders — including paramedics, sheriff's deputies, and others in high-risk jobs — must receive that training through a federal mental health agency.

117-hr-2467.one_liner: Require the EPA to limit PFAS chemicals in drinking water, air, and soil
provisions: Requires the EPA to label two common PFAS chemicals — PFOA and PFOS — as hazardous, which means companies must clean them up when they are found in the environment.
Requires the EPA to set a legal limit for PFAS in tap water, including limits for PFOA and PFOS specifically.
Gives the EPA five years to decide whether other PFAS chemicals should also be treated as hazardous.
Requires the EPA to add PFOA and PFOS to the list of harmful air pollutants, which would trigger rules on how much can be released into the air.
Requires the EPA to test all PFAS chemicals to see how dangerous they are to human health.
Sets rules for how materials that contain PFAS can be thrown away or disposed of.
Gives money to local water systems to help them filter PFAS out of drinking water.

117-hr-2668.one_liner: Let the FTC sue companies in court to get money back for consumers
provisions: The FTC can take companies to federal court when they use false advertising, fraud, or other illegal business practices.
Courts can order companies to pay back money consumers paid because of illegal practices.
Courts can cancel or change contracts that were made through illegal business practices.
The FTC can also ask courts to make companies give up any profits they made from those illegal practices.
This law overturns a 2021 Supreme Court decision that blocked the FTC from getting this kind of money back in court.

117-hr-2497.one_liner: Make a Colorado World War II prison camp a national historic site
provisions: A site in Granada, Colorado called Amache will become part of the National Park System.
It will preserve history about Japanese Americans who were imprisoned there during World War II.
It also preserves history about people held at Amache who served in the U.S. military during the war.
The National Park Service can buy or accept donated land to make the site work.
The Park Service must write a plan for how the site will be managed.
The Park Service can partner with outside groups to run visitor services and store historical items.

117-hr-2547.one_liner: Restrict debt collectors and add protections for people with student loans and medical debt
provisions: Private student loans must be canceled if the borrower dies or becomes fully and permanently disabled.
Medical debt from a procedure your doctor said you needed cannot be put on your credit report.
Debt collectors cannot lie to military members and say that not paying will get them demoted or punished.
Debt collectors cannot text or email you without your permission.
Lenders cannot make you sign away your right to sue them if you fall behind on a loan.
The rules on how debt collectors must treat people now apply to debts owed to the government and to states.
These rules also now cover companies that buy debt from other lenders.

117-hr-256.one_liner: Remove the 2002 law that allowed the U.S. to invade Iraq
provisions: Takes away the legal permission Congress gave the President in 2002 to use military force in Iraq
The 2002 law has been used to justify military action in the Middle East for over 20 years
After this bill passes, the President would no longer have that standing war permission for Iraq

118-hres-1143.one_liner: Condemn Iran's attack on Israel and call for stronger sanctions against Iran
provisions: The House says it condemns Iran for launching drones and missiles at Israel.
The House says the U.S. stands behind Israel's right to defend itself and fight back.
The House praises U.S. troops, the UK, France, and Jordan for shooting down Iranian drones and missiles.
The House calls on the U.S. government to fully enforce existing sanctions and trade restrictions against Iran.

117-hr-2911.one_liner: Require the VA to report how it spends COVID relief money
provisions: Requires the Department of Veterans Affairs to submit a plan showing how it will spend COVID relief funds
Requires the VA to send reports every two weeks on how much COVID money has been spent and what it plans to spend until all funds are used
Requires the VA's Inspector General to review and report on how COVID funds were spent
Requires the Government Accountability Office to submit two reports — one midway through and one final — reviewing how the VA spent its COVID money

117-hr-2685.one_liner: Require a federal study on how safe mobile phone networks are from hackers
provisions: Requires a federal agency called NTIA to study how safe mobile phone networks are from hackers and foreign governments
The study looks at whether phone companies have fixed known security weaknesses in their networks
It checks whether phone companies are following security best practices
It estimates how widely encryption and authentication methods are used to protect calls, texts, and devices
NTIA must send a report of its findings to Congress

117-hr-2758.one_liner: Give the Lumbee Tribe of North Carolina federal recognition and access to government services
provisions: Gives the Lumbee Tribe of North Carolina official federal recognition as a tribe.
Opens up federal programs and services for Lumbee members — the same ones available to members of other federally recognized tribes.
Tribal members living in Robeson, Cumberland, Hoke, and Scotland counties in North Carolina are considered within the area where those services will be delivered.
The federal government must work with the tribe to figure out what services and programs the tribe needs.
The federal government can hold land in trust for the tribe, which gives the tribe legal protections on that land.
North Carolina handles crimes and civil cases on tribal land, unless the tribe and state agree to hand that power to the federal government.

117-hr-2877.one_liner: Create guidelines for school teams that identify students showing warning signs of harmful behavior
provisions: Requires the Department of Health and Human Services to create best practices for setting up behavioral intervention teams in schools and colleges.
These teams are made up of experts who watch for students showing signs they may hurt themselves or others.
The teams connect those students with mental health support before harm occurs.
HHS must also offer help to schools on how to set up and run these teams.

117-hr-2662.one_liner: Give inspectors general more protection and power to investigate wrongdoing
provisions: Inspectors general — the officials who catch fraud and waste inside federal agencies — can only be fired for a specific reason, like proven misconduct, not just because the President wants them gone.
Before an inspector general is put on leave or sidelined, Congress must be told.
If the President does not pick someone to fill an inspector general job, they must explain why to Congress.
Inspectors general can now require private citizens and former government workers to show up and answer questions under oath.
The inspector general at the Department of Justice can now investigate DOJ lawyers for wrongdoing.
If a federal agency blocks an inspector general from seeing information they asked for, the inspector general must tell Congress.
The oversight committee that handles complaints about inspectors general must report to Congress and the President twice a year.

117-hr-3110.one_liner: Give salaried workers and others the right to take pumping breaks at work
provisions: Under existing federal law, hourly workers already had the right to take breaks to pump breast milk at work.
This law adds salaried workers and other groups that were left out of that rule — giving them the same protections.
If a mother pumps at work while also doing job tasks, that time counts as paid work hours.

117-hr-2989.one_liner: Require federal financial regulators to use standard data formats for searchability
provisions: Tells all federal financial regulatory agencies to use the same data formats when they publish information.
The published data must be searchable online.
Sets rules for how data is labeled and organized so information from different agencies can be compared.
Agencies covered include those that oversee stocks, bank deposits, and trading in goods like oil and grain.

117-hr-2930.one_liner: Ban exports of illegally obtained Native American cultural items and raise prison sentences
provisions: Makes it illegal to send Native American cultural items or human remains out of the United States if they were stolen or taken illegally.
Doubles the maximum prison sentence for selling, buying, or moving illegally obtained Native American human remains or cultural items — from 5 years to 10 years.
Creates a process for returning stolen or illegally taken cultural items back to Native American tribes and Native Hawaiian groups, including through voluntary returns.
Requires the Department of the Interior and the Department of State to each assign a person whose job is to help tribes get their items back, including through training sessions.
Sets up a working group made up of representatives from Native American tribes and Native Hawaiian groups to give advice on stopping illegal trade in cultural items and human remains.

117-hr-3193.one_liner: Fund grants to bring or improve high-speed internet to rural areas
provisions: Lets the Department of Commerce give out grants to help bring high-speed internet to places that don't have it or need better service.
Grant money can be used for planning, buying land, building, or improving internet infrastructure.
Public agencies and nonprofits that receive grant money must keep ownership of the property for as long as the project is in use.
Grant money can be combined with other federal funding to cover the cost of a project.

117-hr-3005.one_liner: Remove all Confederate statues from the Capitol and replace a bust with Thurgood Marshall's
provisions: Take down the bust of Roger Brooke Taney from the Old Supreme Court room in the Capitol and put up a bust of Thurgood Marshall in its place.
Remove all statues and busts of people who voluntarily fought for the Confederacy from parts of the Capitol that visitors can walk through.
Also remove statues of three people listed by name: Charles Brantley Aycock, John Caldwell Calhoun, and James Paul Clarke.
Store all removed statues in a Capitol storage area.
Let states take back a removed statue if the state agrees to pay for shipping.
Let states send a new statue to replace any of theirs that gets removed.
Stop any new statues of people who served the Confederacy from being placed in National Statuary Hall.

117-hr-3537.one_liner: Fund research and speed up access to new ALS treatments
provisions: Gives grants to groups that help ALS patients get experimental drugs that are not yet fully approved
Gives grants to researchers working on drugs that treat ALS and other brain-wasting diseases
Creates a partnership between the NIH, the FDA, and outside groups like universities and nonprofits to work on ALS drugs together
Requires the FDA to post a 5-year plan on its website for how it will help develop new drugs for rare brain diseases

117-hr-3469.one_liner: Give the Boots to Business program official legal standing under the SBA
provisions: Makes the Boots to Business program an official part of the Small Business Administration by writing it into law.
The program teaches veterans and active-duty military members how to start and run a business.
Before this bill, the program ran without a permanent legal home — this bill locks it in place.

117-hr-3325.one_liner: Award four congressional gold medals to police who protected the Capitol on January 6, 2021
provisions: Gives four congressional gold medals to the U.S. Capitol Police and the D.C. Metropolitan Police Department for their actions on January 6, 2021.
The medals go to the two police agencies as a group, not to individual officers.
Congressional gold medals are one of the highest honors Congress can give to a person or group.
Congress has given out fewer than 200 of these medals in U.S. history.

117-hr-3462.one_liner: Require the SBA to publish yearly reports on its computer security
provisions: The Small Business Administration must publish a report every year about its computer security systems.
Each report must rate how strong the SBA's current computer systems are and lay out a plan to improve them.
Each report must list all SBA computer equipment made by companies based in China.
Each report must describe any security breaches or threats the SBA faced in the past two years, and what steps the SBA took to respond.

117-hr-3533.one_liner: Create official job categories for tech workers in the federal government
provisions: The Office of Personnel Management must create official job categories for federal workers in software development, software engineering, data science, and data management.
OPM can create one shared category covering all four tech fields, or separate categories for each field.
These job categories apply only to federal government positions, not private-sector jobs.

117-hr-3599.one_liner: Let federal cybersecurity workers temporarily swap jobs across agencies
provisions: Federal workers in tech and cybersecurity jobs can take temporary assignments at other federal agencies.
Each agency decides which of its tech jobs can take part in the program.
The Office of Personnel Management writes the rules for how workers move between agencies.
The Government Accountability Office checks whether the program is working and how many agencies and workers have joined.

117-hr-3635.one_liner: Change how the government stores, maintains, and shares its emergency medical supply stockpile
provisions: The government can share emergency supplies from the national stockpile with other federal agencies through September 2024.
The government must keep all stockpile supplies in working order and can hire companies to maintain them.
The government must build U.S.-made reserves of certain supplies and can partner with manufacturers to produce them through September 2024.
States can get grants to build their own stockpiles of emergency supplies for public health crises.
The government must publish clear rules for how it decides who gets supplies from the stockpile.
It must also explain when requests are denied or only partly filled.
During the COVID-19 emergency, the government must release monthly reports showing what states, tribes, and local governments asked for and received.

117-hr-3616.one_liner: Study whether Bear River areas in Utah and Idaho should become a National Heritage Area
provisions: The Department of the Interior must study land along the Bear River in Utah and Idaho
The study checks whether this area should be named a National Heritage Area
No final decision is made by this bill — it only calls for the study

117-hr-3709.one_liner: Review and improve how FEMA checks damage after disasters
provisions: FEMA must send Congress a report explaining how it checks damage after disasters, covering the last five years.
FEMA must form a panel of advisors to help improve how those damage checks are done.

117-hr-3593.one_liner: Fund new science research programs at the Department of Energy
provisions: Sets up new research programs at the Department of Energy covering topics like energy, climate, coastal zones, and the basic building blocks of matter.
Creates a program called QUEST that gives more scientists access to quantum computing tools.
Keeps U.S. scientists involved in the Large Hadron Collider, a major physics experiment based in Europe.
Creates a research program on fusion energy, which uses the same process as the sun to produce power.
Starts a high-powered laser research program.
Requires the Department of Energy to hire more science, technology, engineering, and math workers and bring in people from more backgrounds.

117-hr-3730.one_liner: Create a VA advisory committee for veterans in U.S. territories and Pacific island nations
provisions: Creates a new group inside the Department of Veterans Affairs made up of advisors who focus on veterans living in U.S. territories and nearby Pacific nations.
The committee covers eight places: American Samoa, Guam, Puerto Rico, the Northern Mariana Islands, the U.S. Virgin Islands, Micronesia, the Marshall Islands, and Palau.
The committee will review VA programs and services and suggest ways to better reach veterans in those areas.

117-hr-3985.one_liner: Add 8,000 more visas for Afghans who helped U.S. or NATO forces
provisions: Adds 8,000 more special visas for Afghan people who worked for the U.S. government or a NATO mission in Afghanistan
These visas are available until all 8,000 have been given out — there is no deadline to use them
Spouses and children of the main applicant do not count against the 8,000 limit
Removes the rule that required applicants to submit a sworn statement describing the danger they face because of their work
Removes the rule that required certain applicants to prove their job duties were sensitive or trusted

117-hr-391.one_liner: Create a U.S. council to coordinate responses to global disease outbreaks
provisions: Creates a new government council to coordinate how U.S. agencies work together on global disease threats.
The council gives policy recommendations, helps agencies do their jobs, and checks whether the U.S. is meeting its commitments.
The bill covers help given to other countries to prepare for disease outbreaks.
The President picks a single person to lead and report on the U.S. response when a global health emergency happens.

117-hr-3919.one_liner: Stop the FCC from approving equipment that poses a national security risk
provisions: The FCC must stop reviewing or approving new applications for equipment it has flagged as a national security risk
Equipment already on the FCC's risk list cannot get new government approval to be used in the U.S.
The FCC must write new rules putting this ban into effect

117-hr-390.one_liner: Rename a federal building in Memphis after Odell Horton
provisions: Changes the official name of the federal building at 167 North Main Street in Memphis, Tennessee
The building was previously named the Clifford Davis and Odell Horton Federal Building
After this bill, the building is officially called the Odell Horton Federal Building

117-hr-4026.one_liner: Require a federal report on how HHS tracks health factors like income and education
provisions: The GAO, a federal watchdog office, must write a report on what HHS has done about social factors that affect health.
The report covers how HHS collects data on factors like income, education, and where people live.
The report checks whether that data collection follows privacy laws.
