117-hr-8876.one_liner: Extend and increase funding for home visits for new and expecting parents through 2027
provisions: Keeps the Maternal, Infant, and Early Childhood Home Visiting Program running through 2027
Increases the total amount of money the program receives each year
Sets rules for how that money gets divided among states and groups
Gives tribal communities a larger share of program funds than before
Creates a public website where anyone can see how the program is performing
Requires the program to find ways to reduce paperwork and reporting for staff
Lets home visitors meet with families online instead of in person, under certain conditions

117-hres-1130.one_liner: Express support for Finland and Sweden joining NATO
provisions: The U.S. Congress says it supports Finland and Sweden applying to join NATO.
Congress says it opposes any move by Russia to stop Finland and Sweden from joining.
Congress calls on all NATO member countries to approve Finland and Sweden's membership quickly.

117-hr-8987.one_liner: Send one-time payments to 9/11 victims and their families from an existing fund
provisions: 9/11 victims, their spouses, and their children get one-time catch-up payments from the U.S. Victims of State Sponsored Terrorism Fund
The money to pay for this comes from leftover Small Business Administration funds that were set aside for the Paycheck Protection Program but never used

117-hr-8873.one_liner: Change the rules for how electoral votes are cast and counted in presidential elections
provisions: Each state must use laws passed before Election Day to pick its electors, the people who officially cast electoral votes for that state.
A state can only extend its voting time because of a major disaster, terrorist attack, or widespread power outage.
The event must stop a large number of people from voting or destroy many ballots already cast.
Each state's governor must officially sign off on which electors the state is sending.
When Congress meets to count electoral votes, the Vice President's only job is to keep the process moving, not to decide which votes count.
To object to a state's electoral votes in Congress, at least one-third of both the House and Senate must agree.
Before this bill, just one member from each chamber could raise an objection.

117-hres-1168.one_liner: Urge the President to strengthen trade between the US and Caribbean nations
provisions: The US Congress states that trade with Caribbean countries is important to the US economy.
Congress calls on the President to make Caribbean trade programs a priority.
The resolution supports trade deals with Caribbean nations that build long-term economic stability in the region.

117-hres-1254.one_liner: Set House debate rules for three bills on health, trails, and pensions
provisions: Lets the House vote on a bill to study cardiovascular health in South Asian Americans.
Lets the House vote on a bill to finish the Continental Divide National Scenic Trail.
Lets the House vote on a bill to raise guaranteed pension payouts for certain retirees.
This rule does not change any law on its own.
It only sets up how the three bills will be debated on the House floor.

117-hres-1224.one_liner: Set the rules for debating five separate bills in the House
provisions: This bill set the rules for how the House would debate and vote on five other bills.
One of those bills funded the military and set troop levels for 2023.
One would have improved college grants for children of soldiers killed in Iraq or Afghanistan.
Two bills dealt with abortion access. One would protect people's ability to get an abortion. The other would stop states from blocking people from traveling out of state to get one.
One bill would have created a national alert system to warn the public about active shooter situations.

117-hres-1232.one_liner: Set the rules for how Congress debates three separate bills
provisions: Lets Congress vote on a bill to fund transportation and housing programs through September 2023
Lets Congress vote on a bill about the legal right to use contraception
Lets Congress vote on a bill about federal marriage rules
Sets time limits and debate rules for how each of those three bills gets discussed on the House floor

117-hres-1204.one_liner: Set rules for how Congress votes on three separate bills
provisions: Lets Congress vote on renaming a federal courthouse in Tallahassee, Florida after Joseph Woodrow Hatchett
Lets Congress vote on extending a program that gives schools flexibility in how they serve meals to children
Lets Congress vote on funding for the Legislative Branch for the year ending September 30, 2022

117-hres-1300.one_liner: Change House rules to speed up how certain resolutions get scheduled for a vote
provisions: Lets the House vote on certain rules committee resolutions the same day they are introduced, instead of waiting a day
Applies this change through July 29, 2022
Changes how bills on the Consensus Calendar — a list of bills with broad support — get scheduled for a vote

117-hres-1289.one_liner: Set the rules for how Congress votes on a spending bill for its own operations
provisions: Sets the steps the House must follow to vote on a spending deal that the Senate changed
Covers government spending for Congress itself for the year ending September 30, 2022
Sets rules for how Congress runs its business between August 1 and September 12, 2022

117-hres-1316.one_liner: Set the House rules for debating a Senate budget bill
provisions: The House set specific rules for how it would debate and vote on the Senate's version of H.R. 5376, a budget bill.
H.R. 5376 was originally passed using a budget process called reconciliation, which lets Congress change spending and tax rules with a simple majority vote.
The rule controlled how much time members of Congress could spend debating the Senate's changes before voting.

117-hres-1256.one_liner: Set the rules for debating two bills in the House
provisions: This bill sets the time limits and debate rules for two other bills before the House votes on them
One of the two bills would change rules about keeping certain wild animals in captivity
The other bill would extend the ability of Medicare patients to see doctors by video or phone call

117-hres-1302.one_liner: Set the debate and voting rules for a bill that would limit assault weapons
provisions: This is a procedural rule — it sets the terms for how the House of Representatives debates and votes on a bill.
The bill being debated, H.R. 1808, is a separate piece of legislation that would put limits on who can own certain guns and what types of guns can be sold.
The rule gives both sides a set amount of time to speak before a vote is taken.
This rule does not change any gun laws on its own — only the final vote on H.R. 1808 would do that.

117-hres-1339.one_liner: Set the rules for debating three bills about federal jobs and the Census
provisions: Decides how long Congress can debate a bill that limits which government jobs can be removed from standard hiring rules
Decides how long Congress can debate a bill that adds protections for federal workers who report wrongdoing
Decides how long Congress can debate a bill that changes how the Census Bureau runs

117-hres-1372.one_liner: Set the House floor debate rules for a bill on counting electoral votes
provisions: Allows H.R. 8873, a bill about how Congress counts electoral votes, to be brought up for a vote in the House.
Sets how much time members of Congress can spend debating the bill before a vote is held.
Controls which changes to the bill members can propose during the debate.

117-hres-1377.one_liner: Set House debate rules for four bills on violence, policing, and mental health
provisions: This bill sets the House debate rules for four other bills — it does not create programs itself.
One bill would give money to community groups that work to reduce violence.
A second bill would fund a program to help solve violent crimes using new technology.
A third bill would give money to police departments with fewer than 200 officers.
A fourth bill would fund states and tribes to hire mental health workers.
Those workers would respond to emergencies involving people with mental illness instead of police.

117-hres-1361.one_liner: Set debate rules in Congress for a bill to let borrowers split joint student loans
provisions: This sets the rules for how Congress will debate and vote on S. 1098.
S. 1098 would let borrowers who have a joint consolidation loan split it into two separate loans.
Right now, borrowers who took out joint consolidation loans cannot split them into separate loans.
Joint consolidation loans are federal student loans that two borrowers combined into one single loan.

117-hres-1396.one_liner: Set the rules for debating three bills in the House
provisions: This bill sets the time limits and rules for how the House debates three other bills.
The first bill changes the fees companies pay before merging and adds money for antitrust enforcement.
The second bill funds mental health and drug treatment support for students and school staff.
The third bill lets voting access grants go to a U.S. territory and American Indian tribal groups.

117-hres-720.one_liner: Condemn ISIS attacks in northern Mozambique and call for action to protect civilians
provisions: The U.S. Congress condemns terrorist attacks carried out by an ISIS group in the Cabo Delgado region of Mozambique.
The resolution calls on the Mozambique government to take steps to stop the violence and keep its people safe.
No U.S. laws change and no U.S. money is spent — this is a statement of position only.

117-hres-892.one_liner: Call on Rwanda to release Paul Rusesabagina and let him return to the US
provisions: Calls on the government of Rwanda to release Paul Rusesabagina, who is being held in prison there
Calls on Rwanda to give Rusesabagina access to doctors and the medical care he needs
Calls on the US government to push Rwanda to release him in every meeting between the two countries
Expresses support for Rusesabagina's family as they work to bring him home

117-hres-1499.one_liner: Set the rules for debating four bills in the House
provisions: This bill sets the time limits and debate rules the House follows when voting on four other bills
One of those bills would give money to nonprofits that help people leaving prison find housing, jobs, and services
Another bill would set rules for medical care for pregnant women who are in prison
A third bill would keep funding a program that sends nurses or social workers to visit new and expecting parents at home
The fourth measure would end a labor dispute between railroad companies and some of their workers

117-hres-1464.one_liner: Set the debate rules for a bill about silencing agreements in sexual assault cases
provisions: This is a procedural rule that sets the terms for how the House of Representatives will debate another bill.
The underlying bill would stop courts from enforcing contracts that require people to stay silent about sexual assault or harassment before any dispute happens.
Those silencing agreements are sometimes signed before people are hired or as part of other deals.
This rule decides how much time lawmakers get to debate, what changes they can propose, and when they vote.

117-hres-1404.one_liner: Set the rules for the House to vote on two bills
provisions: This bill sets the terms for how the House of Representatives will debate and vote on two separate pieces of legislation.
One of those bills would cap how much people pay out of pocket for insulin.
The other would set aside money to pay victims of terrorism sponsored by foreign governments who have not yet received their full payment.

117-s-144.one_liner: Let a health agency buy land and build a road to a California youth center
provisions: Lets the Indian Health Service buy private land in Hemet, California at a fair price
Requires the agency to build a paved road on that land
The road gives people a way to reach the Desert Sage Youth Wellness Center, which serves Native American youth
Requires the agency to either maintain the road itself or make an agreement with Riverside County to maintain it

117-s-1098.one_liner: Let student loan borrowers split a joint loan into two separate loans
provisions: Right now, some people took out a single joint federal student loan with another borrower and cannot separate it.
This bill lets both borrowers apply together to the Department of Education to split their shared loan into two separate loans.
If one borrower is facing abuse — including financial control — by the other, or cannot reach them, they can apply alone.
They do not need the other person's agreement to split the loan in those cases.

117-s-2293.one_liner: Give FEMA disaster reservists job protections when they leave for a deployment
provisions: FEMA keeps a group of reservists, workers who can be called up when disasters hit.
This bill gives those workers job protection when they leave for a deployment.
Employers must give these workers their old jobs back when they return from a deployment.
These job protections apply even if the worker could not tell their employer before leaving.

117-s-231.one_liner: Require FEMA to create safety guides for firefighters on avoiding harmful chemicals in foam
provisions: Tells FEMA to write guides for firefighters on how to avoid contact with PFAS chemicals.
PFAS chemicals are man-made substances found in some firefighting foams and have been linked to health problems.
Tells FEMA to create guides on foam, gear, and tools that do not contain PFAS chemicals.
Tells FEMA to build a public website where firefighters can find best practices for reducing exposure to these chemicals.

117-s-2089.one_liner: Let states bury National Guard and Reserve members at state veterans cemeteries
provisions: States that get VA grant money for veterans cemeteries can now choose to bury National Guard and Reserve members who left service with an honorable discharge.
ROTC members who died while in the program under honorable conditions can also be buried at these state cemeteries.
Spouses and children of these members can be buried at the same state cemeteries.
The VA cannot turn down a state's grant application just because the state plans to bury these members.
The VA cannot enforce old grant rules, set before this bill passed, that blocked states from burying these members.
Families of eligible members can receive money to help pay for a burial plot at these cemeteries.

117-s-2794.one_liner: Raise the life insurance cap for service members and veterans from $400,000 to $500,000
provisions: Raises the maximum life insurance payout for active and former service members from $400,000 to $500,000.
This applies to two government life insurance programs: one for people currently serving and one for veterans.
If a covered service member or veteran dies, their family can receive up to $100,000 more than before.

117-s-2551.one_liner: Require federal workers who buy goods and services to take AI training
provisions: The federal office that oversees government budgets must create a training program about artificial intelligence for government workers who handle purchasing and contracts.
The training covers what AI can do and what risks come with using it.
The program must be updated at least every two years.
The office must track how many workers complete the training and collect feedback from them.

117-s-2490.one_liner: Create a national historic site in Texas honoring a school that taught Mexican-American children
provisions: Makes the Blackwell School in Marfa, Texas part of the National Park System.
The school educated children of Mexican descent from 1885 to 1965, during a time when Texas schools were segregated by race.
The site cannot open until the federal government signs an agreement with the Marfa school district to share or receive the property.
The government can only get the land through donations, donated money, or trades — not by forcing anyone to give it up.
No private or local government land can be added to the site without the written permission of the owner.
The National Park Service must write a plan for how to manage the site.

117-s-3157.one_liner: Study why some workers cannot find jobs that match their credentials from other countries
provisions: The Department of Labor must research why some people cannot find jobs that match their foreign credentials.
The bill covers people who are legally in the country but not yet citizens, and people who have become naturalized citizens.
The study must include suggestions for how the government could help these workers find jobs that match their skills.
The Department of Labor must send the results of the study to Congress.

117-s-3115.one_liner: Make permanent a rule requiring federal judges to hold yearly events for abuse survivors
provisions: Each federal district's chief judge must hold at least one public event per year.
The event must connect survivors of domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, or stalking with free legal help.
Without this bill, the rule would have ended automatically after four years.
Judges would no longer be required to hold these events once the rule expired.
This bill removes the expiration date so the rule stays in place going forward.

117-s-3369.one_liner: Rename the VA medical center in Atlanta, Georgia after veteran Max Cleland
provisions: Renames the VA medical center in Atlanta, Georgia after Joseph Maxwell 'Max' Cleland.
Max Cleland is a Vietnam War veteran who lost three limbs in combat.
He later served as a U.S. Senator from Georgia and as head of the VA.
This is a name change only — no funding, programs, or services change.

117-s-3662.one_liner: Fund airports to temporarily test fire suppression systems without releasing PFAS chemicals
provisions: The federal government will pay 100% of the cost for airports to buy equipment that tests fire suppression systems without releasing PFAS chemicals into the ground or water.
PFAS are man-made chemicals found in some fire-suppression foam used at airports.
Right now, airports often have to release PFAS into the ground or water just to test their fire systems.
This new equipment lets them run the same test without releasing any PFAS.
Scientists have linked PFAS exposure to possible health problems in humans.

117-s-3846.one_liner: Keep funding grants that connect police and courts with mental health services
provisions: Keeps the Justice and Mental Health Collaboration Program running through the year starting October 2025
Gives grants to states, cities, and tribes to help police and courts work with people who have mental health problems
Lets grant money pay for training prosecutors on how to redirect people away from jail and into treatment
Lets grant money pay for programs where police officers and mental health workers respond to crisis calls together
Opens up grants to cover suicide prevention programs, case management, and the 988 mental health phone line
Keeps the Department of Justice's job of tracking and reporting how many people with mental illness are in prisons and jails

117-s-3470.one_liner: Require agencies to report contractors linked to human trafficking to oversight offices
provisions: When a government agency gets a report confirming that a contractor, grant recipient, or their partners took part in human trafficking, the agency must report them to its suspension and debarment office — the office that can bar companies from getting future government contracts.
Under current law, agencies only have to consider reporting these contractors. This bill makes reporting required.
The Office of Management and Budget must send Congress a report on how well the government is following its own rules against human trafficking in contracts.

117-s-3451.one_liner: Speed up federal permits for tech projects including semiconductors and artificial intelligence
provisions: Six types of tech projects can now use a faster federal permitting process.
Those types include the semiconductor industry, artificial intelligence systems, and high-performance computing and advanced hardware.
Quantum computing and science, data storage and management, and cybersecurity are also included.
This faster process requires government agencies to review a project at the same time instead of one after another.

117-s-4359.one_liner: Rename the VA office in Atlanta, Georgia after Senator Johnny Isakson
provisions: The Department of Veterans Affairs office in Atlanta, Georgia will be officially renamed the Senator Johnny Isakson Department of Veterans Affairs Atlanta Regional Office.
The office can also be called the Isakson VA Atlanta Regional Office for short.
Johnny Isakson was a U.S. Senator from Georgia who served from 2005 until he resigned in December 2019 due to health problems.

117-s-4003.one_liner: Create federal training programs to help police de-escalate crises
provisions: The Department of Justice will create training programs for police officers and mental health professionals.
The programs cover how to de-escalate tense situations and avoid using force.
They also teach officers how to respond when someone is having a mental health or suicidal crisis.
The federal government will give money to states to pay for this training.

117-s-442.one_liner: Require federal buildings to use the most energy-efficient lighting available
provisions: Federal buildings run by the General Services Administration must use the most efficient lighting systems available, not just any energy-efficient bulb.
The new rule covers the full lighting system — including sensors and how light is spread across a room — not just the bulbs.
When the government buys new lighting, it must choose the option that costs the least over the full life of the product, including energy costs.
The General Services Administration must share information with state, local, and tribal governments about how to buy and use these lighting systems.

117-s-3895.one_liner: Keep the U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom operating through 2024
provisions: Keeps the U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom running through the end of 2024.
The commission tracks how countries around the world treat people because of their religion.
Without this bill, the commission would have lost its power to operate after 2022.
The commission sends yearly reports to Congress and the President listing countries with serious religious freedom problems.

117-s-4524.one_liner: Stop courts from enforcing silence agreements in sexual harassment or assault cases
provisions: If someone signs a nondisclosure or nondisparagement agreement before a sexual harassment or assault dispute starts, that agreement cannot be enforced in court.
This applies to cases under federal, tribal, or state law.
Courts cannot use these pre-signed agreements to stop a person from speaking about sexual harassment or assault they experienced.

117-s-958.one_liner: Let health centers use federal grants to build clinics or mobile medical units
provisions: Health centers can now use federal grant money to construct or renovate buildings where they provide care.
Health centers can also use that same grant money to set up mobile medical clinics — vehicles or portable units that bring care to patients.
Before this bill, mobile clinics could only get grant funding if they were connected to a permanent, full-time location. Now they can qualify on their own.
These grants go to health centers that serve communities where people have trouble getting medical care.

117-s-4785.one_liner: Extend a $5,000 fee on convicted sex traffickers by 19 days
provisions: People or companies convicted of sex abuse or human trafficking crimes must pay a $5,000 fee on top of other penalties.
This fee was set to end on September 11, 2022, but the bill moves that end date to September 30, 2022.
Money from this fee goes into a fund for victims of human trafficking inside the U.S.

117-s-4900.one_liner: Extend and add security rules to federal small business research grant programs
provisions: Keeps two federal programs running through the year starting October 2024 — these programs give money to small businesses to do research that could turn into products.
Stops small businesses from getting grants if they have financial ties to certain foreign countries.
Requires government agencies that run these programs to check whether applicants have connections to foreign governments before approving their grants.
Small businesses that have already received many grants must meet stricter performance standards to keep getting money.
Government inspectors must audit small businesses that are subject to those stricter standards.
The Defense Department, Energy Department, Health and Human Services, and National Science Foundation must each report on whether these programs create national security risks.

119-hconres-40.one_liner: Order the President to pull U.S. troops out of fighting with Iran
provisions: Tells the President to stop using U.S. military forces in any fighting against Iran.
The President must stop unless Congress officially declares war or votes to allow military action against Iran.
U.S. forces can stay if they are defending the United States, an ally, or a partner from an attack that is happening right now.
Under existing law, the President has up to 60 days to use military force before needing Congress to approve it.

119-hr-1011.one_liner: Give farmers and forest owners more money upfront to recover from natural disasters
provisions: Farmers can now get up to 75% of the cost of rebuilding or fixing farmland paid upfront, before the work is done — up from 25%
Farmers can get 50% of repair costs paid upfront, also up from 25%
Wildfire damage now counts for disaster payments even if the fire was started by humans or the government, as long as it spread naturally
Forest owners on private land can now get up to 75% of emergency costs paid upfront — currently they get nothing upfront
Forest owners must spend the money within 180 days of receiving it

119-hr-1689.one_liner: Give Haitians in the US temporary permission to stay and work for 18 months
provisions: Gives Haitians in the US a temporary legal status called TPS starting August 3, 2025, lasting 18 months.
While they have this status, they can get a work permit.
While they have this status, they cannot be held by immigration officials just because of their immigration status.
While they have this status, they cannot be deported.

119-hr-7613.one_liner: Require military and civilian aircraft to share location signals and strengthen air safety rules
provisions: Military helicopters must broadcast their location when flying in shared airspace, unless doing so would give away a secret mission.
Military helicopters on special missions in the Washington, DC area are not required to broadcast their location.
Those helicopters must go through a safety review and take steps to reduce the risk of a crash.
By December 31, 2031, military aircraft must be able to receive location signals from other planes and helicopters.
By December 31, 2031, civilian aircraft already required to broadcast their location must also be able to receive location signals.
The FAA must set limits on how long supervisory air traffic controllers can stay at their post without a break.
The FAA must notify people involved in close-call incidents in the air and review helicopter flight paths near Reagan National Airport.

119-hres-1156.one_liner: Express support for tax policies that help working families
provisions: This is a resolution, not a law — it does not create new rules or change anything on its own.
It states that Congress supports tax policies for working families and recognizes the tax relief passed in the 2025 reconciliation act.
It only states a position and has no legal effect.

119-hr-6398.one_liner: Remove EPA review of federal projects already reviewed under another law
provisions: Right now, the EPA must review and give comments on big federal construction projects and other major federal actions. This bill removes that requirement.
Federal projects already go through a review process under a law called NEPA. This bill stops the EPA from doing a second review on top of that.
The change applies to new federal construction projects and proposed federal rules that already require NEPA review.

119-hr-6409.one_liner: Exempt states from air quality penalties when outside sources like wildfires cause the pollution
provisions: States can avoid federal sanctions if outside pollution — like wildfire smoke — causes their air quality problems.
This applies to areas rated severe or extreme for ozone, or serious for particle pollution.
States can also avoid federal fees for missing air quality targets if outside pollution is the cause.
To keep the exemption, states must prove every five years that outside pollution is still the cause.
An area cannot be labeled as failing air quality standards if the pollution comes from outside the United States.
Pollution from other countries counts as an outside source even when caused by human activity, not just natural events.

119-hres-965.one_liner: Set the rules for debating a bill about Haiti temporary protected status
provisions: This resolution sets the rules for how the House of Representatives will debate and vote on a separate bill called H.R. 1689.
The bill being debated would require the U.S. government to give Haitians temporary protected status.
Temporary protected status lets people from a certain country stay and work legally in the U.S. for a set time.
The U.S. grants this status to people whose home country has gone through a disaster, war, or other serious crisis.
This resolution is not the Haiti bill itself — it only controls how that bill gets debated on the House floor.

119-hres-1174.one_liner: Set the rules for debating four bills about clean air and taxes
provisions: Lets Congress debate a bill that changes how the EPA handles air quality data when wildfires or other events affect the readings
Lets Congress debate a bill that changes how the EPA reviews laws proposed by Congress before they pass
Lets Congress debate a bill that sets rules for pollution that comes into the U.S. from other countries
Lets Congress debate a resolution that says tax rules should support working families

119-sjres-138.one_liner: Block a proposed U.S. weapons sale to Israel
provisions: Congress votes to stop a proposed sale of U.S. weapons and military equipment to Israel.
Under U.S. law, Congress can pass a resolution to block any proposed weapons sale to a foreign country before it goes through.
If this resolution passes both chambers and becomes law, the sale cannot happen.
The resolution does not cancel existing weapons already delivered — it only stops this specific proposed sale.

119-sjres-123.one_liner: Order U.S. troops out of military action against Iran without a vote from Congress
provisions: Tells the President to stop any U.S. military attacks on or inside Iran
Says those attacks have not been approved by Congress
Uses the War Powers Resolution, a 1973 law that lets Congress pull back troops when war has not been declared

119-hres-1175.one_liner: Set the debate rules for a vote on extending a U.S. surveillance law
provisions: This resolution sets the rules for how the House of Representatives will debate and vote on a separate bill about U.S. surveillance powers.
The bill being debated would extend the government's power to collect foreign intelligence under the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) through October 20, 2027.
FISA lets the U.S. government collect information on people outside the country who may be threats to national security.
This bill would keep those powers active through October 20, 2027.
This resolution itself does not change any law — it only controls how the debate in the House is run.

119-hr-4690.one_liner: Remove the rule requiring federal buildings to stop using fossil fuels by 2030
provisions: Cancels the rule that required new and renovated federal buildings to phase out fossil fuels by 2030
Tells the Department of Energy to act as if the phase-out rule never existed until new rules are written
Stops green building certification programs from blocking federal buildings from getting certified just because they use fossil fuels

119-hr-2493.one_liner: Renew federal grants for health care in rural areas through 2030
provisions: Federal money for rural health care is renewed through 2030.
One set of grants helps rural doctors, clinics, and hospitals offer more services to more people.
A second set of grants helps local health care groups work together and share resources.
A third set of grants helps small rural health care providers give better care.
Grant money must be used to reach people in rural areas who have trouble getting health care.
Those same communities must be involved in planning how the money is spent.

119-hr-5200.one_liner: Require the FCC to study 911 outages and hold yearly public hearings on disasters
provisions: The FCC must publish a report on 911 outages that are not currently required to be reported to the government.
The report must also look at whether phone companies should include images or video when reporting outages.
The FCC must recommend rule changes to fix gaps in how outages are reported.
The FCC must hold public hearings once a year after any major event that knocked out phone or internet service for at least a week.
After each hearing, the FCC must release a public report on how many outages happened, how long they lasted, and steps to make networks more reliable.
All reports must be posted on the FCC's public website.

119-sjres-32.one_liner: Block a proposed U.S. weapons sale to Israel
provisions: Stops the U.S. government from going through with a planned sale of weapons and military equipment to Israel.
Congress would use its power to reject the sale before it is completed.
The specific weapons and equipment in the sale are listed in the original sale proposal but not named in the resolution.

119-hr-1681.one_liner: Create a team to speed up federal reviews of broadband permits on public land
provisions: Creates a team made up of heads of federal land agencies to help those agencies process broadband permit requests.
The team holds regular calls to make sure each agency is keeping up with its backlog of permit requests.
The team sets goals for how fast permit requests should be reviewed and tracks whether agencies hit those goals.
The team must send Congress a report on how well it is working.

119-hr-5201.one_liner: Require the FCC to report on whether companies follow the direct-dial 911 law
provisions: Requires the FCC to publish a report on whether companies that make multi-line phone systems are following the direct-dial 911 law.
Multi-line phone systems are used in places like offices, hotels, and schools.
The report must describe how well companies are following the rule and what is making it hard for others to comply.
The report must also include suggestions for changes to FCC rules or new laws if needed.

119-hres-1189.one_liner: Set the rules for House floor debate on four energy and environment bills
provisions: This resolution sets the rules for how the House will debate and vote on four other bills.
One bill removes federal rules that set energy efficiency standards for buildings.
One is a House statement expressing support for rural communities — it does not change any laws.

One bill changes the Endangered Species Act to speed up permits for landowners and reward private landowners who protect wildlife on their property. It also requires the government to publicly report on progress recovering at-risk species.
One bill removes the requirement to get a federal drilling permit for some geothermal energy projects. It also removes the environmental review requirement for those same projects.

119-hres-1182.one_liner: State that the House supports rural communities in the 119th Congress
provisions: The House says it has supported rural areas through rules on energy, health care, manufacturing, and internet access.
This resolution does not create new laws, change any rules, or spend any money.
It is a statement of support only.

119-hr-5587.one_liner: Remove federal permit and review requirements for geothermal drilling on state and private land
provisions: Geothermal energy comes from heat stored underground and can be used to generate electricity or heat buildings.
Companies on private or state land no longer need a federal drilling permit for geothermal work.
This applies when they hold a state permit and the federal government owns less than half of the underground heat resources.
These projects do not need to go through a federal environmental review.
These projects do not need to check whether they might harm endangered plants or animals.
Historic preservation review is skipped unless the state has no law protecting historic sites.
These exemptions do not apply on land where Native American tribes hold ownership.

119-hr-6387.one_liner: Expand what counts as an exceptional event for federal air quality rules
provisions: The EPA must leave certain pollution data out when checking if a state broke federal air quality rules.
A state can request this by proving a specific event — not everyday pollution from cars or factories — caused the spike.
Controlled burns and other human actions designed to copy natural events now count as valid exceptional events.
States can now point to hot, dry weather or still air as causes of their pollution readings; those conditions were not recognized as valid causes before.
The EPA must update its rules for handling air quality data affected by actions taken to reduce wildfire risk.
When several states file about the same event, the EPA must do a regional study covering all of them.

119-s-1020.one_liner: Give hydropower projects more time to start construction
provisions: Hydropower projects that got a license before March 13, 2020 can ask for more time before they have to start building.
Right now, these projects can get up to 8 extra years to start construction. This bill adds up to 6 more years on top of that.
The extra time comes in three 2-year blocks, so projects can ask for more time as they need it.
If a project's license already expired, FERC can bring it back to life as if it never ran out.

119-hr-227.one_liner: Give clergy a two-year window to undo their Social Security and Medicare tax exemption
provisions: Some clergy and Christian Science practitioners can apply to skip paying Social Security and Medicare taxes on their church pay.
That exemption has been permanent — once granted, they could not undo it.
This bill opens a two-year window for those clergy to cancel their exemption and start paying into Social Security and Medicare.
Clergy who do not opt back in will have no Social Security or Medicare benefits from their church work.
That changes only if they have enough credits from other jobs.
The IRS must create a plan to let clergy know they can now undo their exemption.

119-sjres-114.one_liner: Order U.S. military forces out of fighting Iran that Congress never approved
provisions: Congress has not voted to allow military action against Iran, but U.S. forces have been involved in fighting there.
This resolution uses a 1973 law called the War Powers Resolution to require the President to pull U.S. forces back.
The President would be required to end U.S. involvement in the fighting after the resolution passes.

119-sconres-33.one_liner: Set the federal government's spending and revenue targets for 2026 through 2035
provisions: Sets targets for how much the government plans to spend and take in each year from 2026 through 2035.
Tells four committees — covering homeland security, immigration law, courts, and government operations — to send budget proposals by May 15, 2026.
Those proposals can add no more than $70 billion total to the deficit across 2026–2035.
In the Senate, these budget bills can pass with 51 votes instead of the usual 60, skipping a step that normally lets senators delay a vote.
Sets aside budget room for border security and immigration changes that do not add to the deficit.

119-hr-7567.one_liner: Renew federal farm and food programs through 2031
provisions: Keeps USDA farm and food programs running through 2031, when Congress will need to renew them again
Continues food assistance — known as SNAP or food stamps — for the roughly 42 million Americans who use it to buy groceries
Renews crop insurance that pays farmers when weather or other problems wipe out their crops
Keeps programs that pay farmers to protect soil, water, and wildlife on their land
Continues government loans that help farmers buy land, equipment, and supplies
Updates rules on who can buy U.S. farmland from outside the country
Funds farm research and programs for people living in rural towns and communities

119-s-1318.one_liner: Find Jewish veterans buried abroad under wrong grave markers and notify their families
provisions: Find Jewish veterans buried abroad in U.S. military cemeteries under grave markers that did not show they were Jewish.
Reach out to the families and descendants of those veterans.
The government must try to hire a nonprofit group to run this program for the first 10 years after the bill passes.

119-hr-7959.one_liner: Strengthen protections and payment rules for people who report tax cheats to the IRS
provisions: People who report tax fraud to the IRS can now keep their name private in court.
A judge can reveal their name only if the public benefit of knowing outweighs the risk to them.
When a whistleblower disputes their award, the judge must take a fresh look at the full case, not just check for obvious errors.
If the IRS is late notifying a whistleblower about their award, the IRS must pay interest on top of the award amount.
Whistleblowers can deduct lawyer's fees from their taxes, whether the award came through the required or optional payment program.
The IRS must include a list of up to 10 top tax avoidance schemes reported by whistleblowers in its yearly report to Congress.

119-sjres-124.one_liner: Order U.S. military forces to stop fighting in or against Cuba without a vote from Congress
provisions: Tells the President to pull U.S. military forces out of any fighting in or against Cuba
Says Congress has not approved any military action against Cuba
Uses the War Powers Resolution, a 1973 law that lets Congress stop military operations the President started without approval

119-s-4465.one_liner: Extend the government's legal authority to monitor foreign communications for national security
provisions: Lets U.S. intelligence agencies collect electronic messages and calls of people outside the United States without getting a separate warrant for each person
Requires the government to get a court order before searching collected messages for information about an individual U.S. citizen or resident
Keeps the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court in charge of reviewing and approving the rules that govern how these collections work
Extends these collection powers for 5 more years, through 2031

119-hres-1224.one_liner: Set the rules for debating five separate bills in Congress
provisions: Sets the time limits and debate rules for five bills before the full House
One of the five bills covers farm programs through 2031
One bill requires parents to approve any changes to a child's name, pronouns, or bathroom access at public schools
One bill sets the federal government's spending plan for 2026 through 2035
One bill creates a program to find and correct grave markers for Jewish American soldiers buried overseas under wrong symbols
One bill changes clean air rules related to ethanol content in gas

119-sres-690.one_liner: Let the Senate vote on multiple nominations at the same time
provisions: Lets the Senate group certain nominations together and vote on all of them in one vote, instead of voting on each person one at a time.
The nominations being grouped are already listed on the Senate's Executive Calendar — the waiting list of people nominated for government jobs.
This only changes how the Senate holds the vote, not who is nominated or what the positions are.

119-hconres-75.one_liner: Order the President to pull U.S. troops out of fighting against Iran
provisions: Tells the President to stop U.S. military forces from taking part in attacks on Iran by March 30, 2026.
The order does not apply if Congress votes to declare war on Iran or approves military action before that date.
U.S. forces can still defend themselves, American diplomats, military bases, or allied countries if attacked.

119-sjres-184.one_liner: Order US military forces to stop fighting Iran without a vote from Congress
provisions: Tells the President to pull US military forces out of any fighting with Iran
Says Congress has not voted to approve military action against Iran
Uses the War Powers Act, a law that lets Congress stop a President from keeping troops in a war zone without approval
Applies to any US forces currently involved in attacks on or inside Iran

119-sjres-139.one_liner: Cancel the EPA rule that blocked Colorado's regional haze plan
provisions: Regional haze is air pollution that makes it harder to see clearly in national parks and wilderness areas.
Colorado made its own plan to reduce that kind of air pollution, as required by federal law.
The EPA reviewed Colorado's plan and rejected it with a formal rule.
When the EPA rejects a state's plan, the EPA puts its own federal plan in place for that state instead.
This resolution cancels the EPA's rejection rule, so the EPA's federal plan does not take over and Colorado's state plan is no longer blocked.

119-sjres-99.one_liner: Bring back automatic work permit renewals for certain non-citizens
provisions: Right now, some non-citizens can keep working while waiting for their work permit to be renewed — this is called an automatic extension.
A government rule ended that automatic extension for certain people, meaning their work permits expired while they waited.
This resolution cancels that rule, bringing back the automatic extension so those non-citizens can keep working during the wait.
The people affected are non-citizens who already have work permits and applied to renew them before the permit ran out.

119-hconres-96.one_liner: Express support for law enforcement officers and their contributions
provisions: Congress states that it supports law enforcement officers.
Congress recognizes the work that law enforcement officers do.
Congress recognizes the risks they take on the job.

119-hr-5625.one_liner: List states that free people charged with violent, sexual, or public disorder crimes before trial
provisions: The Department of Justice must publish a list every year of states and cities that release people before trial without requiring bail.
The list covers people charged with violent, sexual, or public disorder crimes — like murder, rape, break-ins, looting, or vandalism.
People on those charges can be released by signing a promise to appear in court, with no money paid upfront.
This bill does not change any state's bail laws — it only collects and publishes information about which states use this practice.

119-hr-2853.one_liner: Crack down on organized theft rings that steal and resell goods across state lines
provisions: Lets prosecutors add up stolen goods over 12 months to reach the dollar amount needed for federal charges, instead of counting each theft separately.
Lets the government seize money and property tied to organized retail theft.
Makes organized retail theft a crime that can also be charged under federal money laundering laws.
Expands money laundering laws to cover people who use prepaid cards or gift cards to move stolen money.
Creates a center inside the Department of Homeland Security to coordinate federal agencies fighting organized retail theft rings.

119-hr-2071.one_liner: Block U.S. money from going to foreign shrimp farms through international banks
provisions: Stops U.S. government money from going to international banks — like the International Monetary Fund — if those banks use the money to fund shrimp farms, shrimp processing, or shrimp exports in other countries.
Requires the Treasury Department to attach this condition every time it sends money to these international banks.

Requires a government watchdog agency to check every year whether U.S. representatives at these banks are following existing rules against funding foreign goods that compete with American farmers, and report the findings to Congress.

119-hr-1346.one_liner: Let gas stations sell higher-ethanol fuel year-round in all states
provisions: Gas with 15% ethanol, called E15, can be sold during summer months — right now, most states cannot sell it in summer because it evaporates faster in heat and can worsen air quality
States that had already put rules in place to block E15 summer sales lose those rules when this bill passes, but they can apply to get new ones after that
Small oil refineries that are required to blend renewable fuel into their gas or diesel can get unused blending credits back from the EPA in some cases
The bill changes a Clean Air Act rule that set limits on how much summer gas is allowed to evaporate — those limits now apply the same way to E15 as they already do to regular E10 gas

119-hres-1251.one_liner: Call on leaders to speak out against antisemitism and honor Jewish-American servicemembers
provisions: Calls on elected officials to publicly condemn antisemitism and take action against it
Calls on faith leaders and community leaders to do the same
Honors Jewish Americans who have served in the U.S. military
Commits to protecting all Americans, including Jewish Americans, from violence or persecution while worshipping

119-hres-1252.one_liner: Honor law enforcement officers and express condolences to families of those killed on the job
provisions: States that Congress supports police and other law enforcement officers across the country.
States that Congress recognizes the need to give officers the equipment, training, and resources to stay safe while protecting the public.
States that Congress honors law enforcement officers for their acts of heroism and sacrifice.
States that Congress offers condolences and thanks to the families of officers who died in the line of duty.

119-hr-8365.one_liner: Add rules for court-appointed monitors who oversee local police departments
provisions: When a court orders a city or police department to make changes, it can appoint a monitor — an outside person who checks that those changes happen.
Before a monitor is picked, the public must be told and given a chance to comment.
One person can only be a monitor for one case at a time.
Monitors can only serve for up to five years.
Monitors must publicly report what they charge and what work they do.
There is a cap on how much monitors can be paid.
Monitors are allowed to do some of the work for free.

119-hr-8469.one_liner: Fund building projects on military bases and veterans services through September 2027
provisions: Gives money to the Army, Navy, Marine Corps, Air Force, and National Guard to build and repair military bases
Funds VA hospitals, veterans benefit payments, and military cemeteries for the year ending September 2027
Sets aside money to build and fix housing for military families who live on or near bases
Funds housing for service members who live on base without their families
Pays for the court that hears cases when veterans are denied benefits
Funds the upkeep of American war memorials and cemeteries in other countries
Sets rules for how all of these funds can and cannot be spent

119-hr-6260.one_liner: Treat organizations that pay bail for defendants as insurance businesses under federal law
provisions: Groups that pay bail money for defendants must follow the same federal and state rules that apply to insurance companies.
This includes nonprofits and charities that pay bail for people who cannot afford it.
These groups must get a license from their state, just like insurance companies do.
State insurance boards can now oversee and regulate any group that pays bail.
The rule covers three types of bail: cash bail, criminal bail bonds, and immigration bail bonds.

119-hres-1259.one_liner: Ask the President to push China to release five named people held in detention
provisions: Calls on the President to raise the cases of Pastor Jin Mingri, Pastor Gao Quanfu, his wife Pang Yu, Dr. Gulshan Abbas, and Jimmy Lai whenever he meets with China's leader Xi Jinping.
Asks the President to get proof that these people are alive and in good health.
Calls for these detainees to have access to lawyers of their choosing and to contact their families.
States that the U.S. stands for the right of people to practice their religion and speak freely without being jailed for it.

119-hres-1274.one_liner: Remove a rule requiring two bills to be combined in the farm bill
provisions: A rule passed on April 29, 2026 said that a bill about fuel choices at gas stations had to be added into the farm bill before it could pass.
This resolution cancels that rule, so the farm bill can move forward without the fuel bill attached to it.
The fuel choice bill — which deals with what kinds of fuel gas stations can sell — would continue on its own separate path.

119-hres-1275.one_liner: Set House debate rules for four bills and one resolution on bail, courts, and veterans
provisions: Lets the House vote on a bill that would make public a list of states and cities that allow cashless bail
Lets the House vote on a bill that would make it illegal to lie or cheat when paying bail to get out of jail
Lets the House vote on a bill that sets rules for when a court can appoint an outside person to watch over a government agency
Lets the House vote on a resolution that expresses support for law enforcement officers
Lets the House vote on a spending bill for military bases and the Department of Veterans Affairs for the year ending September 30, 2027

119-sjres-132.one_liner: Bring back financial inspections to protect active-duty military members
provisions: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau had stopped doing special financial inspections of lenders who serve active-duty troops and their families
This resolution cancels that decision, so those inspections start again
The inspections check whether banks and lenders are following rules that protect military members from unfair loan terms and fees

119-sjres-130.one_liner: Bring back federal guidance that some bank overdraft sign-up practices break the law
provisions: Since 2010, banks must get your permission before they can charge overdraft fees on debit card or ATM purchases.
In 2024, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau said some banks were collecting that permission in ways that broke the law.
That guidance was later cancelled.
This bill cancels that cancellation, making the 2024 guidance active again.
Under the restored guidance, banks that use those sign-up practices can be investigated and penalized by federal regulators.

119-hr-1041.one_liner: Stop the VA from reporting veterans to the gun background check system based only on having a financial manager
provisions: Right now, the VA sends names to a federal gun background check system when a veteran needs someone else to manage their benefits money.
This bill stops the VA from sending that information unless a judge has ruled that the veteran is a danger to themselves or others.
Veterans who have a money manager handling their VA benefits would no longer lose access to guns just because of that.
The change applies to both veterans and other people who get VA benefits.

119-hr-1329.one_liner: Set a location and rules for a new Smithsonian museum about women's history
provisions: The museum will be built on the National Mall in Washington, DC, on a piece of land across from the National Museum of African American History and Culture.
The President has 180 days after the bill passes to pick a different location if needed.
The Smithsonian Board must get approval from federal agencies before the museum can be planned, designed, or built.
The museum will focus on the history and experiences of biological women in the United States.
The museum cannot describe or show any biological male as a female.
The advisory council must get input from people with different political viewpoints when creating exhibits and programs.

119-sres-526.one_liner: Stop Senator pay on every day the government shuts down
provisions: Senators would not receive pay on any day the government is shut down.
Senators currently earn $174,000 a year, and this bill would pause those payments during any shutdown.
Federal workers already lose pay during shutdowns — this bill would make Senators lose pay too.

119-sjres-163.one_liner: Remove U.S. troops from any fighting with Iran that Congress has not approved
provisions: Troops must be pulled out of any fighting with or inside Iran.
The removal only applies if Congress has not passed a war declaration or a vote allowing the use of force against Iran.
This does not stop U.S. forces from defending against attacks on American people or U.S. buildings in other countries.

119-sjres-141.one_liner: Keep rules limiting how debt collectors can go after people over medical bills
provisions: The CFPB, which is the federal agency that oversees banks and lenders, tried to cancel its own rules about medical debt collection — this resolution blocks that cancellation.
The original rules stay in place, meaning debt collectors still have to follow them when trying to collect money owed on medical bills.
Debt collectors cannot use deceptive or unfair methods to collect medical debt from people.
People who owe medical bills keep the protections that were already written into the original CFPB rule.

119-hr-2616.one_liner: Require schools to get parent permission before changing a student's gender records
provisions: Public elementary and middle schools must ask parents before changing a student's name, pronouns, or gender on any school form.
Schools must ask parents before moving a student to a different locker room or bathroom based on gender.
Schools that do not get parent permission can lose certain federal education funding.

119-hr-1993.one_liner: Create a coin marking the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks
provisions: The U.S. Treasury will make and sell special coins to mark the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001 attacks.
Each coin sold will include an extra fee on top of the purchase price.
That extra fee goes to the National September 11 Memorial and Museum in New York City to help pay for its upkeep.
If too many of these coins are made in a given year and they go over a legal limit, the extra fee is dropped from those coins.

119-hr-4544.one_liner: Make it easier to apply to start a new bank or credit union
provisions: Federal banking regulators must review how people apply to start a new bank or credit union and reduce duplicate requests for information.
If an applicant asks, regulators must assign one employee to guide them through the application process.
If an applicant asks, regulators must provide a list of similar banks or credit unions that are willing to act as mentors.
Regulators must look at the rules around how new banks raise startup money, while keeping protections for investors in place.
Each regulator must create a plan to help states and other groups understand how to apply to start a new bank or credit union.

119-hr-5317.one_liner: Change rules so some small bank deposits no longer count as brokered deposits
provisions: Right now, some deposits are labeled 'brokered,' which means banks face more government oversight for holding them.
This bill removes that label from certain deposits held at banks with less than $10 billion in total assets.
To qualify, those deposits must make up less than 20% of the bank's total money owed to others.
The bank must also be in good financial standing, or have a special exception from the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC).
Banks that take in these deposits must still follow the same interest rate rules that apply to banks in weaker financial shape.

119-hr-3234.one_liner: Let local banks hold more customer deposits through shared deposit networks
provisions: Raises the cap on how much money banks can hold through deposit-sharing networks, where banks split up large deposits to give customers more insurance coverage
Sets different caps based on the size of the bank — bigger banks can hold more, smaller banks hold less
Opens up deposit-sharing to more banks by letting banks with a health rating of 1, 2, or 3 (on a 1–5 scale, where 1 is best) qualify, instead of only the top two ratings

119-s-1003.one_liner: Let the government send shark attack warnings to cell phones
provisions: The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) is the government agency that runs emergency text alerts sent to cell phones.
Right now, the government can send emergency alerts for things like bad weather, missing children, and other dangers to people's lives.
This bill adds shark attacks to the approved list of emergencies that can trigger those alerts.

119-s-2393.one_liner: Let the VA build a new medical facility in St. Louis, Missouri
provisions: Lets the Department of Veterans Affairs build a new medical complex at its St. Louis, Missouri location during the year starting October 2025.
The project includes a new building with patient beds, expanded clinic space, a combined office and warehouse building, a utility plant, and parking garages.
Sets a maximum dollar amount the government can spend on the project, though the exact cap is detailed in the full bill text.

119-hres-1299.one_liner: Create new federal housing programs and update housing rules
provisions: Creates new programs to help people get access to housing
Updates federal rules around how housing programs work
Changes requirements for who can qualify for housing help
Sets new rules for how housing money is spent at the federal level

119-hres-1300.one_liner: Set the rules for House floor votes on three separate bills
provisions: Lets the House vote on a bill to stop the VA from sharing veteran records with the gun background check system.
Lets the House vote on a bill to raise disability pay for veterans and benefits for their surviving families.
Lets the House vote on a bill to place a Smithsonian museum about American women's history on the National Mall.
Skips a House rule that would normally delay a vote on certain resolutions from the Rules Committee.

119-hr-6047.one_liner: Add monthly payments and expand home loans for disabled veterans and survivors
provisions: Gives disabled veterans who already get a monthly payment for needing help with daily care an extra $833.33 per month
Raises monthly payments to surviving family members of veterans who died from a service-connected cause by an extra 1% at the next inflation increase, then 0.5% more at the one after that
Lets National Guard and reserve members qualify for VA home loans after 14 days of active duty, including annual training time
Extends current VA home loan fee rates through September 30, 2036
Raises fees for some VA loan refinancing and loan takeovers
Keeps a cap on pension payments for veterans living in hospitals or care facilities through September 30, 2036

119-hr-7618.one_liner: Extend federal grants to protect U.S. battle sites through 2036
provisions: Keeps three National Park Service grant programs running through 2036, instead of ending in 2028.
These grants pay for buying, fixing, and adding information displays at U.S. battle sites.
Tells the National Park Service to study battle sites from the French and Indian War (1754–1763) for possible protection.
Tells the National Park Service to study battle sites from the Mexican-American War (1846–1848) for possible protection.

119-hr-2860.one_liner: Renew a marine protection program covering Washington's Strait of Juan de Fuca and Puget Sound
provisions: Renews a program for seven years that protects marine waters, habitats, and wildlife in Washington's Strait of Juan de Fuca and Puget Sound.
Keeps a commission in place that gives resources and technical support to local groups working to protect those waters.
The commission must use science to create plans for restoring and protecting the marine environment.
The commission holds open meetings where the public can talk about policy for the marine ecosystem.

119-hconres-86.one_liner: Order the President to pull U.S. troops out of fighting with Iran
provisions: The President must remove U.S. military forces from any fighting against Iran unless Congress officially declares war or passes a law allowing it.
U.S. troops that are defending the U.S., an ally, or a partner from an immediate attack do not have to be pulled out right away.
If troops stay to defend against an immediate threat, the President must follow the War Powers Resolution, which gives a 60-day limit on military action without Congress approving it.

119-sjres-185.one_liner: Order U.S. military forces to stop fighting Iran without a vote from Congress
provisions: Tells the President to pull U.S. armed forces out of any fighting against Iran
Says Congress has not voted to approve this military action
Uses the War Powers Act, which lets Congress order troops home if they were sent to war without a congressional vote

119-hconres-84.one_liner: Order the President to pull U.S. troops out of Lebanon within seven days
provisions: Tells the President to remove all U.S. Armed Forces from Lebanon within seven days of this resolution passing.
Uses the War Powers Resolution, a 1973 law that lets Congress direct the President to end military operations.

119-hres-518.one_liner: Set the rules for how the House debates and votes on Ukraine aid
provisions: This resolution sets the time limits and debate rules the House must follow when voting on H.R. 2913, the Ukraine Support Act.
It controls which changes to the bill members of Congress can propose during the debate.
After the House passes H.R. 2913, the Clerk of the House must send the bill to the Senate within one week.
This resolution only controls the debate process — it does not change U.S. policy toward Ukraine on its own.

119-hr-7726.one_liner: Require the federal government to cut funding to states that misuse child care money
provisions: Right now, the federal government can cut funding to states that misuse child care money — but it does not have to.
This bill changes that: if a state is found to have broken the rules of the Child Care and Development Block Grant program, the federal government must take action.
The strongest punishment is cutting off the state from receiving any more money from the program.
The program gives money to states to help low-income working families pay for child care.

119-hres-1336.one_liner: Let the House vote on a budget bill the same day it is proposed
provisions: Normally, the House must wait one day before voting on a rules proposal, unless two-thirds of members agree to skip the wait.
This resolution removes that two-thirds vote requirement for one specific budget bill.
The House can now vote on the budget rules the same day they are introduced, through June 5, 2026.

119-s-2.one_liner: Fund border patrol and immigration enforcement agencies through 2029
provisions: Gives money to Customs and Border Protection for more staff, border technology, and enforcement activities.
Gives money to Immigration and Customs Enforcement for more staff, investigations, transportation, computers, and buildings.
Pays for ICE to make arrests related to immigration enforcement.
Lets state and local police departments work with ICE on immigration enforcement.
Gives extra money to the Department of Homeland Security to work with state and local agencies on enforcement.
All of this funding stays available through the end of 2029.

119-hres-1333.one_liner: Allow House votes on agriculture funding, child care grants, FAFSA fraud checks, and welfare rules
provisions: Allows the House to debate and vote on four separate bills at once
One bill funds the U.S. Department of Agriculture, rural programs, and the FDA through September 2027
One bill would cut child care grant money to states that don't follow federal rules
One bill would require a fraud check on every student financial aid (FAFSA) application to spot identity theft
One bill changes how welfare cash assistance (TANF) works — directing money to low-income families and adding steps to track and reduce incorrect payments

119-sjres-188.one_liner: Bring back air pollution limits on coal and oil-fired power plants
provisions: The EPA had a rule that limited harmful gases — including mercury — released by coal and oil-fired power plants.
The EPA then canceled those limits.
This bill cancels the EPA's cancellation, so the original pollution limits go back into effect.
Coal and oil-fired power plants would again have to meet the rules that were in place before the EPA repealed them.

119-s-254.one_liner: Let Alaska Natives sell, trade, and own ivory and bone products in any state
provisions: States cannot ban Alaska Natives from importing, selling, trading, giving, or owning ivory, bone, or baleen from marine animals.
Baleen is the stiff material inside a whale's mouth, often used in traditional crafts.
These products must be legally made by Alaska Natives as part of their traditional crafts or clothing.
This applies in all 50 states — no state can pass its own law to stop these sales.
